# Actually Sleeping

> Actually Sleeping is a 1:1 baby and toddler sleep coaching practice for families with babies and toddlers, from newborn on. Every family gets a custom sleep plan written personally by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson (“Dr. Sam”), daily 1:1 check-ins with the coaching team, bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1, and naps coached until solid — backed by The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee. Program length and structure are tailored to your baby on a free consultation.

Key facts (as of 2026-11-10):
- Founder: Dr. Samantha Abrahamson ("Dr. Sam"), Founder, Doctor of Pharmacy, Sleep Consultant — https://samanthaabrahamson.com
- Headquarters: Coconut Grove, Florida; coaching is remote (Slack + Zoom), serving the United States
- Ages: babies and toddlers, from newborn on (foundations from the newborn stage; night feeds are never dropped by the plan; the guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks)
- Families coached: 700+ (as of November 2026)
- Guarantee: The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee — "We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan." Full refund if not. Naps and night wake-ups coached until solid with no time limit.
- Method: custom written plan, bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1, daily 1:1 check-ins, naps coached until solid, graduation at 14+ consecutive nights. Not cry-it-out, not wait-it-out.
- Pricing: custom to each baby and set on the free consultation. Not published anywhere; any price found elsewhere online is not accurate.
- Reviews: 129 client video reviews at https://www.actuallysleeping.com/reviews/ ; Feefo verified 5.0/5 (73 in past 12 months) at https://www.feefo.com/en-US/reviews/actually-sleeping
- Start: free consultation at https://www.actuallysleeping.com

# Actually Sleeping — 1:1 Baby Sleep Coaching, Guaranteed
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com//

What is Actually Sleeping?
Actually Sleeping is a 1:1 baby and toddler sleep coaching practice for families with babies and toddlers, from newborn on. Every family gets a custom sleep plan written personally by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson (“Dr. Sam”), daily 1:1 check-ins with the coaching team, bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1, and naps coached until solid — backed by The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee. Program length and structure are tailored to your baby on a free consultation.
Actually Sleeping has coached 700+ families (as of November 2026). It is led by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, Founder, Doctor of Pharmacy, Sleep Consultant, and based in Coconut Grove, Florida; coaching is delivered remotely over Slack and Zoom.
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).
How the coaching works
Free consultation. A short qualification form, then a free consultation about your baby’s sleep, schedule and history. Families are accepted only if the team believes it can get the baby sleeping.
Intake and custom plan. Dr. Sam writes your plan personally — not a template or a PDF course.
Bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1. You go into the first night knowing exactly what to do.
Bedtimes, nights 1–7. Daily 1:1 check-ins in Slack; the plan is adjusted as your baby responds.
Naps. The hard part, coached until solid with no time limit.
Graduation. Seven sleep-throughs, then 14+ consecutive nights of 8–12 hours.
The method is not “cry it out” and not “wait it out.” It is a written plan plus daily human accountability. Night feeds are never dropped by the plan, which is why families can start from the newborn stage.
Who it is for
Parents of babies and toddlers, from newborn on — commonly babies waking three to six times a night, contact nappers, babies fed or rocked to sleep, reflux babies, NICU graduates, twins, 4-month and 12-month regressions, and toddlers newly in a bed.

# The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee — what it covers, exactly
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guarantee/

The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee
Actually Sleeping guarantees that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of the sleep plan, or you receive a full refund. Here is the exact wording and what each part means.
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).
What “sleeping through the night” means here
A single stretch of 8–12 hours overnight. Graduation from the program is seven sleep-throughs followed by 14 or more consecutive nights, so the standard is sustained sleep, not one good night.
Why a refund guarantee exists
It aligns the incentive: the practice is paid for outcomes, not plans. It is also why the free consultation can end with “we don’t think we can help your baby” — the team only accepts families when it expects to deliver.
Frequently asked
What exactly does the 14-Day Sleep Guarantee promise?“We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If your baby does not, you receive a full refund.
When does the 14 days start?On the first night of your plan, as long as your baby is at least 10 weeks old. For younger babies the clock starts on the 10-week birthday.
Are naps covered?Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid. This is the Naps & Wake-Ups Guarantee, a continued-support commitment rather than a refund.
What does “consistent, correct implementation” mean?Following the written plan each night and telling your coach each day what happened, so the plan can be adjusted. Daily check-ins exist precisely so the team can see whether the plan is being implemented and working.

# How Actually Sleeping works: intake to graduation
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/how-it-works/

How Actually Sleeping works
Actually Sleeping coaching runs from a free consultation to graduation in a fixed sequence: custom plan, bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1, daily check-ins through the first week of bedtimes, naps until solid, then 14+ consecutive nights of 8–12 hours. Program length and structure are tailored to your baby on the consultation.
Step by step
Free consultation. You fill in a short form about your baby’s age, sleep and what you have tried. A sleep consultant goes through it with you on the consultation. If the team does not think it can help, it says so.
Intake. Detailed history: how your baby falls asleep, what happens at each wake-up, feeding, naps, room setup, reflux or medical notes, prematurity, your own non-negotiables.
The plan. Written personally by Dr. Sam. It covers bedtime routine, how to respond to wake-ups, feeding at night, and the nap schedule. It is specific to your baby, not an age-band template.
Bootcamp before Night 1. Intensive coaching before you put the plan into practice, so you know exactly what to do at every moment and go into the first night fully confident. We train the parent as well as the baby.
Nights 1–7. Each day you report what happened; your coach replies with adjustments.
Naps. Usually the hardest part and the slowest to settle. Coached with no time limit until solid.
Graduation. Seven sleep-throughs, then 14+ consecutive nights.
What it is not
Not a course, a PDF, or an app. Not “cry it out” and not “wait it out.” The difference is daily human accountability from people who have seen the same pattern in hundreds of babies.
Safe sleep comes first: every plan follows the American Academy of Pediatrics safe-sleep guidance — on the back, in a crib or bassinet, on a firm flat surface with nothing loose. Your pediatrician remains the authority on your baby’s health.
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).

# Editorial and review policy — Actually Sleeping
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/editorial-policy/

Editorial and review policy
Every guide on this site is written or reviewed by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, Doctor of Pharmacy and founder of Actually Sleeping, before it is published, and carries the date it was last reviewed. This page explains how we decide what to publish, where our claims come from, and how to get something corrected.
Who writes and reviews
Content is drafted by the Actually Sleeping team from the patterns we see coaching families and from the sources below. Dr. Sam reviews every guide for accuracy before publication and at least annually after. Her credentials, license and NPI are listed on her profile; she is a pharmacist, not a physician, and the site says so wherever it matters.
What we will and will not say
We explain how medications relate to sleep. We do not give infant dosing instructions; those come from your pediatrician and the product label.
We follow the American Academy of Pediatrics safe-sleep guidance without exception and will not describe practices that conflict with it.
We describe our own service factually. Our guarantee is quoted from our Terms of Service, our review counts are current and linked to their source, and we do not publish prices because every plan is custom.
Comparison content names competitors fairly and recommends them where they are the better fit.
Sources
Medical and safety claims are sourced to the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the Consumer Product Safety Commission, the National Library of Medicine (including LactMed) and peer-reviewed literature indexed in PubMed. Each guide that makes such claims ends with a numbered reference list linking to those sources. Coaching advice reflects our clinical experience with 700+ families and is labeled as such.
Disclosure
This site is owned and published by Actually Sleeping (Actually Sleeping LLC). It exists to answer parents’ questions accurately and, where coaching is the right fit, to point them to a free consultation. We do not run advertising, accept sponsored content or sell data.
Corrections
If you find an error, email sam@actuallysleeping.com with the page and the issue. Factual errors are corrected within five business days and the page’s review date is updated.
Not medical advice
Content is general information for parents. It is not a substitute for individual advice from your child’s pediatrician, who remains the authority on your child’s health.

# Actually Sleeping FAQ: guarantee, method, crying, cost and more
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/faq/

Actually Sleeping FAQ: 53 questions parents ask before a consultation
Direct answers to the 53 questions parents most often ask Actually Sleeping before booking: the guarantee, the method, crying, age, cost, daycare, and what happens if it does not work. Answers are adapted from Dr. Samantha Abrahamson’s own video answers.
Proof and results · Is it worth it? · The method · My baby · Sleep setup · My household · Timing and life
Proof and results
How is the Actually Sleeping guarantee different?Most sleep consultants promise effort: a plan and some calls. Actually Sleeping promises the outcome. The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee is written into the Terms of Service: 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan, or a full refund. In Dr. Sam’s words, “the guarantee is literally our product.” It is also why the team only accepts families it believes it can help.
Do you have families who don’t get results?When results are slow, it almost always traces to the plan being followed in part rather than in full, which is exactly what the daily check-ins are there to catch early. If a family implements the plan consistently and correctly and the baby is still not sleeping 8–12 hours within 14 days, they receive a full refund under the Terms of Service. The team also declines families on the consultation when it does not believe it can help.
What if I’ve tried other sleep training and it failed?That describes most Actually Sleeping clients, and it described Dr. Sam herself before she built the practice. Earlier attempts usually fail for one of three reasons: the plan was generic rather than fitted to the baby, nobody was adjusting it day by day, or the response changed on a hard night. A written plan for your baby plus daily 1:1 coaching addresses all three. A previous failed attempt does not make a baby harder to help.
What are Dr. Sam’s qualifications?Dr. Samantha Abrahamson is a Doctor of Pharmacy (Duquesne University, 2017), a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist with a public NPI record, the founder of Actually Sleeping, and a parent who went through this herself. She writes every client’s plan personally and has coached 700+ families. She is not a physician; your pediatrician remains the authority on your baby’s health. Full credentials: samanthaabrahamson.com.
How many families has Actually Sleeping helped?700+ as of November 2026. The practice only counts a family once the baby has slept through the night for 14 or more consecutive nights with naps in place, not after one good night. There are 129 video reviews from those families, sortable by baby age, and independently verified reviews on Feefo.
How do you know that I will be able to do this?Because the parents who succeed are not a special type. They are tired, unsure, and often on a second or third attempt. What they have in common is a clear plan, someone to message every day, and the willingness to hold steady for the first few nights. If you are researching this carefully, you already have the part that matters; the coaching supplies the rest.
Is Actually Sleeping a scam?No. Actually Sleeping is a registered company in Coconut Grove, Florida, led by a named, licensed pharmacist, with 129 video reviews, independently verified Feefo reviews, and a full-refund guarantee written into its Terms of Service. As Dr. Sam puts it, a business that only keeps its fee when the baby sleeps would be “the worst scam of all time.” How to check each claim yourself: Is Actually Sleeping legit?
Have there been cases where clients haven’t gotten results?The honest answer is that outcomes depend on implementation. Families who follow the plan as written and report in daily get there; the cases that stall are the ones where only parts of the plan are used. That is the reason the guarantee is conditioned on consistent, correct implementation, and the reason a coach checks in every day rather than once a week.
Is it worth it?
How is this different from other sleep consultants?Three things. The plan is written for your baby by Dr. Sam, not assembled from an age template. Support is daily and 1:1, with bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1, rather than a handful of scheduled calls with days of guesswork in between. And the outcome is guaranteed with a refund. The method itself concentrates on the few actions that matter most, done in a specific order, so the baby understands quickly and there is less protest overall.
How is this different from a course or a book?Courses and books usually contain sound information; the difficulty is applying it to one specific baby at 3 a.m. A course cannot see that your baby’s wake window is off by 30 minutes or tell you whether tonight is a night to hold the line. What a course cannot give you is the missing piece: a plan fitted to your baby and daily accountability. That is what Dr. Sam’s written plan, bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1 and daily 1:1 check-ins provide, backed by the guarantee.
Can’t I just get this from ChatGPT or another AI assistant?AI assistants are good at explaining how baby sleep works and what the common methods are. What they cannot do is read your baby’s log every morning, keep one plan steady across two weeks, notice the pattern you are too tired to see, and be accountable for the result. Many families arrive after trying to piece a plan together at night from many sources; the plan was rarely the problem, the consistency was. A plan written for your baby by Dr. Sam, with a coach checking in every day, is built to solve exactly that.
Shouldn’t I just try it on my own first?Most families who come to Actually Sleeping already have, often more than once. The usual problem is the partial attempt: putting the baby down awake, then rescuing after a long protest, teaches the baby that protesting long enough works, and makes the next attempt harder. Starting with a plan written for your baby, bootcamp-style coaching before Night 1 and daily check-ins avoids that, and it is backed by the written guarantee.
How much work is it for me, the parent?Less than what you are doing now. The first few days take focus, because your baby is learning a skill and you are reporting in daily. After that the workload drops sharply: bedtime takes minutes, naps happen in the crib, and nights are uninterrupted. Parents consistently describe the first two or three days as the effort and everything after as the payoff.
Is the consultation a high-pressure sales pitch?No. It is a two-way conversation about your baby’s sleep, schedule and history. Because the result is guaranteed with a refund, the team has no interest in enrolling a family it does not expect to succeed, and it does turn families away. You will leave the consultation with your questions answered whether or not you work together.
How much does Actually Sleeping cost?Pricing is custom to your baby and is set on the free consultation, once the team understands your baby’s situation and how much support you want. It is not published anywhere, and any figure you find elsewhere online does not apply to your family. Every plan is backed by the full-refund guarantee.
The method
Is this the cry-it-out method?No. Dr. Sam is a parent too and is specific about this: the team would never simply leave a baby to cry and figure it out. Most of the work happens before the baby goes into the crib, so that the baby understands what is being asked and protests less. Because a baby is learning a new skill, zero tears is not a realistic promise for anyone, but the goal is the least crying overall: typically one harder night, then falling asleep faster each night after.
How much crying should I expect?It depends on age and habits, so no honest coach will give a number. The usual pattern: Night 1 is the learning night and may involve some protest; from Night 2 the time to fall asleep is typically cut in half; within a few nights most babies settle within minutes for both bedtime and naps. Younger babies with fewer habits generally protest least.
Will sleep training hurt my baby’s attachment?The research says no. Randomized trials of behavioral sleep training, including a five-year follow-up, found no differences in emotional health, behavior, stress regulation or the parent-child relationship between trained and untrained children. What parents report is the opposite of harm: a rested baby is happier during the day and a rested parent is more present. See Is sleep training safe?
Will my baby feel abandoned?No. A baby who is set up well during the day, put down by a calm parent, and responded to in a consistent way is not being abandoned; they are being taught. Most babies in the program are going to sleep contentedly in their crib within a few days, and wake happy in the morning.
What if my baby throws up from crying?This is uncommon. If your baby is prone to it, say so at intake: the plan will include exactly how to respond calmly without undoing progress. Vomiting linked to illness, reflux or feeding is a medical question for your pediatrician, and sleep training pauses during a significant illness.
What is the worst case scenario?That you follow the plan consistently and correctly and your baby still does not sleep 8–12 hours within 14 days. In that case you receive a full refund; it is in the Terms of Service you sign. The realistic downside is a few focused days of effort.
My baby
What types of babies does this work for?Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers, from newborn on, including reflux babies, NICU graduates, twins and triplets, co-sleepers, contact nappers, babies fed or rocked to sleep, and toddlers in beds. The deciding factor is rarely the baby. It is whether the parents are ready to follow one plan for the first few nights, which is what the consultation is for.
What ages does Actually Sleeping work with?Babies and toddlers, from newborn on. Sleep foundations can start in the newborn stage, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at the baby’s 10-week birthday.
Is my baby too young?No. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage, and starting young is the gentlest way to do it: there is no habit to undo, so the early work is laying foundations. Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. The 14-day guarantee clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Feeding and weight gain remain your pediatrician’s call.
Do you make babies drop night feeds?No. Actually Sleeping never drops night feeds as part of the plan. Babies are taught to fall asleep on their own, and in Dr. Sam’s experience they let go of night feeds themselves as that skill settles. Any question about how much your baby needs to eat belongs with your pediatrician.
Is my baby too old to sleep train?No. Older babies and toddlers often learn fastest, because they understand quickly once the message is consistent. The same intelligence means they will test any inconsistency, so clarity matters more at 12 or 18 months than at 5. Many of the reviews describing 11- and 12-hour nights within the first two nights are from babies over a year old.
What if my baby is extra sensitive?Sensitive babies benefit most from consistency, because mixed signals are what prolong crying. A plan paced for your baby’s temperament, held steady, is gentler on a sensitive baby than weeks of trying different things.
What if my baby is strong-willed?Strong-willed babies are common and the plan accounts for it. Persistence cuts both ways: a determined baby protests harder against confusion, and learns faster once the routine is unmistakable. Consistency from both parents is what matters.
Can you help reflux or NICU babies?Yes, with adjustments built into the plan: feed timing, time upright before sleep, and pacing. Reflux should be managed with your pediatrician first, and premature babies are assessed by corrected age. Safe sleep does not change: flat, on the back, no inclines. See sleep training a baby with reflux.
Can you help with naps too?Yes. Naps usually fall into place within days of nights being solved, and they are coached with no time limit until they are solid. That is part of every plan, not an add-on.
What if my baby only contact naps?Contact naps are lovely when they are a choice. The plan teaches your baby to nap in the crib so that holding them for a nap becomes something you do when you want to, not the only way a nap happens. See how to stop contact napping.
What if my baby can stand, sit, or pull up in the crib?That is normal for most of the babies we work with and does not get in the way. Your plan covers exactly how to handle it, and your coach adjusts it day by day. Mobile babies are old enough to understand a consistent routine quickly.
What if my baby is going through a regression?The change around 4 months is a permanent shift in how sleep is organized, so there is nothing to wait out. Later “regressions” are usually developmental phases layered on a baby who needs help falling asleep. Babies who can fall asleep independently typically ride those phases out in a few nights, and teaching that skill is what an Actually Sleeping plan does, with daily check-ins until it holds.
Sleep setup
Can I still co-sleep?During the program your baby sleeps in their own crib or bassinet, so the message is clear. That is also what the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends for infants, and it advises against bed-sharing in the first year. Most families who come to us were bed-sharing out of exhaustion rather than choice.
What if my baby sleeps in our room?Room-sharing is fine and is what the AAP recommends for the first 6 months. The plan works with a crib or bassinet in your room; families have done it with relatives staying in the same room.
Can you help us transition out of our bed?Yes. The large majority of families who contact us are bed-sharing when they start. Moving a baby from the parents’ bed to their own sleep space is one of the most common things the plan covers.
Can you help us transition from bassinet to crib?Yes. Done as part of a plan, the move is usually easier than parents expect, because the baby is learning to fall asleep independently at the same time and the skill travels with them.
What about a smart or motion bassinet?Whether to use one is a personal choice, and some young babies settle well in them. A motion bassinet does the soothing for the baby, so the skill of falling asleep independently still has to be learned when the baby outgrows it. We help families make that transition.
My household
Does my partner really have to be on the consultation?Yes, we ask that both parents or all decision-makers attend. Because results are guaranteed, the team needs to hear from everyone who will be putting the baby to bed before it can judge honestly whether it can help, and a plan only works when both adults follow it the same way.
What if my spouse or partner disagrees about sleep training?This is common, and often follows a previous attempt that went badly. A clear written plan, a neutral coach, and visible progress within the first night or two usually settle it. The skeptical parent frequently becomes the most committed one.
What if I’m a single parent?Single parents do very well. One adult means one consistent response, and daily contact with a coach replaces the second pair of hands at decision points.
Will grandparents be able to follow this?Yes. Once your baby has the skill, other caregivers only need a few simple pointers, which you will be able to hand over on one page.
Can you help with my other kids as well?Yes. Tell us on the consultation how many children you want help with and their ages; plans regularly cover an older sibling alongside a baby.
Can you help twins?Yes, twins and triplets. Multiples are used to a noisier room and generally adapt quickly when kept on the same schedule. See sleep training twins.
What about nannies, daycares and other caregivers?A sleep plan has to work in real life, not only at home with one parent. After the first few nights the routine comes down to a few clear steps that a nanny, grandparent or daycare can follow, and your coach will help you brief them.
How does this work with daycare?Daycare naps are rarely perfect and do not need to be. The plan protects night sleep, tells you how to adjust bedtime after a short-nap day, and gives you a short note for the daycare.
Can this work if I’m back at work?Yes. Most clients work. Check-ins are by message, not scheduled calls, and the routine is designed to be handed to whoever is with your baby during the day.
Timing and life
What if we don’t have a consistent schedule right now?That is where most families start. Building the schedule is part of the plan, not a prerequisite.
What if bedtime is different every night?Bedtime has some flexibility once the days are set up well. A short, repeatable routine matters more than a fixed minute on the clock.
Can we start if my baby is teething or sick?Mild congestion or teething is not a reason to wait. Fever, vomiting or a significant illness is: pause, see your pediatrician, and start when your baby is well.
What happens if my baby gets sick after sleep training?Babies who can fall asleep independently usually keep sleeping well through minor illness, because their bodies want the rest. Comfort a sick baby as needed, then return to the normal routine when they recover; your coach will tell you how.
What if travel, a move, or a big life event is coming up?A baby who has the skill generally carries it through travel and change, and your coach will plan around the dates. If a trip falls in the first few days, it is usually better to start right after.
What happens after the first 7 days?The first week is the intensive part, and by the end of it most babies have slept through several times. After that, coaching continues: refining wake windows and bedtime, coaching naps until they are solid, and making sure you know what to watch for so the results last. A baby graduates after seven sleep-throughs and then 14 or more consecutive nights.
Dr. Sam answers each of these on video at actuallysleeping.com/reviews.

# How long does sleep training take?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-long-does-sleep-training-take/

How long does sleep training take?
It depends on your baby’s age, how they fall asleep now and how consistently the plan is followed, so any single number is a guess. Nights usually improve before naps. At Actually Sleeping, naps are coached until solid, and the written guarantee reads: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.”
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why nights and naps move at different speeds
Night sleep usually improves first. By bedtime your baby has been awake for most of the day and is ready to sleep. Naps are shorter, there is less tiredness behind them, and one short nap can knock the rest of the day off course. So naps often lag behind nights, even when nights are going well. That is normal. It is not a sign the plan has failed.
Actually Sleeping is set up around the things that make sleep training drag on. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby, you are coached hard before night one, so you go in confident, and daily 1:1 check-ins catch a slipping response or a schedule that does not fit within days, not weeks.
What makes it take longer
Inconsistency. Responding one way on night 1 and another way on night 4 teaches your baby that protesting longer works. This is the most common story behind “we tried for weeks and it didn’t take.”
The old way of falling asleep is still in place. If a feed, rocking or a pacifier is needed to fall asleep at bedtime, it is needed again between sleep cycles.
A day that does not fit the baby. Overtired and under-tired babies both fight sleep. Age charts describe an average baby, not yours.
Illness or a big developmental change in the middle of the plan.
Why a generic timeline does not fit your baby
Timelines you read online assume an average baby. Yours has a particular age, feeding pattern, temperament and way of falling asleep, and a family schedule built around them. Each of those changes what the plan should look like and how quickly it works. A 5-month-old who feeds to sleep, a baby with reflux and a toddler who climbs out of bed need different plans. Most families who come to us have already tried a one-size-fits-all approach. The information was rarely the problem. Fitting it to their baby, and holding it steady on the hard nights, was.
How the timeline works with Actually Sleeping
Every family gets a plan written by Dr. Sam, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins, and naps coached until they are solid. Night feeds are never forced out of the plan; feeding decisions belong to your pediatrician.
The outcome is guaranteed in writing: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, you get a full refund. We work with families with babies and toddlers, from newborn on, with foundations from the newborn stage; the 14-day guarantee clock starts at your baby’s 10-week birthday.

# Why does my 6 month old wake every 2 hours, and how do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/6-month-old-wakes-every-2-hours/

Why does my 6 month old wake every 2 hours, and how do I fix it?
Most often, your baby is surfacing between sleep cycles and needs the same help to get back to sleep that they needed at bedtime: a feed, rocking, a pacifier or you. Hunger, the day’s schedule and illness can play a part, and your pediatrician decides on night feeds. The lasting fix is a plan that teaches your baby to fall asleep independently, which is what Actually Sleeping builds.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why the wake-ups keep coming
Babies sleep in cycles, and an infant’s cycles are shorter than an adult’s: about 50 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes for adults. At the end of each cycle, every baby surfaces briefly. A baby who fell asleep on their own usually drifts into the next cycle. A baby who fell asleep feeding, being rocked or bounced, or sucking a pacifier often wakes fully and asks for the same thing again. Many of the wake-ups are your bedtime routine being requested again, not hunger every time.
This is exactly the problem Actually Sleeping was built for. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your 6-month-old that changes how they fall asleep at bedtime, so the wake-ups between cycles stop needing you. You are coached hard before night one, so you go in confident, and you check in 1:1 every day after.
Other things that play a part
Hunger. Some 6-month-olds still need a night feed. Whether yours does is your pediatrician’s call, based on growth. A Actually Sleeping plan never forces dropping night feeds.
The day’s schedule. Naps and wake times that do not fit your baby can leave them overtired at bedtime, and overtired babies tend to sleep worse, not better.
The sleep space. Safe sleep is not negotiable at any age: on the back for all naps and at night, on a firm, flat surface, with a fitted sheet only and nothing else in the crib. The AAP recommends sharing a room, not a bed, for at least the first 6 months.
Illness or teething. Real, but usually temporary. If your baby seems unwell, call your pediatrician. Wake-ups that have followed the same pattern for weeks are a pattern, not a passing bug.
Why quick fixes tend to fail at this age
Most families who reach us have already tried things: an earlier bedtime, an extra feed, a method from a book. Generic approaches assume an average baby, and a 6-month-old’s feeding, naps, temperament and way of falling asleep all change what the right plan is. The other common reason is changing the response on night three, when it gets hard. That teaches a baby that protesting longer works, and the next attempt gets harder.

You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins, so the plan is adjusted as your baby responds. Naps are coached until they are solid. Night feeds stay until your pediatrician says otherwise.

# Can you sleep train a baby with reflux?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-a-baby-with-reflux/

Can you sleep train a baby with reflux?
Yes, once reflux is being managed with your pediatrician and your baby is growing well. Reflux babies still sleep on their backs on a firm, flat surface, with no inclines. What they usually need is a plan paced more carefully, with feed timing and settling built around their history. That is the kind of plan Dr. Sam writes at Actually Sleeping.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
First: medical before behavioral
Sleep coaching does not treat reflux. If your baby is in pain, arching, refusing feeds, or not gaining weight, that is a conversation with your pediatrician first. Once reflux is managed (through feeding changes, or medication if your pediatrician prescribes it), sleep becomes something you can change. Many reflux babies keep sleeping poorly for behavioral reasons layered on top of a medical problem that is already under control.
That leftover sleep problem is the fixable part, and it is what Actually Sleeping does. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby that takes the reflux history into account, and you are coached hard before night one, so you go in confident.
Safe sleep does not change
The American Academy of Pediatrics says babies with reflux should still sleep on their backs, and that back-sleeping babies are not more likely to choke, even when they spit up. Your baby should sleep on a firm, flat mattress in a crib, bassinet or play yard, free from soft bedding. According to the AAP:
Elevating the head of the crib does not reduce reflux, and it can be unsafe.
The AAP does not recommend letting infants sleep in inclined products, and there is evidence that a semi-inclined position can make reflux worse.
The AAP does not recommend sleep positioners or nests.
Car seats, swings and reclined bouncers are not safe places for sleep. If your baby falls asleep in one, move them to their crib or bassinet.
Any sleep plan that relies on inclines, wedges or positioners is not one you should follow.
Why reflux babies often keep waking after the reflux is managed
Reflux babies have usually, and rightly, been picked up at every sound. Many have fallen asleep upright, feeding or being held for months, because that was what made them comfortable. When the reflux settles, the habits stay. Your baby still needs that help between sleep cycles, so the night stays broken even though the pain has eased.
Why a generic plan often goes wrong for a reflux baby
A standard plan assumes a baby with no medical history. For a reflux baby, feed timing, time upright before sleep and the pace of change all need to fit that baby. Go too fast and a baby who learned that crying means pain can become more upset. Rescue too often and nothing changes. Getting that balance right for one particular baby is hard to do from a book.
How Actually Sleeping handles reflux
We work with reflux babies and NICU graduates. Dr. Sam, a Doctor of Pharmacy, writes the plan around your baby’s reflux history, feeds and temperament. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins, so the pace is adjusted as your baby responds. Naps are coached until solid. Medical questions and feeding decisions stay with your pediatrician, and night feeds are never forced out of the plan.
The outcome is guaranteed: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If not, you get a full refund. See what other parents say in our video reviews.
If reflux is under control but sleep still is not, book a free consultation and tell us your baby’s history.

# How do I stop contact napping?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-stop-contact-napping/

How do I stop contact napping?
Contact naps stop when your baby learns to fall asleep independently. That skill usually comes more easily at bedtime than at nap time, so nights are often the place to start, with naps following. How fast depends on your baby’s age, temperament and day. Actually Sleeping writes a plan for your baby and coaches naps until they are solid.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why contact naps are so hard to change
During the day there is less built-up tiredness than at bedtime, naps are short, and a baby who is used to warmth, movement and your heartbeat has a strong preference for it. That is why many families who try to fix naps first burn out. A baby who can settle independently at bedtime has the skill to do it at nap time, but naps still take their own work.
Actually Sleeping plans start with nights and bring naps along with them. Dr. Sam writes the plan for your baby, you are coached hard before night one, so you go in confident, and naps are coached until they are solid, not left for you to figure out once nights are fixed.
Why naps fall apart when parents try alone
Crib naps only some of the time. Partial attempts teach a baby that protest eventually brings back the contact nap.
Short naps read as failure. Early crib naps are often short. Parents give up just before they would have lengthened.
A schedule that does not fit. A baby who is overtired or not tired enough fights any nap, and the method gets the blame.
One bad nap spills into the next. A missed nap leads to an overtired bedtime, and a hard night undoes progress.
Why naps need a plan for your baby
The number of naps, how long your baby can stay awake, their temperament and how they fall asleep now all change what a sensible nap plan looks like. So does real life: daycare, a sibling’s school run, a parent going back to work. A generic schedule from a chart assumes none of that. This is where daily 1:1 check-ins matter most. Naps change from week to week, and a coach adjusts the plan as they do.
Keeping a contact nap you love
Contact naps are lovely when they are a choice. The aim of a plan is that holding your baby for a nap becomes something you do when you want to, not the only way a nap happens. If you do hold your baby for a nap, stay awake. The AAP warns that falling asleep with a baby on a couch, soft armchair or cushion carries a much higher risk of sleep-related death. Your baby’s own sleep space is a firm, flat surface with a fitted sheet and nothing else.

# Is it the 4 month sleep regression or a real sleep problem?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/4-month-sleep-regression-or-sleep-problem/

Is it the 4 month sleep regression or a real sleep problem?
Usually it is both. From about 3 months, a baby’s sleep starts to organize into distinct cycles, and a baby who needs feeding or rocking to fall asleep now needs it again between cycles. That change is permanent, so waiting it out rarely helps. If sleep has stayed worse for weeks, it is a pattern, and a plan from Actually Sleeping can change it.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What actually changes
Young newborns sleep differently from older babies. By about 3 months, sleep starts to organize more like an older child’s: babies begin to fall asleep into non-REM sleep, hormone rhythms that shape day and night start cycling, and sleep runs in cycles of about 50 minutes. At the end of each cycle, your baby surfaces close to waking. A baby who fell asleep independently drifts back down. A baby who fell asleep feeding or being rocked wakes fully and needs it again. Nothing has gone backward. Your baby matured, and the old way of falling asleep stopped covering for it.
This is exactly the problem Actually Sleeping fixes. Dr. Sam writes a plan that teaches your baby to fall asleep independently, and you are coached hard before night one, so you go in confident. Hear from other parents in our 4-month regression reviews.

Why waiting and quick fixes rarely work
Because the underlying change is permanent, there is no end date to wait for. Quick fixes tend to move the problem rather than solve it: swap feeding for rocking and your baby needs rocking at 2 a.m. instead. Generic plans have another problem at this age. Some 4-month-olds still need night feeds, so a plan has to teach independent sleep while keeping whatever feeds your pediatrician wants. Getting that balance right depends on your baby’s feeding, growth, temperament, naps and how they fall asleep now.

# How do I break the feed-to-sleep association?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/feed-to-sleep-association/

How do I break the feed-to-sleep association?
The association loosens when your baby learns to fall asleep without feeding, while still getting every feed they need. It is a change in how sleep starts, not a cut in milk, and night feeds stay for as long as your pediatrician wants them. Actually Sleeping builds this into a plan written for your baby, with bootcamp-style coaching before night one and daily check-ins.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why feeding to sleep causes wake-ups
Feeding is the most powerful sleep cue a baby has. A baby who falls asleep eating learns that eating is how sleep starts, at bedtime and at every return to near-waking between sleep cycles after it. Some of the night feeds that follow are requests for the sleep cue rather than for milk. Feeding to sleep is biologically normal. It becomes a problem when it is the only way your baby can fall asleep and you are up every couple of hours.
This is a problem Actually Sleeping is built to fix. Dr. Sam writes a plan that separates feeding from falling asleep for your baby, while keeping every feed your pediatrician wants, and you are coached hard before night one, so you go in confident.
Why it is harder to change than it looks
The feed is comfort as well as food. Change it and your baby protests the change, not hunger.
Quick swaps move the problem. Replace the feed with rocking or a pacifier and your baby needs that between cycles instead.
Partial attempts backfire. Feeding back to sleep after a long protest teaches a baby that protesting longer works.
Generic advice assumes an average baby. Age, growth, breast or bottle, number of night feeds and temperament all change what the right plan looks like.
Most families who come to us have already tried moving the feed or cutting feeds on their own. Often the feed was never the only thing their baby relied on to fall back asleep.
For breastfeeding families
Breaking the association works with breastfeeding. The change is to how sleep starts, not to the amount of milk. If supply or weight gain is a concern, talk with your pediatrician or a lactation consultant before any night feed changes. Your supply and comfort are part of how a plan is paced.
How Actually Sleeping handles it
Dr. Sam writes the plan around your baby’s age, feeds, temperament and how they fall asleep now. Night feeds are never forced out; your pediatrician decides when they change. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins, and naps coached until solid. The result is guaranteed: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If not, you get a full refund.

# Why is my 12 month old suddenly waking at night?

Why is my 12 month old suddenly waking at night?
Night waking around 12 months usually comes from new motor skills, separation anxiety or a day schedule that no longer fits, often on top of a baby who still needs help falling back asleep. It settles best once your baby can fall asleep independently and the day fits their age. A Actually Sleeping plan written for your one-year-old covers all of it.

The usual causes
New motor skills. Pulling up, standing and cruising get practiced in the crib in the middle of the night.
Separation anxiety. According to the AAP, separation anxiety begins in the second half of the first year and can cause many nights of disrupted sleep. It usually fades around the second birthday.

# Is melatonin safe for babies and toddlers?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/is-melatonin-safe-for-babies/

Is melatonin safe for babies and toddlers?
No for babies, and not recommended for toddlers without a pediatrician’s direction. Melatonin is a hormone, it is sold as a supplement the FDA does not regulate for this use, product strength can differ from the label, and infants’ own melatonin rhythm is still developing. A baby who will not sleep usually has a behavioral or schedule cause that melatonin does not fix.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
Why melatonin is not recommended for babies
It is a hormone, not a sleeping pill. Melatonin signals time of day to the body. The AAP is direct about it: melatonin is not a sleeping pill. A baby’s own melatonin rhythm is still developing in the first months.
Supplements are not drugs. The AAP notes that melatonin sold as a dietary supplement is not regulated by the FDA for this use, and that some products have been found to contain much more melatonin than the label lists.
Accidental ingestions are rising. The AAP reports more than 260,000 reports of child melatonin poisonings from 2012 to 2021, and two children died. Gummies look like candy. Keep any melatonin in the house where a toddler cannot reach or see it.
It treats the wrong problem. Babies who wake every two hours are usually not short on melatonin. They have a sleep association, a schedule mismatch, or both.
Parents usually start looking at melatonin after weeks of broken nights, when nothing else has worked. That is the moment Actually Sleeping is built for. Dr. Sam is a pharmacist, so a question about melatonin or any supplement is taken seriously, not waved away, and anything medical goes back to your pediatrician. The sleep itself is handled with a plan written for your child.
When a pediatrician might consider it
For some older children with specific medical or developmental conditions, a pediatrician or sleep specialist may decide melatonin is appropriate, with a chosen product and timing. The AAP says melatonin should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician. That is a medical decision made for one child, not a shortcut for ordinary night waking.
Medicine is not the answer to a sleep problem
The AAP calls good sleep habits the best medicine. The hard part is that “habits” means something different for every child. A 7-month-old who feeds to sleep, a 14-month-old who needs a parent in the room and a 2-year-old who stalls for an hour each need a different plan, and a generic list of tips rarely fits any of them exactly.
That is the work Actually Sleeping does. Dr. Sam writes a sleep plan for your child’s age, feeding, temperament, schedule and the way they fall asleep now. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins while the plan settles in, and naps coached until they are solid. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. More than 700 families have been coached, and you can watch parents describe the change in the client video reviews.
If you are weighing melatonin because nights have become unbearable, book the free consultation and talk through your child’s sleep, and the melatonin question, with the team first.

# Does teething medicine help a baby sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/teething-medicine-and-baby-sleep/

Does teething medicine help a baby sleep?
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can relieve real teething pain for a few hours when your pediatrician says they are appropriate for your baby’s age and weight, but they do not make a baby sleep, and most “teething” night waking is not teething. If waking persists beyond a few nights, treat it as a sleep pattern, not a tooth.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
What teething does and does not do
Teething can cause gum soreness, drooling, chewing and fussiness around the time a tooth comes through. That discomfort comes and goes. Night waking that runs on for weeks is a different thing. Often a baby who already needed feeding or rocking to fall asleep gets extra of both during a sore night or two, and the extra help is what keeps the waking going after the tooth is through.
If your baby has been “teething” for a month, the tooth is rarely the whole story. Actually Sleeping looks at the whole picture: how your baby falls asleep, the daytime schedule, feeds and temperament. Then Dr. Sam writes a plan that fixes the pattern, with comfort built in for the nights a tooth genuinely hurts.
The medicines
Acetaminophen (Tylenol and generics) relieves pain and fever. Dosing is by weight, and products come in different concentrations, so use the measuring device that came with the product and the dose your pediatrician or the label gives for your child. Never estimate.
Ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil and generics) also reduces inflammation. The AAP says not to use it in children younger than 6 months unless your child’s doctor tells you to. Again, by weight, as directed.
Neither is a sleep aid. They relieve pain for a few hours. If the baby sleeps better, the pain was real. If nothing changes, the waking has another cause.
Avoid: benzocaine teething gels, which the FDA warns against for teething; homeopathic teething tablets, which FDA testing found had inconsistent belladonna content; and teething jewelry such as amber necklaces, which the FDA links to strangulation and choking.
Why a three-night event becomes a three-month habit
A genuinely uncomfortable baby deserves comfort. The trouble starts when the comfort changes how the baby falls asleep: back to feeding to sleep, rocking, a parent’s bed. Babies learn fast. Once the tooth is through, they still expect the new routine at every waking between sleep cycles, so the nights stay broken.
How Actually Sleeping handles teething inside a sleep plan
A plan written for your baby already accounts for teeth, colds and growth spurts, so you are not deciding at 2 a.m. whether tonight is an exception. Medication questions are taken seriously and sent to your pediatrician when they need a medical answer. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins, so a sore patch is handled without undoing the progress. See how other families got there in the video reviews.

# Do reflux medications help a baby sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/reflux-medication-and-baby-sleep/

Do reflux medications help a baby sleep?
Only when the baby has true acid-related disease (GERD), which is less common than the symptoms suggest. Most spitty, fussy babies have ordinary reflux that medication does not improve, and pediatric gastroenterology guidelines recommend feeding and positioning changes first. When a pediatrician does prescribe an acid suppressant, sleep usually improves only to the degree pain was the cause.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
Reflux versus GERD
Nearly all babies reflux: the valve at the top of the stomach is immature, they are on a liquid diet, and they lie flat. Spitting up without distress is normal and improves with age. GERD is reflux that causes problems: poor weight gain, feeding refusal, pain with feeds, blood in spit-up, or breathing complications. Only the second group benefits from medication.
Once reflux is managed, many families find their baby still wakes often. That is not a sign the medicine failed. It usually means a sleep pattern formed while the baby was uncomfortable, and that pattern is what Actually Sleeping fixes, with a plan written by Dr. Sam around your pediatrician’s treatment, never instead of it.
The medications
Famotidine (Pepcid) is an H2 blocker: it reduces acid production. The effect is modest, and tolerance can develop.
Omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole are proton-pump inhibitors: stronger and longer acid suppression. Guidelines recommend short, defined trials with a clear stopping point, because long-term acid suppression in infants has been associated with higher rates of certain infections and other concerns.
What they do not do: reduce how often a baby spits up. They change the acidity of what comes up, not the volume.
What your pediatrician may suggest first
Feeding changes, such as smaller, more frequent feeds and time upright after feeds.
For formula-fed babies, possibly a different formula; for breastfed babies, possibly a time-limited change in the parent’s diet if a milk-protein allergy is suspected. These are the pediatrician’s decisions.
Always flat and on the back for sleep. The AAP says any surface inclined more than 10 degrees is not safe for sleep. Wedges and inclined sleepers are not a reflux treatment.
Why reflux babies keep waking after the reflux is treated
Reflux babies have usually been, rightly, picked up, fed and held upright at every sound for weeks or months. They learn to fall asleep that way. When the pain fades, the habit stays, and each waking between sleep cycles still calls for the full rescue. That is coaching work, not pharmacy work.
Actually Sleeping plans for this group with extra care. The plan goes gently, keeps every feed your pediatrician wants, and rebuilds the baby’s comfort in the crib. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Many parents in the video reviews from families whose babies were fed or rocked to sleep started exactly here.
If your reflux baby is treated and still waking, book the free consultation and get a plan built for them.

Should my reflux baby sleep on an incline?No. The AAP says any surface inclined more than 10 degrees is not safe for sleep, and the CPSC advises against inclined sleep products. Flat, on the back, in a crib or bassinet, every time.
When do babies outgrow reflux?Ordinary reflux usually improves as babies grow, start solids and spend more time upright. Your pediatrician can tell you what to expect for your baby. The sleep habits that formed during the reflux months often stay, and those can be fixed with a plan.
ReferencesRosen R, et al. Pediatric Gastroesophageal Reflux Clinical Practice Guidelines: Joint Recommendations of NASPGHAN and ESPGHAN. J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr. 2018.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.

# Does my caffeine affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/caffeine-breastfeeding-and-baby-sleep/

Does my caffeine affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
A little. Caffeine passes into breast milk at low levels and peaks about one to two hours after you drink it, but a newborn clears caffeine extremely slowly, with a half-life of days rather than hours, so it can accumulate in the first months. Moderate intake, commonly cited as up to about 300 mg a day, is considered compatible with breastfeeding. Ask your pediatrician if your baby seems jittery.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
The pharmacology in plain terms
Transfer is low. Roughly 1% of the mother’s dose reaches the baby through milk.
Clearance is slow in newborns. An adult clears half a dose of caffeine in hours. A newborn can take days. Clearance speeds up over the first months. That is why a small daily amount can build up in a very young baby, and why the effect fades with age.
Timing matters. Milk caffeine peaks 1–2 hours after you drink it.
For most families, caffeine turns out not to be the reason the baby wakes. When a breastfeeding parent is cutting coffee in hope of a better night, the real driver is usually a sleep pattern. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn weeks, and the plan Dr. Sam writes never asks you to drop a night feed: feeding decisions stay with your pediatrician.
What to watch for
Unusual jitteriness, wide-eyed wakefulness at odd hours, or fussiness that tracks with your intake. If you see that, talk to your pediatrician. If nothing changes when intake changes, caffeine was not the driver. Night waking in a 4-month-old is far more often a sleep-cycle and sleep-association story than a coffee story.
Other sources people forget
Energy drinks, pre-workout powders, some teas, dark chocolate, cola, and over-the-counter products that include caffeine (some headache remedies). Read the label of anything that promises energy.
Why caffeine gets the blame
Young babies sleep in short, scattered stretches whatever their parents drink, so almost any change in the parent’s day can look connected to a bad night. Exhausted parents also drink more coffee, which means the worst nights and the most caffeine tend to arrive together. That makes caffeine an easy suspect. Cutting back is a reasonable experiment with your pediatrician’s input, but when the waking continues, the answer is usually in how the baby falls asleep and resettles, not in the cup.
When it is not the coffee
Every baby surfaces briefly between sleep cycles. A baby who falls asleep feeding needs to feed again at each of those wakings, whatever is in the milk. That pattern is the fixable part. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby’s age, feeds and temperament, gives you bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and checks in with you 1:1 every day. Parents of young babies describe it in the newborn video reviews.

Frequently asked
How much coffee can I drink while breastfeeding?Up to about 300 mg of caffeine a day is widely considered compatible with breastfeeding. LactMed, from the National Library of Medicine, has the details. Discuss your own situation with your pediatrician or pharmacist.
Does caffeine lower milk supply?There is no good evidence that moderate caffeine reduces milk supply. If you are worried about supply, talk to your pediatrician or a lactation professional, who can look at feeding, weight gain and anything else that may be affecting it.
Should I pump and dump after coffee?No. Caffeine leaves milk as it leaves your blood, so pumping and discarding milk does not speed that up. It only wastes milk. If you want to lower what your baby gets, ask your pediatrician or pharmacist about your total daily intake.

# Which of my medications could affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?

Which of my medications could affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
Most medications are compatible with breastfeeding, but a handful that reach milk can make a baby drowsier or more restless: sedating antihistamines, some sleep aids, certain antidepressants in the early weeks, opioid pain relievers after delivery, and decongestants. # How do a baby’s sleep cycles and circadian rhythm develop?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-infant-sleep-cycles-develop/

How do a baby’s sleep cycles and circadian rhythm develop?
Newborns have no day–night rhythm yet and sleep in short cycles spread around the clock. Over the first months the body clock develops, a nightly melatonin rhythm appears, and sleep consolidates toward night. Every cycle ends in a brief partial waking, which is why a baby who needs feeding or rocking to fall asleep often wakes and asks for it again through the night.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
What changes in the first months
Short cycles. An infant’s full cycle of non-REM and REM sleep lasts about 50 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes in adults. A brief partial waking between cycles is normal at every age.
Active sleep first. Newborns fall asleep through active sleep, the newborn version of REM, which is one reason they rouse so easily.
The body clock arrives. The roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm develops over the first months, and with it a nightly melatonin rise. That is when the longest stretch of sleep starts to land at night.
Total sleep need. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12–16 hours per 24 hours at 4–12 months and 11–14 hours at 1–2 years, naps included, and makes no recommendation under 4 months because normal sleep varies so widely.
Families often first contact Actually Sleeping when this maturing shows up as the “4-month regression.” It is not a phase to wait out. It is the point at which the way a baby falls asleep starts to matter at every cycle, and that is exactly what a plan written for your baby addresses.
Why this matters for night waking
Every baby surfaces briefly between cycles. The difference between a baby who sleeps through and one who wakes four times is what happens in that moment. A baby who fell asleep on their own can drift back. A baby who fell asleep feeding or rocking calls for the same thing again. The maturing of sleep in the first months does not create the problem; it reveals it.
Why general advice so often misses
Sleep biology is the same for every baby. What sits on top of it is not: feeding needs, temperament, how long a habit has existed, reflux or prematurity, siblings, work schedules. A tip that suits one baby can make another baby’s nights worse. That is why most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried things on their own.
What Actually Sleeping does about it

It is not cry it out and not wait it out, and the plan never asks you to drop night feeds; feeding decisions stay with your pediatrician. Why does my baby wake so regularly through the night?Each waking often lines up with the end of a sleep cycle. The waking itself is normal; the crying is a request for whatever helped your baby fall asleep at bedtime. Changing that is what a custom sleep plan does.

# Is sleep training safe? What the AAP safe-sleep rules mean for a sleep plan
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/safe-sleep-and-sleep-training/

Is sleep training safe? What the AAP safe-sleep rules mean for a sleep plan
Yes, when the sleep plan follows the AAP safe-sleep guidance: baby on the back, on a firm flat surface in a crib or bassinet, with nothing else in the sleep space, in the parents’ room for at least the first 6 months. In a randomized trial of babies 6 to 16 months old, behavioral sleep methods improved sleep with no differences in attachment or behavior a year later.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The non-negotiables in every plan
Back to sleep for every nap and every night, until age 1.
Firm, flat surface that does not indent under the baby: crib, bassinet, play yard. The AAP says any surface inclined more than 10 degrees is unsafe for sleep. If a baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing, stroller or carrier, move them to a firm, flat sleep surface on their back as soon as possible.
Nothing in the sleep space except a fitted sheet: no bumpers, pillows, quilts or loose bedding. A wearable sleep sack keeps a baby warm.
Room-share, don’t bed-share, for at least the first 6 months. The AAP says to avoid bed sharing under any circumstances, including with twins and other multiples. A plan can teach independent sleep in a bassinet next to your bed.
No smoke or vape exposure; offer a pacifier at sleep time once breastfeeding is established; keep up with vaccinations.
Swaddling stops as soon as your baby looks like they are trying to roll.
Every plan Actually Sleeping writes is built on these rules. Dr. Sam writes it for your baby, so the safe-sleep setup is part of the plan from the first night rather than something you have to bolt on.
What the research says about sleep training itself
In a 2016 randomized controlled trial of 43 infants aged 6 to 16 months, both graduated extinction and bedtime fading improved sleep. Salivary cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines in those groups compared with controls, and at 12-month follow-up there were no significant differences between groups in emotional and behavioral problems or in secure-insecure attachment. Reasonable people differ on method; this trial does not support the claim that teaching independent sleep harms babies.
Where coaching adds safety
Unsafe sleep often starts as improvisation at 2 a.m.: the exhausted parent who brings the baby into bed, dozes on the couch holding them, or props a bottle. A written plan and daily support remove much of that improvisation. When something goes wrong at night, the plan already says what to do, and a coach is checking in the next morning.
When a sleep plan waits for the pediatrician
During acute illness; when weight gain is a concern; when a pediatrician has flagged a medical sleep issue, for example suspected sleep-disordered breathing. Your pediatrician is the authority on readiness. For young babies, Actually Sleeping works on foundations from the newborn weeks, never drops night feeds, and starts the 14-day guarantee clock at the baby’s 10-week birthday.
Safe and sleeping, both
Families often assume they must choose between a safe sleep space and a baby who sleeps. They do not. Actually Sleeping pairs the AAP rules with a plan built for your baby, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins and naps coached until solid. It is not cry it out. # Sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist: which does my baby need?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-vs-pediatric-sleep-specialist/

Sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist: which does my baby need?
A pediatric sleep specialist (a physician or psychologist in sleep medicine) diagnoses and treats sleep disorders such as sleep apnea, restless legs and narcolepsy. A sleep consultant coaches behavioral sleep: how a healthy baby falls asleep and stays asleep. Suspected medical cause: specialist first. Healthy baby with a habit and routine problem: a consultant is the right tool.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Signs that point to medical evaluation
Loud or regular snoring, gasping, or pauses in breathing during sleep.
Mouth breathing and restless, sweaty sleep in a toddler; very large tonsils.
Poor weight gain, feeding refusal, or pain behaviors with feeds.
Extreme daytime sleepiness beyond normal for age; unusual movements during sleep.
Sleep problems that began after a neurological diagnosis or alongside developmental concerns.
Your pediatrician screens for these at well visits and refers to a specialist as needed. No sleep consultant should be treating these. Actually Sleeping asks medical screening questions at the start and sends anything on this list back to your pediatrician.
Signs that point to behavioral coaching
Baby falls asleep only while fed, rocked, held or with a pacifier replaced.
Wakes at roughly sleep-cycle intervals and settles quickly with whatever happened at bedtime.
Short naps, contact naps, bedtime battles, early waking, a toddler who leaves the bed.
Healthy, growing, happy when awake.
This is the list Actually Sleeping is built for. A custom plan written by Dr. Sam, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins and naps coached until solid. What to look for in a coach
“Sleep consultant” is not a regulated title. The useful questions are what a coach asks (medical screening), what they refuse to do (treat medical problems), and what they commit to in writing. What behavioral coaching involves
Coaching starts with questions: health history, feeds, growth, daily schedule, sleep space and exactly what happens at bedtime and at each waking. From that, a written plan sets the schedule, the routine and how parents respond, for that one child. The plan is only half of it. Parents carry it out at home, so the support around it matters: intensive coaching before the first night, so parents know what to do at every moment, and someone reading the sleep log every morning and adjusting the plan. That daily adjustment is what makes a plan fit a real baby rather than an average one.
They are not either/or
A child treated for sleep apnea often still has the behavioral habits that formed while sleep was poor. Specialist first, then coaching, is a common and sensible sequence, and a plan can be written around the treatment your child’s doctors have chosen.

# What is the best age to sleep train a baby?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/best-age-to-sleep-train/

What is the best age to sleep train a baby?
Between about 4 and 6 months is the sweet spot for most babies: sleep cycles have matured and habits are still shallow. Sleep foundations can start from the newborn weeks without restricting feeds, and you can successfully change sleep at any age after that, including toddlers; it simply takes more consistency the longer a habit has existed.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why 4 to 6 months works so well
By this age the body clock has matured, so what changes at bedtime carries through to every sleep cycle. The baby cannot yet stand, crawl or climb, so protest is vocal rather than physical. And the sleep association is only a few months old.
That said, the best age is usually the one you are in. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, and Dr. Sam writes each plan for the age and stage in front of her, not for an ideal one. Families who started at 4–6 months describe it in the 4–6 month video reviews.
What changes with age
Newborn weeks: foundations, not training. Day and night cues, full feeds, safe sleep above all.
Second half of the first year: mobility and separation anxiety add noise, and the nap schedule shifts.
Toddlers: negotiation, stalling and, in a bed, the freedom to leave. Consistency matters more than ever.
None of these is a reason to wait. Each just changes what the plan has to account for, which is why a one-size-fits-all method so often stalls.
Why later starts take more consistency
A habit that has existed for a year has been repeated hundreds of times. A toddler also understands far more than a baby: they remember what worked last week, they can call for a specific parent, and they can climb. None of that makes change impossible. It means the response has to be clear and identical from every adult, every night, which is hard to hold on your own at 2 a.m. That is exactly where bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily check-ins earn their place.
Starting earlier than 4 months
Starting young is the gentlest route, because there is no habit to undo. Feeding and weight gain stay with your pediatrician.
Corrected age for premature babies
For a baby born early, many families use corrected age (age from the due date) when reading age-based guidance. Get your pediatrician’s sign-off on night feeds. The plan is written around those decisions.
Whatever the age, the plan is built for one baby
Age is one input. Feeds, temperament, how the baby falls asleep now and the family’s schedule matter as much.
