# What are the right wake windows by age?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/wake-windows-by-age/

What are the right wake windows by age?
Roughly 45–90 minutes for newborns, 1.5–2.5 hours at 4–6 months, 2–3.5 hours at 6–9 months, 3–4 hours at 9–12 months, and 4–6 hours once a toddler is on one nap. These are rule-of-thumb starting points from practice, not research findings, and the right window for your baby depends on far more than age.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What a wake window is
A wake window is the stretch of time a baby is awake between one sleep and the next. The idea behind it is sleep pressure: the longer a baby is awake, the stronger the drive to sleep. Too little pressure and the baby lies in the crib chatting. Too much and the baby becomes overtired, fussy and harder to settle. The ranges below are where many babies of each age land.
Rule-of-thumb ranges
AgeWake window (rule of thumb)Naps per day (rule of thumb)AASM total sleep per 24 h
0–4 weeks45–60 min5+No AASM recommendation under 4 months
1–3 months60–90 min4–5No AASM recommendation under 4 months

9–12 months3–4 h212–16 h

18–36 months5–6 h111–14 h at 1–2 years; 10–13 h at 3–5 years
Only the last column is a research recommendation, from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. Wake windows are averages from practice. They describe a typical baby, and no baby is typical in every way.
Why the chart so often fails a real baby
Too short and too long look alike. A window that is too short and one that is too long both produce short naps and early waking. From the outside you cannot tell which one you have.
Timing is rarely the only cause. If your baby falls asleep being fed or rocked, perfect timing still produces a 30-minute nap. Parents spend weeks adjusting the clock when the problem is how the baby falls asleep.
Every change takes days to read. Sleep varies night to night anyway, so it is easy to chase noise.

A calculator gives an average; a plan fits your baby
The wake window calculator will give you a typical day. The hard part is getting your particular baby to follow it. # When do babies drop naps, and how do I handle the 3-to-2 and 2-to-1 transitions?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/nap-transitions-3-to-2-to-1/

When do babies drop naps, and how do I handle the 3-to-2 and 2-to-1 transitions?
As a rule of thumb from practice, many babies go from 3 naps to 2 at around 6 to 8 months, and from 2 naps to 1 at around 14 to 18 months. The sign is a pattern, not a bad day: the last nap is refused or pushes bedtime late for two weeks or more. Transitions go best gradually and timed to your child.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What a nap transition is
As children get older, they can stay awake longer and need less daytime sleep. At some point the day no longer fits the number of naps it used to hold, and one nap has to go. The weeks in between are the transition. They are uneven by nature: some days the child needs the old number of naps and some days the new one. Because total sleep across 24 hours still matters, a nap lost during the day has to be made up somewhere, usually with an earlier bedtime, or it shows up as a harder night.
Signs a transition is real (versus a bad week)
The last nap is consistently refused or takes a long time to happen, for a couple of weeks.
Naps are fine but bedtime is being pushed late to fit them.
Early morning waking appears with no other change.
One bad day, an illness or travel is not a transition.
Telling a real transition from a rough patch is one of the most common reasons parents contact Actually Sleeping. A plan written for your child by Dr. Sam sets the timing, and daily check-ins catch the moment the schedule needs to change.
Why transitions go wrong
Too early. A few refused naps around the first birthday look like readiness for one nap. Often they are a passing regression. Dropping a nap too soon tends to show up as weeks of night waking and early rising.
Too abrupt. A child who goes from two naps to one overnight is awake for a long stretch they are not ready for, and the overtiredness spills into the night.
Without a cushion. Days during a transition are uneven. Without a bedtime that moves to match, a short-nap day becomes a bad night.
One plan for every child. Some children move through a transition in days, others take weeks. A generic schedule cannot tell you which you have.
How Actually Sleeping handles nap transitions
Naps are coached until they are solid, and that includes the weeks when the number of naps is changing. Dr. Sam writes the plan around your child’s age, current naps, night sleep, temperament and your family’s day. The team checks in with you 1:1 every day and adjusts the schedule as the transition unfolds, so you are not guessing from one bad day. Families describe this stage in the 7–9 month video reviews.
If your child’s naps are falling apart, book the free consultation and get the transition planned for them.

# Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/early-morning-waking/

Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?
Early waking usually comes from a schedule problem, a light problem, or a sleep-association problem, often more than one at once. A late bedtime, long or late naps, light in the room and a baby who cannot resettle alone all produce the same 5 a.m. waking. Finding which one drives your baby’s is the fix, and that is what a plan built for your baby does.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What counts as early waking
Many babies wake for the day between 6 and 7 a.m., and that is normal. Early waking is a baby who starts the day at 5 a.m. or earlier, is clearly tired soon after, and often needs an early first nap, which then keeps the cycle going. It is one of the most common reasons parents look for help, and one of the most stubborn when tackled one tip at a time.
The usual causes
Bedtime too late. An overtired baby sleeps lighter in the early morning. Counterintuitively, a later bedtime often makes early waking worse.
Naps too long or too late. Too much daytime sleep, or a nap late in the afternoon, lowers sleep pressure for the end of the night.
Light. Early-morning sleep is the lightest of the night. Sunrise or a hallway light becomes a cue to wake.
Sleep association. The 5 a.m. waking is a cycle transition, and the baby cannot get back down without whatever helped at bedtime.
Reinforced waking. If 5 a.m. brings milk, a parent’s bed or a screen, it becomes the best part of the day.
Hunger is sometimes real in a young baby. Night feeds are your pediatrician’s call, and a sleep plan never asks you to drop them.
Most early risers have two or three of these at once, which is why fixing one at a time can take weeks with nothing to show for it. Actually Sleeping looks at all of them together. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby’s schedule, sleep setup, feeds and way of falling asleep, and the team adjusts it with you every day.
Why early waking is so stubborn
Early-morning sleep is lighter, sleep pressure is at its lowest, and the body clock is starting to signal morning. All of that makes the last stretch of the night the hardest one for a baby to return to sleep. Small mistakes in the schedule show up here first. And because parents are exhausted at 5 a.m., the response often varies from one morning to the next, which keeps the waking going.
How Actually Sleeping fixes early waking
The plan sets a schedule built for your baby, the sleep setup and a single consistent response for early wakings. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins, so if 5 a.m. persists the cause is tracked down instead of guessed at. Naps are coached until they are solid, because nap timing and early waking are linked. # Why does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/short-naps-30-minutes/

Why does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?
A 30–45 minute nap is about one sleep cycle; the baby wakes at the transition and cannot link to the next cycle. The usual causes are a wake window that is slightly off, a way of falling asleep the baby cannot repeat at the transition, or a room that is too bright. Naps lengthen once your baby’s cause is found, which is the job of a custom plan.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What a 30-minute nap tells you
A nap that ends at 30 to 45 minutes almost always ends at the same point: the transition from one sleep cycle to the next. The baby surfaces briefly, as every sleeper does, and either drifts into the next cycle or wakes fully. A baby who wakes fully at that point, nap after nap, is telling you something specific about timing, the room or how they fell asleep in the first place.
Why naps are the last thing to improve
Daytime sleep pressure is lower, naps are short by nature in the first months, and the body clock does not help as it does at night. Many young babies take short naps whatever their parents do; it is developmental. As babies get older, consistent short naps usually have a cause.
The usual causes
Timing. Both too short and too long a wake window produce a 30-minute nap, and they look the same from the outside.
How the baby falls asleep. If the baby falls asleep being fed or rocked, the cycle transition reproduces the problem: they wake and need the same help again.
Environment. Light, noise or temperature that is fine at night can be enough to wake a baby from a light daytime sleep.
The rescue. Going in at the first sound ends the nap, but waiting too long can tip a baby into full crying. Where the line sits is different for every baby.
Overtiredness snowballing. A short nap makes the next window too long, which makes the next nap short too.
Parents often spend weeks testing these one at a time. Actually Sleeping looks at them together. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby’s age, feeds, temperament, schedule and current way of falling asleep, and naps are coached until they are solid, not just nights.
Why generic nap advice stalls
Nap advice tends to assume the cause. The baby whose naps are short because of a feed-to-sleep habit needs a different plan from the baby whose naps are short because the morning window is too long. Applying the wrong fix makes naps worse and loses weeks. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried several fixes on their own.
How Actually Sleeping lengthens naps
You get a custom plan, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Nights usually come first, and the team keeps coaching naps until they hold. # My toddler won’t stay in bed. How do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed/

My toddler won’t stay in bed. How do I fix it?
Most toddlers who will not stay in bed have learned that getting up works: it brings a parent, a drink, a story or a spot in the big bed. Many also left the crib before they had the self-control a bed demands. It is fixable with a clear routine and the same response every time, set by a plan built for your toddler.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why toddlers get up
It works. Every return that comes with a conversation, a cuddle or a negotiation teaches the toddler that getting up is worth it.
Freedom before self-control. A bed gives a young toddler freedom to leave with little ability to stop themselves. Many families who moved early find the crib was holding everything together.
Inconsistency. Two parents with two responses, or a response that changes after the tenth trip, gives a toddler a reason to keep testing.
Real fears. Fears of the dark and of separation appear in the toddler years and are real. How they are handled decides whether they fade or grow.
Parents usually reach Actually Sleeping after weeks of bedtime battles. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your toddler, built around age, temperament, the bed or crib, siblings and your evening, and the team supports you every day while it takes hold.
Crib or bed
A crib does a lot of quiet work. It sets a physical limit, so the only question at bedtime is whether the child falls asleep, not whether they stay put. A bed removes that limit and hands the decision to a toddler who is still learning to control impulses. Families often move to a bed because of a new sibling, a climbing toddler or a sense that it is time. Whether to stay in the crib, move back, or make the bed work is a decision that depends on the child, the reason for the move and safety, and it is one of the first things a plan settles.
Safety first
A toddler who can leave the bed will sometimes be up alone. Make the room safe for that: furniture anchored to the wall, outlets covered, cords out of reach, windows secured, nothing to climb. Many families use a gate at the door. If your toddler climbs out of a crib, talk to your pediatrician about the safest setup.
Why the usual fixes stall
Most of what parents try is reasonable. It stalls because toddlers are expert at finding the one thing that still works, and because exhausted parents vary at 9 p.m. A plan written for your child removes the guessing, and daily check-ins keep both parents on the same response.

# Why is my 8, 9 or 10 month old suddenly waking at night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/8-to-10-month-sleep-regression/

Why is my 8, 9 or 10 month old suddenly waking at night?
The 8–10 month period stacks three things at once: new motor skills (crawling, pulling to stand) that get practiced in the crib, separation anxiety, and a nap transition. A baby who was sleeping independently usually returns to baseline once the response stays consistent; a baby who never slept independently often gets worse, because each new skill and fear lands on a habit that was already fragile.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is happening
Motor leaps. A baby who just learned to stand will stand up in the crib at 2 a.m. and may not know how to get down.
Separation anxiety. Babies this age now understand that you exist when you leave the room, and many protest. It is a normal stage of emotional development.
Nap transition. Naps are shifting, and a day with too little daytime sleep produces a worse night.
Teething and illness ride along but rarely explain weeks of waking.
When all of this lands at once, many families contact Actually Sleeping. Dr. Sam writes a plan that takes the new skills, the separation anxiety and the nap shift into account, so the regression is handled without new habits forming.
What it looks like at night
Parents describe the same few patterns. A baby who used to sleep through starts waking once or twice and will not settle without being picked up. A baby who stands up in the crib and cries because they cannot get back down. A baby who protests hard the moment a parent leaves the room at bedtime. Naps get shorter or are refused, and bedtime drifts later. Any one of these is manageable. All of them together, in a baby who already needed help to fall asleep, is why so many families hit their limit at this age.
Why it lasts longer for some babies
A regression becomes a long-term problem when the response changes: night feeds return, rocking to sleep returns, or the baby moves into the parents’ bed. Each change makes sense on the night. Together they turn a few weeks into months. Babies who never learned to fall asleep on their own have nothing to return to once the stage passes.
Separation anxiety is not a reason to wait. A plan accounts for it, with a predictable routine and a response your baby learns to trust.

# Is the 18 month sleep regression real, and what do I do about it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/18-month-sleep-regression/

Is the 18 month sleep regression real, and what do I do about it?
Yes, and it is mostly a toddler-development story: new independence and testing, language growing faster than self-control, separation anxiety returning, molars, and the move to one nap. The fix is boundaries, not new comforts: a tight routine, the same response every night and a nap schedule that fits, set by a plan built for your toddler.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why 18 months is different
Earlier regressions are about sleep physiology. This one is about a person: an 18-month-old wants control, has opinions, and has discovered that bedtime protest gets a reaction. It overlaps with molars (real but usually brief), the nap transition (real and often long), and a second wave of separation anxiety.
At this age, generic advice runs into a toddler who is very good at finding the one thing that still works. Actually Sleeping plans for that. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your toddler’s temperament, naps, routine and the way they fall asleep now, and the team checks in every day while it settles.
What it looks like
Bedtime stretches as the toddler asks for one more book, one more drink, one more hug. A child who went down easily starts crying the moment a parent leaves, or calls out for a specific parent. Night waking returns in a child who had been sleeping through. Naps get refused, especially the morning nap in a child who still takes two. Parents often feel they have gone backward months. They have not; the child has moved forward, and the plan needs to catch up.
What makes it worse
New comforts that stay. Lying down with them “just tonight,” extra milk, a parent’s bed. Each is reasonable on the night and hard to undo.
A move to a big bed. Changing to a bed during a regression adds freedom at the moment self-control is weakest.
Dropping the second nap too soon, or holding it too long. Either produces a tired toddler at bedtime.
Different responses from different adults. Toddlers notice and test the gap.
Molars and medicine
Molars can hurt. Pain relief for a clearly uncomfortable toddler, as your pediatrician directs and as the label says, is reasonable for a night or two. A new sleep habit started during those nights will outlast the tooth by months. For more, see teething medicine and sleep.

# How do you sleep train twins?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-twins/

How do you sleep train twins?
On a shared schedule, in a safe shared room with a separate sleep surface for each baby, with a plan that still treats each twin as an individual. One twin usually wakes the other less often than parents fear. Twins add logistics, two temperaments and half the parental capacity, which is why a plan built for both babies and daily support matter even more.

What makes twins different
Logistics. Two feeding patterns and two nap patterns can mean no one in the house ever sleeps if the babies drift apart.
Two temperaments. One twin may adapt in days and the other take longer. Holding the easier sleeper to the harder one’s pace, or the reverse, causes problems for both.
Noise. Parents worry that one baby will wake the other. Babies often get used to a roommate faster than adults expect.
Capacity. Twice as much to track every night with half as much energy to track it.
Actually Sleeping works with twin and triplet families regularly. Dr. Sam writes one plan that covers both babies and treats each as an individual within it, built around their ages (corrected, if they were born early), feeds, temperaments and your household.
Why a single-baby method often stalls with twins
Most sleep advice is written for one baby and one set of parents taking turns. With twins, the parent responding to one baby is often needed by the other at the same moment. A response that works for a calm twin may not work for an intense one. And when one twin has a bad night, the plan for the other has to hold anyway. Twin families do best with a plan that decides these things in advance: who responds to which baby, what happens when both wake, and how to keep the two schedules together.
Safety with twins
Each baby needs their own safe sleep surface. The AAP says to avoid bed sharing under any circumstances, including with twins and other multiples. Room sharing without bed sharing is recommended for at least the first 6 months.
Premature twins
Many twins arrive early. Corrected age matters for readiness, and your pediatrician decides night feeds for each baby separately. Weight gain, not the calendar, decides when night feeds go, and the plan works around those decisions.
Why coaching helps even more with twins
There is twice as much information every night and half as much capacity to make sense of it. A coach reading both babies’ logs each morning and telling you which adjustment to make removes most of the guesswork. # How do I sleep train my baby? A step-by-step guide
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-sleep-train-a-baby/

How do I sleep train my baby? A step-by-step guide
Sleep training means teaching a baby to fall asleep in the crib without being fed, rocked or held to sleep, so they can link sleep cycles on their own overnight. The AAP’s parent site notes that babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months. It works best with a plan built for your baby, followed consistently, with someone adjusting it as you go.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
What sleep training actually changes
Every baby wakes briefly between sleep cycles, many times a night. A baby who falls asleep being fed, rocked or held expects the same help at each of those wakings. The AAP’s parent site makes the same point: babies who are held or rocked to sleep may have trouble falling back asleep when they wake in the night. From about 4 months, it advises putting babies to bed drowsy rather than waiting until they are asleep. Sleep training is the work of moving that last step, falling asleep, from you to your baby.
That sounds simple. In practice the sticking points are specific to each baby: the right bedtime for this baby, which night feeds stay, how this baby reacts when you are in the room, and what to change when night 3 looks nothing like night 1.
That is the gap Actually Sleeping fills. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby from a detailed intake, coaches you bootcamp-style before night one, checks in with you daily, and keeps coaching naps until they are solid. It is not cry it out and not wait it out.
The stages, start to finish
Every successful plan moves through the same stages. What happens inside each one is where babies differ.
Readiness. Age, health, growth, night-feed needs and a safe sleep space. Your pediatrician has the final word on health and feeds.
Foundations. Schedule, routine and room. A baby who is badly overtired or not tired enough will protest any approach, which is why a plan starts here and not with the response at the crib.
The response. How you respond at bedtime and at night, chosen to fit your baby’s temperament and your limits, and kept the same by every adult.
The first nights. Protest is normal while a baby learns something new. Knowing which changes are progress and which mean the plan needs adjusting is the hardest part to judge alone at 2 a.m.
Naps. Daytime sleep usually lags behind nights and needs its own attention.
Why generic plans stall
Age-band templates. Two 6-month-olds can need different bedtimes, different feeds and different responses.
Mixing methods from several sources, or switching after a hard night.
Inconsistency at 2 a.m. Holding steady at bedtime and giving in later teaches a baby to protest longer.
Bedtime only. A plan that changes bedtime but leaves night wakings and naps unplanned keeps the old habit alive.
No one to adjust it. A written method cannot tell you which detail to change for your baby on night 4.
Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried things on their own. They usually did a lot right and were missing one or two details.
What the research says
A review of 52 treatment studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that 94% reported behavioral interventions for bedtime problems and night wakings were effective, and over 80% of children treated showed clinically significant improvement, maintained for 3 to 6 months. The methods are well supported. The method names compared side by side are in methods compared, and the full evidence is in what the research says.
Safety comes first, every night
Whatever plan you follow, your baby sleeps on the back, alone, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface without pillows, blankets, soft toys or bedding, as the AAP advises. Call your pediatrician before any sleep plan if your baby snores or gasps in sleep, seems to be in pain, is feeding poorly or is not gaining weight.

# How do I get my baby to sleep through the night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-get-baby-to-sleep-through-the-night/

How do I get my baby to sleep through the night?
Babies sleep through the night when they can fall asleep on their own at bedtime, their daytime schedule and feeding suit their age, and any night feeds they still need are planned with the pediatrician. Every baby still wakes briefly between sleep cycles; the difference is settling back without help. Before about 4 months, night waking to feed is normal.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
What “through the night” really means
Every baby wakes briefly between sleep cycles all night long. A baby who “sleeps through” wakes too, and goes back to sleep without help. The AAP’s parent site notes that babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months, and that babies who are held or rocked to sleep may have trouble falling back asleep when they wake. So the question is rarely “why does my baby wake” and almost always “why does my baby need me to get back to sleep.” See how infant sleep cycles develop.
Why babies keep waking
How they fall asleep at bedtime. This is the largest factor. Whatever helps your baby fall asleep at 7 p.m. is what they look for at 11 p.m., 1 a.m. and 3 a.m.
A schedule that does not fit. Bedtime too late, too early, or daytime sleep that leaves your baby overtired or not tired enough.
Night feeds without a plan. Some feeds are needed. Others have become the way a baby gets back to sleep. Telling them apart is a question of age, growth and pattern, and your pediatrician decides what your baby needs.
Responses that change from night to night or from one adult to another.
The room. Early light, noise, or a sleep space that is not set up for sleep.
Most babies have two or three of these at once, which is why fixing one at a time often seems to do nothing.
Actually Sleeping exists for exactly this. Dr. Sam looks at all of it together, writes one plan for your baby, and adjusts it with you every day until nights hold. Night feeds your pediatrician wants kept stay in the plan.
Why generic advice often fails
Most advice is written for an age band. Your baby is not an age band. A bedtime that suits one 7-month-old leaves another overtired. A response that calms one baby winds another up. When a general plan stalls, parents usually change several things at once, and the baby gets a new set of rules every few nights. A plan built from your baby’s age, feeding, temperament, how they fall asleep now and your family’s schedule avoids most of that.
What does not help
Cereal in the bottle. The AAP advises against it because it can increase the likelihood of gagging or inhaling the thickened mixture into the lungs.
Inclined sleepers, wedges or positioners. The AAP advises a firm, flat, non-inclined sleep surface.
Keeping your baby up later or cutting naps in the hope of a longer night. Overtired babies tend to sleep worse, not better.
If your baby used to sleep through and stopped
Illness, a new skill such as rolling or standing, a nap transition, or a regression at 4 months, 8 to 10 months or 12 months can all set sleep back. When new habits creep in during the disruption, they tend to stay after it passes.
When it is not behavioral
Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, persistent mouth breathing, poor weight gain, eczema that itches at night or frequent painful spit-up are reasons to see your pediatrician before any sleep plan.

# What is the Ferber method, and does it work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/ferber-method-explained/

What is the Ferber method, and does it work?
The Ferber method, also called graduated extinction or timed checks, means putting your baby down awake, leaving the room, and returning for brief checks at gradually longer intervals until they fall asleep. It has randomized-trial support in babies 6 to 16 months. It is not cry it out, because you keep checking, but it does involve crying, and it does not suit every baby.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What it is
Graduated extinction is a set script. After the bedtime routine your baby goes into the crib awake and you leave. If your baby cries, you return briefly at set intervals that lengthen over the night and over the week, offering a calm word but not picking up or feeding to sleep. The same script applies at night wakings, apart from planned feeds.
Does it work? What the research says
A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found support for graduated extinction; its strongest support was for unmodified extinction and preventive parent education. In a 2016 randomized trial of 43 babies aged 6 to 16 months, graduated extinction produced large reductions in the time to fall asleep and in the number of night wakings compared with a control group. Infant cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines compared with controls, and 12 months later the groups did not differ in emotional or behavioral problems or in attachment.
So the method can work. The question for a parent is whether it is the right fit for this baby, in this family, right now.
Who it tends to fail for, and why
Babies who escalate at every check. For some babies, a parent appearing and leaving again is more upsetting than no visit at all. The script keeps sending you in.
Parents who know they will pick up after a long cry. Holding out for 40 minutes and then rocking to sleep teaches a baby to cry for 40 minutes.
Babies whose schedule is working against them. An overtired or under-tired baby protests any method. The intervals do not fix the timing.
Babies with unclear night-feed needs. The script cannot tell a hungry waking from a habit waking. Your pediatrician has to decide which feeds stay.
Families who apply it at bedtime only, and feed or rock back to sleep later in the night.
Young babies, or any baby who is ill. The trial evidence is in babies 6 months and older.
The method is a general script. It does not know your baby’s temperament, feeds, bedtime or room, and those matter as much as the intervals.
How Actually Sleeping is different
Actually Sleeping does not hand you an interval chart. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby from a detailed intake: age, feeding, temperament, how your baby falls asleep now and your family’s schedule. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. You get bootcamp-style coaching before night one, so you already know how to make the decisions that usually derail timed checks. Daily 1:1 check-ins adjust the plan as your baby responds, and naps are coached until solid.
The result is guaranteed in writing: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Full refund if not. Many families come to us after a check-based method stalled; their stories are on our reviews from families who had already tried other sleep training.
Safety, whatever approach you use
Your baby sleeps on the back, alone, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface without soft bedding, as the AAP advises. Always go in for illness, vomiting, or anything that sounds different from protest. Ask your pediatrician about night feeds before changing anything.

# What is cry it out (extinction), and is it safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/cry-it-out-extinction-method/

What is cry it out (extinction), and is it safe?
Cry it out, called unmodified extinction in research, means putting a healthy baby down awake after a full bedtime routine and not returning until a planned feed or morning. Randomized trials of behavioral sleep methods have not found harm to children’s emotional health, behavior or attachment. It only suits healthy babies in a safe sleep space, and many families do not want it. Actually Sleeping does not use it.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
What it is, and what it is not
Extinction is a structured method: a loving routine, a fed and dry baby, a safe crib, a set bedtime, planned night feeds if your pediatrician wants them, and a parent who is watching a monitor. After goodnight, you do not go back in for crying alone. It is not ignoring a baby all day, leaving a sick or hungry baby, or closing the door regardless of what happens. You always go in for illness, vomiting, a limb stuck in the crib slats, or anything that sounds wrong.
Is it safe? What the evidence says
A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found the strongest support for unmodified extinction, alongside preventive parent education.
A 2016 randomized trial of graduated extinction (with checks) in 43 babies aged 6 to 16 months found small-to-moderate declines in infant cortisol compared with controls, and no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment 12 months later.
A Melbourne trial in which nurses taught behavioral sleep strategies found, at age 2, no evidence of harm to children’s mental health or to parenting, and fewer mothers with depression symptoms in the intervention group.
The honest limits: samples are modest, most participants were 6 months or older, and the trials with follow-up tested behavioral strategies in general rather than pure extinction. The research supports “no harm found,” which is not the same as proof for every child. See what the research says.
Who it tends to fail for, and why
Families who cannot see it through. Crying for an hour and then being rocked to sleep is harder on everyone than a plan with more parental presence, done consistently.
Babies whose schedule or feeds are the real problem. Leaving the room does not fix a bedtime that is wrong for the baby or a hunger waking.
Young babies. Most of the research involved babies 6 months and older, and many younger babies still need night feeds.
Babies who are ill, in pain, or have unresolved feeding, weight or breathing concerns. See sleep training a baby with reflux.
Any baby not in a safe sleep space. Back to sleep, firm flat surface, empty crib. See safe sleep and sleep training.
How Actually Sleeping is different

Dr. Sam writes a plan around your baby: age, feeding, temperament, how your baby falls asleep now and your family’s schedule. You are not left alone at the door listening. You get bootcamp-style coaching before night one, daily 1:1 check-ins to adjust the plan as your baby responds, and naps coached until solid. Night feeds your pediatrician wants kept stay in the plan.
The outcome is guaranteed in writing: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Full refund if not. Safety, whatever you choose
Your baby sleeps on the back, alone, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface without soft toys, pillows, blankets or bedding. The AAP advises against weighted swaddles and weighted objects on or near a baby. Your pediatrician decides night feeds and anything medical.

# What is the chair method of sleep training?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/chair-method-sleep-training/

What is the chair method of sleep training?
In the chair method you put your baby down awake and sit in a chair beside the crib until they fall asleep, then move the chair farther away over a period of nights until you are out of the room. It is also called camping out or gradual withdrawal. It suits parents who want to stay present, but it is slow, it is not tear-free, and it stalls easily.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What it is
The chair method gradually withdraws your presence. You start right beside the crib, offering a quiet voice and limited touch, and move the chair toward the door in stages until your baby falls asleep without you in the room. Night wakings get the same response from wherever the chair is that night.
Does it work?
The chair method has less direct trial evidence than extinction, graduated extinction or bedtime fading, which are the approaches the American Academy of Sleep Medicine review lists with support. It rests on the same principle: your baby does the final step of falling asleep while your help is reduced. A Melbourne cluster randomized trial in which nurses taught 328 mothers behavioral sleep strategies found fewer infant sleep problems at 10 months (56% vs 68%) and 12 months (39% vs 55%) than usual care, and fewer maternal depression symptoms.
Who it tends to fail for, and why
Babies who are more upset with you in the room. Some babies are frustrated that you are right there and not picking them up. Your presence keeps them awake.
Families who stall at one position. Staying in the same spot for a week creates a new habit: needing you in the chair.
Parents who slide back into doing too much from the chair: picking up, lying down next to the crib, holding hands through the slats.
Babies whose schedule is off. If bedtime is wrong for the baby, the chair just means you sit through the protest.
Exhausted parents. It is slow, and 2 a.m. in a chair for weeks is hard to keep up.
Where it does fit, it tends to be with toddlers, children with separation anxiety, and families who share a room. Even then, the details decide whether it works: when to move, how much to say, what to do when a toddler climbs out.
How Actually Sleeping is different
Actually Sleeping does not give you a chair schedule and wish you luck. Dr. Sam writes a plan around your child: age, feeding, temperament, how they fall asleep now, your room setup and your family’s schedule. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. You get bootcamp-style coaching before night one, daily 1:1 check-ins that adjust the plan as your child responds, and naps coached until solid.
The result is guaranteed in writing: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Full refund if not. Parents of children 12 months and older describe their results on these video reviews.

# Does the pick-up-put-down method work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/pick-up-put-down-method/

Does the pick-up-put-down method work?
It can, mainly for younger babies, and it is slow. You pick your baby up when they cry, calm them, and put them back down awake, repeating until they fall asleep in the crib. We found no controlled trial testing it on its own. In older babies it often backfires, because being picked up and put down repeatedly can stimulate and frustrate more than it calms.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What it is
Pick-up-put-down is a hands-on, responsive approach. When your baby cries in the crib, you lift them until they are calm, not asleep, and put them back down awake. You repeat that until they fall asleep in the crib, and the help is meant to shrink night by night.
What the evidence says
We found no controlled trial that tests pick-up-put-down on its own, so there is no direct research on how well it works compared with other approaches. It rests on the same principle as the studied methods: the baby does the final step of falling asleep in the crib while your help is reduced. That principle is well supported. A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that 94% reported behavioral interventions effective. This particular technique is supported mostly by clinical and parent experience.
Who it tends to fail for, and why
Older babies. Many babies past the early months find being lifted and lowered over and over stimulating. They cry harder at each put-down.
Babies who fall asleep in your arms. The longer each hold, the closer it gets to rocking to sleep, which is the habit you are trying to change.
Tired parents. It is physically demanding and slow, and very hard to keep up at 3 a.m.
Babies whose schedule is off. An overtired baby will not settle with any approach; see wake windows by age.
Babies around 4 months, who are also going through a permanent change in sleep structure, covered in the 4-month sleep regression.
The appeal is real: you never leave a crying baby. The problem is that the method is generic, and whether it helps or winds your baby up depends on your baby.

# Which sleep training method is gentlest? Methods compared
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/gentle-sleep-training-methods-compared/

Which sleep training method is gentlest? Methods compared
Measured by crying per night, bedtime fading and the parent-present methods (the chair method and pick-up-put-down) are usually the gentlest, and they tend to be the slowest. Timed checks and extinction involve more crying at first. Research has not shown that a faster method harms a child or that a slower one protects them. What matters most is a plan that fits your baby.

Methods compared
MethodWhat it isParent presenceWhere it often goes wrong
Bedtime fadingBedtime moved to when the child actually falls asleep, then brought earlierNormalFixes bedtime battles but not a baby who still needs help to fall asleep
Pick up, put downLift to calm when crying, put down awake, repeatHighOverstimulates many older babies; exhausting for parents

What “gentle” means
Parents use the word in three different ways, and they point to different methods:
Least crying on any one night: bedtime fading, then pick-up-put-down and the chair method.
Least crying in total: not clearly any of them. Gradual methods spread protest over more nights, and no study has shown that total crying is lower.
Most parental presence: the chair method and pick-up-put-down.
No method is cry-free. Changing how a baby falls asleep is frustrating for the baby, and crying is how babies express frustration. What you can choose is how you respond to it, and how well the plan fits your baby so that the protest is short.
That fit is what Actually Sleeping provides. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby rather than picking a method name off a list. It is not cry it out and not wait it out, and you get bootcamp-style coaching before night one.
What the research says about gentleness
A 2016 randomized trial of 43 babies aged 6 to 16 months compared graduated extinction, bedtime fading and a sleep-education control. Both methods produced large reductions in the time to fall asleep; only graduated extinction clearly reduced night wakings. Infant cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines in both method groups compared with controls, and 12 months later there were no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment. The evidence does not show that a faster method harms a baby or that a slower one protects them. Details are in what the research says.
Why the method name matters less than the plan
Most stalled attempts are not caused by choosing the wrong method from this table. They come from a bedtime that is wrong for the baby, night feeds without a plan, a response that does not suit the baby’s temperament, or adults responding differently. A well-timed bedtime with a gradual approach does better than a badly timed bedtime with any approach. Much of the crying parents fear comes from those details, not from the method itself.

# What is bedtime fading?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/bedtime-fading/

What is bedtime fading?
Bedtime fading means temporarily moving bedtime later, to the time your child actually falls asleep, so they fall asleep quickly, and then bringing it earlier in small steps until you reach the bedtime you want. It involves little crying and has randomized-trial support in babies 6 to 16 months for falling asleep faster. On its own it does less for night wakings.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What it is, and why it works
Sleep pressure builds the longer a child is awake. If bedtime is earlier than the child’s body is ready for, they lie awake, protest, and learn that bed is a place for struggling. Bedtime fading lines bedtime up with real sleepiness, so the child falls asleep fast and bed becomes linked with sleep again. The body clock is then moved earlier gradually, while the morning wake time stays fixed.
What the research says
Bedtime fading was one of two methods tested in a 2016 randomized controlled trial of 43 infants aged 6 to 16 months. Compared with a control group, babies in the fading group had large reductions in the time it took to fall asleep, and infant cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines. Unlike graduated extinction, fading did not produce a large reduction in night wakings. Twelve months later, there were no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment. A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine also lists bedtime fading with positive routines among the behavioral treatments with supporting evidence.
What it fixes, and what it does not
It helps with: long bedtime battles, a bedtime set too early for the child’s body clock, and bed that has become linked with lying awake.
It does not fix by itself: needing to be fed or rocked to sleep. If your baby is still helped to sleep at the later bedtime, night wakings usually continue.
It is not a fix for early morning waking; a later bedtime rarely produces a later morning.
Who it tends to fail for, and why
Babies whose main problem is night waking rather than bedtime. Fading targets falling asleep at the start of the night.
Families who leave the late bedtime in place for weeks. Total sleep still matters, and a child kept up late can become overtired, with more waking and earlier mornings.
Inconsistent mornings. The method depends on a fixed wake time, which is hard to hold after a late night.
Younger babies. The trial evidence is in babies 6 months and older.
Getting the timing right is the whole method. Starting too late, moving too fast or too slowly, and missing that the real problem is a sleep association are the common reasons it stalls.
How Actually Sleeping is different
Timing is one part of an Actually Sleeping plan, not the whole plan. Dr. Sam looks at how your child falls asleep, night feeds, naps, temperament and your family’s schedule together, and writes one plan that addresses bedtime and night wakings at the same time. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. You get bootcamp-style coaching before night one, daily 1:1 check-ins that adjust timing as your child responds, and naps coached until solid.
The outcome is guaranteed in writing: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Full refund if not. Parents describe their results on our video reviews page.

Whatever the bedtime, your baby sleeps on the back, alone, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface without soft bedding, as the AAP advises. Talk to your pediatrician about any health concern before changing your child’s sleep.

# Can I sleep train and keep breastfeeding?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-while-breastfeeding/

Can I sleep train and keep breastfeeding?
Yes. Sleep training changes how your baby falls asleep, not whether they are breastfed, and you do not have to night wean to do it. A good plan keeps the night feeds your pediatrician recommends and changes only the wakings that are about falling back asleep. Ideally breastfeeding is well established and your baby is growing well before you start.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
Sleep training and night weaning are separate
Sleep trainingNight weaning
What changesHow your baby falls asleepWhether your baby eats overnight
Who decides timingYou, with your pediatrician’s view on readinessYour pediatrician; timing varies widely from baby to baby
Required for the otherNoNo
A baby can fall asleep independently and still have night feeds. Many breastfed babies do exactly that for months.
Why breastfed babies often wake more
Breastfeeding is calming, and many breastfed babies fall asleep at the breast at bedtime. That is natural, and it means the breast becomes the way they fall asleep. When they surface between sleep cycles in the night, they look for the same thing. The AAP’s parent site notes that babies who are helped to sleep may have trouble falling back asleep when they wake. The result is a baby who feeds briefly many times a night, not always from hunger. See the feed-to-sleep association.
Telling hunger feeds from habit feeds, and changing one without touching the other, is the delicate part. It is also where Actually Sleeping spends most of its time with breastfeeding families. Dr. Sam writes the plan around your breastfeeding goals and your pediatrician’s guidance, and the plan never forces dropping night feeds.
Why breastfeeding is worth protecting
The AAP notes that at least partial human milk feeding has been shown to significantly lower the risk of sleep-related infant deaths. That is a strong reason to make sure any change to sleep does not undermine breastfeeding.
Supply and health: when to call someone
These are safety points, not a weaning plan:
If you wake painfully full, express just enough for comfort.
Call your doctor or a lactation consultant if you develop a painful lump, redness or fever.
If wet diapers drop or you are worried about your baby’s intake, pause and call your pediatrician or a lactation consultant.
If you pump at work or have had supply concerns, involve a lactation consultant before any change to night feeds.
Hold off on any sleep plan if your baby has slow weight gain, has latch or supply problems still being worked on, or is ill.
Why a generic plan often fails breastfed babies
Most general methods treat every waking the same way, or treat every feed as a habit. Neither works for a breastfed baby who still needs some night feeds. A breastfed baby who smells milk may also protest harder when the nursing parent responds, which changes who should handle which wakings. These are family-specific decisions, and they change as your baby grows.

# Can I sleep train while room-sharing?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-while-room-sharing/

Can I sleep train while room-sharing?
Yes. The AAP recommends that parents sleep in the same room as their baby, but not in the same bed, preferably for at least the first six months, and you can teach independent sleep in that arrangement. It is usually harder, because your baby can see, hear and smell you. A plan written for a shared room makes it workable.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Room-sharing is not bed-sharing
Room-sharing means your baby sleeps in a crib or bassinet in your room: on the back, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface, with no soft toys, pillows, blankets or bedding. The AAP recommends room-sharing and says it cannot support bed-sharing under any circumstances. It notes the risk is higher on couches and soft armchairs, so never let your baby sleep on a sofa or armchair. Do not use inclined sleepers, wedges or positioners, and never drape fabric over or on the crib.
Why it is harder
Babies stir between sleep cycles, see or smell a parent, and call for the usual help.
Parents hear every grunt and respond before the baby has fully woken. Babies are noisy in light sleep.
Parents’ coughing, phones and movement wake the baby, particularly in the early morning hours.
Many general methods assume you can leave the room. In a shared room you cannot, which changes how almost every response works.
This is a common situation for families who come to Actually Sleeping, including families in apartments where a separate room is not an option. Dr. Sam writes the plan for your actual room, so the response fits the space you have.
Why the setup matters
In a shared room, the distance between beds, what your baby can see from the crib, light at the window and how sound carries all affect how often your baby wakes and what they expect when they do. Getting those right, safely, is part of the plan. Anything you add to the room has to respect safe sleep: nothing in or over the crib, and any divider or screen well away from it.
Why general methods stall in a shared room
Leave-the-room methods do not translate directly to 3 a.m. when you are sleeping a few feet away.
Parent-present methods fit better, but your presence all night means there is no point where you withdraw.
Early mornings are hardest, because your own waking and movement start the day early for your baby.
After 6 months
Moving a baby to their own room after 6 months is a family decision. Many families room-share far longer by choice or necessity, and independent sleep can be taught either way. The same principles apply to siblings sharing a room; see sleep training twins. General safety points are in safe sleep and sleep training.

# Does sleep training work? What the research says
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/does-sleep-training-work-evidence/

Does sleep training work? What the research says
Yes. A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that 94% reported behavioral sleep interventions were effective, and over 80% of treated children improved, with gains maintained for 3 to 6 months. Randomized trials also found fewer maternal depression symptoms and no evidence of harm to children’s emotional health, behavior or attachment. Most studies involved babies 6 months and older.

The key studies
StudyDesignMain findings
Mindell et al., 2006 (Sleep)Review of 52 treatment studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine94% of studies reported the intervention worked; over 80% of treated children showed clinically significant improvement, maintained for 3–6 months. Strongest support for unmodified extinction and preventive parent education; further support for graduated extinction, bedtime fading with positive routines, and scheduled awakenings
Hiscock et al., 2007 (Arch Dis Child)Cluster randomized trial in Melbourne, Australia; 328 mothers who reported an infant sleep problem at 7 months; behavioral strategies taught in structured nurse consultationsFewer sleep problems at 10 months (56% vs 68%) and 12 months (39% vs 55%), and fewer maternal depression symptoms, than usual care
Hiscock et al., 2008 (Pediatrics)Follow-up of the same trial at age 2Fewer intervention mothers had depression symptoms above the community cut point (15.4% vs 26.4%); no marked differences in parenting or child mental health, which the authors read as no evidence of longer-term harm. Sleep problems: 27.3% vs 32.6%
Gradisar et al., 2016 (Pediatrics)Randomized trial of 43 infants aged 6–16 months: graduated extinction, bedtime fading or sleep education onlyBoth methods produced large reductions in time to fall asleep; graduated extinction also reduced night waking. Infant cortisol and maternal stress showed small-to-moderate declines compared with controls. No differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment 12 months later
What the evidence supports
It works for most families. Babies fall asleep faster and wake their parents less.
Parents benefit. Improved maternal mood is among the most consistent findings.
No harm has been found in the trials that looked, at 12 months and at age 2.
More than one approach works. Check-based, extinction and fading approaches all have support.
The research answers whether behavioral sleep methods work. It does not tell you which details will work for your baby. That is the part Actually Sleeping does: Dr. Sam applies what the evidence supports through a plan written for your baby, with daily support while you carry it out.
What the evidence does not show
It does not work for every child on a fixed script. Over 80% of treated children improved in the review, which means some did not. Plans that are adjusted as the baby responds are the practical answer to that.
It is not a one-time fix for life. In the Melbourne trial, the gap in sleep problems narrowed by age 2. Illness, travel and regressions can bring old habits back.
Evidence under 6 months is thin. Most trial participants were 6 months or older.
Some methods have no trials. Pick-up-put-down and many popular approaches have not been tested directly.
The limits, fairly stated
Small samples and parent report. The 2016 trial had 43 babies, and many outcomes rely on parents’ diaries.
Mixed methods. Families in the Melbourne trial were taught behavioral strategies by nurses, so results reflect being offered sleep help, not one specific method.
Absence of evidence. “No harm found” in studies of a few hundred children is reassuring but cannot rule out small effects or effects in particular children.
What this means for your family
The research supports behavioral sleep help as effective and, as far as has been measured, safe for healthy babies. Safe sleep rules apply every night whatever you choose: on the back, alone, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface without soft bedding. Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health and night feeds.

Frequently asked
Is sleep training harmful to babies?Trials have not found harm. A 2016 randomized trial found no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment a year later, with infant cortisol slightly lower in trained babies than controls. A Melbourne trial found no evidence of harm to child mental health or parenting at age 2.
Does sleep training raise cortisol?The randomized trial that measured it found small-to-moderate declines in infant cortisol in the graduated extinction and bedtime fading groups compared with controls, alongside small-to-moderate declines in maternal stress.
Do the effects of sleep training last?A review found improvements maintained for 3 to 6 months, and one trial found fewer sleep problems at 10 and 12 months. By age 2 the gap had narrowed, so the main benefit is earlier relief for the family. Illness and travel can bring old habits back.
Does the AAP recommend sleep training?The AAP’s safe sleep guidance applies whatever you choose. Its parent site advises that from about 4 months you put babies to bed drowsy rather than waiting until they are asleep, so they learn to fall asleep on their own. Ask your pediatrician about timing.

# Sleep training isn’t working. What should I do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-not-working/

Sleep training isn’t working. What should I do?
First rule out a medical cause with your pediatrician. If your baby is healthy and you have been consistent, the cause is nearly always one of five things: inconsistent responses, a baby still fed or rocked to sleep, a schedule that does not fit, night feeds without a plan, or a method that does not suit your baby’s temperament. A plan written for your baby, adjusted daily, fixes these.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
Is it really not working?
Progress is rarely a straight line. These are common and do not mean failure on their own:
A second or third night that is worse than the first.
A burst of crying a few nights in, just before things settle.
Nights improving while naps and early mornings lag behind.
A short relapse in the second week.
Signs of real progress are less time to fall asleep, fewer or shorter wakings, or crying that is less intense. If none of those is moving after a fair stretch of consistency, something in the plan is wrong.
The five usual causes
What you seeLikely cause
Crying is as long or longer after a weekInconsistent response: sometimes rocked, fed or brought into your bed after a long cry
Falls asleep easily at bedtime, then wakes every 2–3 hoursPut down drowsy or nearly asleep, or the feed is still the last step before sleep
Takes a long time to fall asleep, or wakes very earlySchedule mismatch: bedtime too early or too late, too much or too little daytime sleep
Wakes at varying times and feeds a little each timeNo feeding plan; feeds are being used to settle
Cries harder after every check or visitA method that does not suit your baby’s temperament
Most stalled attempts have more than one of these at once. That is why changing one thing, or switching methods, so often seems to do nothing.
This is exactly where most families are when they contact Actually Sleeping. Dr. Sam reviews what you have tried and for how long, finds which of these is driving it for your baby, and writes a plan that addresses all of them together.
When it is medical
Stop and see your pediatrician if your baby screams as if in pain, snores, arches, has breathing pauses, is feeding poorly, or was doing well and suddenly is not. Illness, ear infections, reflux and breathing problems all disrupt sleep, and no sleep plan should work around them.
Other things that quietly undo progress
The room: light leaking in early, white noise on a timer that switches off, a room that is too warm.
New skills: rolling, sitting, pulling to stand. See the 8 to 10 month regression.
Different rules by day and night, or between caregivers.
Too many sleep crutches at once: a pacifier that needs replacing many times a night is a sleep association too.
Switching methods every few nights, which teaches a baby that persistence changes the rules.
Why a second generic attempt usually fails too
When a method stalls, the problem is usually in the details: timing that is off by 20 minutes, a feed in the wrong place, a response that works against this baby’s temperament. Those are hard to see from inside the house at 3 a.m., and a different method from the same kind of source does not reveal them. If the constant waking is the main problem, waking every 2 hours explains the common causes by age.

It is not cry it out and not wait it out, and night feeds your pediatrician wants kept stay in. Families who came to us after other sleep training describe what changed on these video reviews. Book a free consultation and Dr. Sam will tell you where your current plan is breaking down.

How long should I try sleep training before giving up?Look for progress in the time to fall asleep, the number of wakings or the intensity of crying. Why did sleep training work and then stop?Illness, travel, teething, a developmental leap or a nap transition can disrupt sleep, and old habits can return if the response changes during that time. An Actually Sleeping plan includes guidance for these disruptions so progress is not lost.

# What is a realistic newborn sleep schedule (0–8 weeks)?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/newborn-sleep-schedule-0-to-8-weeks/

What is a realistic newborn sleep schedule (0–8 weeks)?
There is no clock schedule for a newborn, only a rhythm: feed on cue, stay awake briefly (a common rule of thumb is 45–60 minutes, rising toward 60–90 minutes by 6–8 weeks), sleep, repeat. Expect 5 or more naps, sleep spread across day and night, often only 1–2 hours at a time at first, a total the AAP puts at about 16–17 hours, and a late “bedtime”.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is typical from 0 to 8 weeks
A newborn day is a loop of feeding, a short time awake and sleep, repeated around the clock. The ranges below describe what is common. They are not targets.
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hoursNo AASM recommendation under 4 months. The AAP’s parent site describes about 16–17 hours a day, often only 1–2 hours at a time
What studies of healthy babies foundAverage 14.6 hours at 0–2 months, with a normal spread of about 9 to 20 hours (Galland 2012)
Night sleep (common practice range)Broken stretches through the night, lengthening over the following weeks
Naps (common practice range)5 or more, from 20 minutes to 2–3 hours, with no pattern yet
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)45–60 minutes at 0–4 weeks; 60–90 minutes by 6–8 weeks, including the feed
Night feedsEvery 2–4 hours on cue is common. Some newborns need to be woken to feed until weight gain is established. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Rows marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation, which the AAP supports. Rows marked Galland 2012 come from a systematic review of observational studies. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings. They describe an average baby; healthy babies sit on both sides of every one of them.
Any newborn schedule you find online is an average of many babies. Yours feeds, settles and wakes on their own pattern, and that pattern changes from one week to the next. That is why Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage with a plan written for one baby, not a timetable. Dr. Sam builds it around your baby’s feeding, temperament and how your household actually runs, and checks in with you 1:1 every day.
What is changing developmentally
A newborn has no settled body clock. Circadian rhythms develop around 2 to 3 months, and by about 3 months melatonin and cortisol follow a day–night cycle, which is why newborn sleep is scattered across 24 hours and why day–night confusion is normal. Newborns fall asleep through active (REM-like) sleep, so grunting, twitching and brief cries during sleep do not always mean the baby is awake. The AAP says fussing usually peaks at about 3 hours a day by 6 weeks and declines by 3 to 4 months.
The AASM consensus on sleep duration deliberately gives no recommendation under 4 months, because normal sleep varies so widely at that age and there is too little evidence linking it to health outcomes. See how infant sleep cycles develop for what comes next.
Why a newborn schedule rarely holds
Day–night confusion: with no body clock yet, night is not different from day. It is expected, and it is why clock times mean little in these weeks.
Only sleeps when held: very common now. Contact sleep is fine while you are fully awake. It becomes something to plan around later; see contact napping.
The evening fussy stretch: the AAP says colicky fussing tends to fall between 6 p.m. and midnight, which is exactly when a printed schedule says “bedtime”.
Overtired by evening: how long a newborn can comfortably stay awake varies more than any chart shows; see wake windows by age.
Safe sleep from the first night
On the back for every sleep, on a firm, flat surface, in an empty bassinet or crib.
Share a room, not a bed, for at least the first 6 months (AAP).
If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing or carrier, move them to a firm, flat surface on their back as soon as you can.
Stop swaddling as soon as your baby shows any sign of trying to roll. The AAP says some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Not with any method that drops feeds or leaves a newborn to cry; those are not for this age. Foundations can start now: safe sleep, full feeds, and a predictable shape to days and nights. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage. Night feeds are never forced out, and feeding decisions stay with your pediatrician. The 14-day guarantee clock starts at your baby’s 10-week birthday: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Frequently asked
Should I wake my newborn to feed?Follow your pediatrician’s guidance. Newborns are often woken to feed until weight gain is established, and only your pediatrician can tell you when longer stretches are fine for your baby. Nothing about sleep should override that decision.
When do newborns start sleeping longer at night?Circadian rhythms develop around 2 to 3 months, and night sleep starts to consolidate from about 2 months. Many babies then begin to produce one longer stretch, usually the first of the night. The range is wide and depends on feeding and growth.
What time should a newborn go to bed?Late is normal in the first weeks, often 9 to 11 p.m. as a rough rule of thumb. Bedtime tends to drift earlier as the body clock develops. Where it lands for your baby depends on feeds and naps, which is what a custom plan from Actually Sleeping maps out.
Can a newborn be on a schedule?Not a clock schedule. A repeating pattern of feed, short awake time and sleep is realistic. Fixed feeding or nap times are not, and feeds should never be delayed to fit a timetable. Actually Sleeping builds foundations from the newborn stage without touching night feeds.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/2-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 month old?
At 2 months most babies take 4–5 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 60–90 minutes at a time. Total sleep varies widely; there is no official hour target under 4 months. Bedtime is still on the late side, around 8–9:30 p.m., and night feeds on cue are normal and expected.

What is typical at 2 months
At 2 months naps do not land at the same times every day yet, and night sleep is broken by feeds. The ranges below are what is common, not a timetable.
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hoursVaries widely; the AASM gives no recommendation under 4 months
What studies of healthy babies foundLongest stretch at 0–5 months averaged 5.7 hours, with a normal spread of about 2 to nearly 10 hours (Galland 2012)
Night sleep (common practice range)Broken by feeds; often one longer first stretch of the night begins to appear
Naps (common practice range)4–5, anywhere from 30 minutes to 2 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)60–90 minutes, including feeding time
Night feedsTypically 2–4 a night, on cue. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Rows marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation, which the AAP supports. Rows marked Galland 2012 come from a systematic review of observational studies. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings. They describe an average baby; healthy babies sit on both sides of every one of them.
The hard part is not knowing the average. It is fitting a day around one baby whose naps, feeds and evenings do not match it. Actually Sleeping starts there: Dr. Sam writes a plan for your 2 month old that keeps every feed your pediatrician wants, and adjusts it with you in daily 1:1 check-ins as your baby changes week to week.
What is changing developmentally
The body clock is starting to work: circadian rhythms develop around 2 to 3 months, and night sleep begins to consolidate from about 2 months, often as one longer stretch early in the night. Daytime naps stay irregular for longer. Social smiling arrives, awake time becomes more alert, and the fussing that the AAP says usually peaks by 6 weeks begins to ease, declining by 3 to 4 months.
The AASM consensus gives no sleep-duration recommendation under 4 months because normal variation is so wide, so your baby’s mood, feeding and growth tell you more than an hour count.
Why the average 2-month schedule often does not fit
Short naps: 30–45 minute naps are common at 2 months. See why naps are only 30 minutes.
Naps only in arms: common, and the reason clock times on a page rarely hold. See contact napping.
Overtired evenings: the same window that suits one baby overtires another. See wake windows by age.
Feeding comes first: a hungry baby feeds, whatever the schedule says. Any plan has to bend around that.
Safe sleep at 2 months
Stop swaddling at the first sign of trying to roll. The AAP says some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months. Move to an arms-free sleep sack, never a weighted one.
Sleep stays on the back, on a firm, flat surface, in an empty crib or bassinet, in your room.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Not with anything that drops feeds or leaves a 2 month old to cry. Foundations can start now. # What is a good sleep schedule for a 3 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/3-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 3 month old?
At 3 months most babies take 4 naps (some 3) and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake about 75 minutes to 2 hours. Total sleep varies widely; there is no official hour target under 4 months. Bedtime moves earlier, to roughly 7:30–8:30 p.m., and many babies still feed 1–3 times overnight.

What is typical at 3 months
Nights often get a little more organized at 3 months while naps stay unpredictable. These are the common ranges.
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hoursVaries widely; the AASM gives no recommendation under 4 months
What studies of healthy babies foundAverage 13.6 hours from 3 months, with a normal spread of about 9 to 18 hours (Galland 2012)
Night sleep (common practice range)10–12 hours, usually with feeds
Naps (common practice range)3–4, totalling about 4–5 hours; the last is often a catnap

What is changing developmentally
By about 3 months, melatonin and cortisol follow a day–night rhythm, so nights lengthen and bedtime settles earlier. Naps are the last piece to organize. Sleep onset also shifts from active sleep to quiet sleep around now, and the AAP says babies have regular sleep cycles from about 4 months, which is what parents often experience as the 4-month regression. How infant sleep cycles develop explains the change.
Why the average 3-month schedule often does not fit
The swaddle transition: it has to end at the first sign of rolling, and sleep often gets worse before it settles. See dropping the swaddle.
30-minute naps: still common, and the main reason clock times drift. See short naps.
Feeding to sleep for every sleep: normal now, and a common root of night waking later. See the feed-to-sleep association.
Sudden frequent waking: it may be the early edge of the 4-month sleep regression.
Each of these depends on the baby. The same schedule that settles one 3 month old leaves another overtired by 5 p.m.
Safe sleep at 3 months
Stop swaddling at the first signs of rolling; use an arms-free sleep sack and no loose blankets.
Back to sleep for every sleep, on a firm, flat, empty surface, in your room for at least the first 6 months (AAP).
Is this age right for sleep training?
Foundations, yes. The AAP’s parent site advises that from 4 months babies go to bed drowsy rather than already asleep, so the next few weeks are a natural time to build toward that.
