# What is a good sleep schedule for a 4 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/4-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 4 month old?
At 4 months most babies take 3–4 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 1.5–2 hours at a time. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24 from 4 months, including naps. Four months is when a schedule on paper and a baby in the crib most often part ways. The sleep cycles change, and a baby who needs feeding or rocking to fall asleep starts needing it again at every cycle. A schedule cannot fix that on its own. Actually Sleeping does it with a plan Dr. Sam writes for your baby, bootcamp-style coaching before night one, and daily 1:1 check-ins. It is not cry it out and not wait it out.
What is changing developmentally
The AAP says babies have regular sleep cycles from about 4 months. In infancy each cycle of light and deep sleep lasts about 50 minutes, with a brief arousal between them. This change is permanent. A baby who falls asleep with help notices that the help is gone at each arousal and calls for it. Rolling arrives for many babies, and feeds get distractible in daylight.
Why the average 4-month schedule often does not fit
Waking every 1–2 hours: often the new sleep cycles meeting an old way of falling asleep. See 4-month sleep regression or sleep problem.
Short naps: one sleep cycle and done, usually for the same reason. See 30-minute naps.
Feeding back to sleep at every waking: see the feed-to-sleep association.
3 naps or 4: the answer depends on how long your baby’s naps run, which no printed schedule can know.
These are the reasons the same timetable produces a calm evening for one family and a 2-hour bedtime for another. Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own.
Safe sleep at 4 months
The swaddle must be gone once rolling attempts begin. Keep placing your baby on the back in an empty crib; the AAP says a baby who rolls both ways comfortably does not need to be turned back.
Room-share without bed-sharing for at least the first 6 months (AAP).
Is this age right for sleep training?
For many families, yes, once the pediatrician is happy with growth and feeding. The AAP’s parent site advises putting babies 4 months and older to bed drowsy rather than asleep. Teaching independent sleep does not require dropping night feeds; those decisions belong to your pediatrician, and Actually Sleeping plans never force them out. # What is a good sleep schedule for a 5 month old?

What is a good sleep schedule for a 5 month old?
At 5 months most babies take 3 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 2–2.5 hours at a time. The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, naps included. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 7:45 p.m., with 11–12 hours overnight and often 0–2 night feeds.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 6 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/6-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 6 month old?
At 6 months most babies take 3 naps, with some starting the move to 2. Wake windows of 2–3 hours are a common rule of thumb, the AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, and bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m. with 11–12 hours overnight.

By 6 months the longest stretch of sleep typically lengthens to around 6 hours. Sitting, rolling freely and reaching for everything. The third nap begins to be resisted on some days, the first sign of the 3-to-2 transition. Safe sleep at 6 months
Back to sleep for every sleep until the first birthday, on a firm, flat, empty surface. The AAP recommends room-sharing for at least the first 6 months.
Lower the mattress before your baby can sit unassisted, and to the lowest setting before standing (MedlinePlus).

Yes, for most healthy babies, and 6 months is one of the most common ages families start. What is a good sleep schedule for a 12 month old?

What is a good sleep schedule for an 18 month old?
Between 15 and 23 months most toddlers settle on one midday nap of 1.5–3 hours. As a rule of thumb, wake windows are about 4.5–5.5 hours just after the switch and 5–6 hours from 18 months. The AASM recommends 11–14 hours of sleep in 24, and bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m.

What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 year old?
Between 2 and 3 years most children take one nap of 1–2 hours and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 5–6 hours on either side of it. The AASM recommends 11–14 hours of sleep in 24 at ages 1–2 and 10–13 hours at ages 3–5, naps included, and bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m.

# When and how do I night wean my baby?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/night-weaning-how-and-when/

When and how do I night wean my baby?
Many healthy, well-growing babies can drop night feeds at some point in the second half of the first year; some need them longer. Timing is your pediatrician’s call. Weaning on its own rarely ends night waking, because a baby who feeds to sleep keeps waking between sleep cycles. Actually Sleeping builds any weaning into a plan written for your baby, once your pediatrician agrees.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Hunger feeds and habit feeds
Young babies need to eat at night, and nothing on this page applies to them. Never restrict or stretch feeds for a newborn or a young baby, and never night wean a baby whose weight gain is in question.
In an older baby, night feeds tend to look like one of two things. A hunger feed is a full, active feed at a fairly predictable time, after which your baby goes straight back to sleep, while daytime intake stays steady. A habit feed is a few minutes of sucking until your baby is asleep again, often every 1.5 to 3 hours, close to the length of a sleep cycle. Babies who get a lot of their calories overnight often eat less, or more distractedly, during the day. Many babies have a mix of both.
Whether your baby still needs night feeds, and how many, is a question for your pediatrician. Babies who were born early, or who have had feeding or growth concerns, often keep them longer.
If you are up several times a night and hoping fewer feeds will mean more sleep, the feeds are usually only half the picture. Actually Sleeping fixes the other half, how your baby falls asleep, with a plan written for your baby and your pediatrician deciding the feeds.
Why cutting feeds alone rarely works
Every baby surfaces briefly between sleep cycles, all night long. A baby who falls asleep feeding at bedtime surfaces and asks for the same thing to get back to sleep. Take the feed away without changing how your baby falls asleep, and you usually trade feeding for rocking, holding or crying. That is why so many parents tell us night weaning “didn’t work”: the feed was never the only thing their baby relied on to get back to sleep. See the feed-to-sleep association.
Generic weaning schedules also assume an average baby. Your baby’s age, growth, number of feeds, breast or bottle, and the way they fall asleep all change what a sensible plan looks like. A schedule that suits one baby can leave another hungry, or simply move the crying to a different hour.
How Actually Sleeping handles night feeds
At Actually Sleeping, night feeds stay in a baby’s plan until the family’s pediatrician says otherwise, and the plan never forces dropping them. What changes first is how your baby falls asleep at bedtime, so the wakings between cycles stop needing a feed. Dr. Sam writes the plan for your baby, you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins adjust feeds and timings as things change. When your pediatrician clears it, any weaning is built into that same plan, at a pace that fits your baby and your milk supply.
Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own. You can hear from some of them in video reviews from families whose babies fed or rocked to sleep.
If you are breastfeeding
Dropping feeds suddenly can leave you engorged or with plugged ducts. If supply is a worry, talk with a lactation consultant before anything changes. Your comfort and supply are part of how a plan is paced.
When feeds come back in
Illness, a growth concern, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who is clearly hungry during the day despite extra offers. Feed, call the pediatrician, and adjust the plan later.
If night feeds and night waking have become tangled together in your house, book a free consultation and tell us your baby’s age and feeding pattern.

# Does a dream feed help a baby sleep longer?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/dream-feed-does-it-work/

Does a dream feed help a baby sleep longer?
Sometimes. A dream feed, feeding your baby around 10–11 p.m. without fully waking them, helps some babies between about 2 and 6 months shift their longest stretch to line up with yours, and does nothing or causes extra waking in others. It addresses hunger only. It does not help a baby who wakes because they need help falling back asleep.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What a dream feed is
You lift your sleeping baby roughly 2–3 hours after bedtime, usually just before you go to bed, feed them while they stay drowsy, and lay them back down. The idea is simple: a baby whose longest stretch runs 7 p.m. to midnight has spent it while you were awake. Topping up at 10:30 may move the next waking to 3 or 4 a.m.
What the evidence says
Not much. One small 1993 randomized study of 26 breastfed newborns combined a “focal feed” between 10 p.m. and midnight with gradually stretching middle-of-the-night feeds and strong day–night cues. By 8 weeks, all 13 babies in that group slept from midnight to 5 a.m., compared with 23% of controls, with no difference in 24-hour milk intake. The late feed was never tested alone, so nobody knows how much of the effect it was responsible for.
If you are considering a dream feed because your baby wakes often, it helps to know what it can and cannot fix. Actually Sleeping looks at the whole night, feeds and falling asleep together, and writes a plan for your baby rather than adding one more feed to try.
Who it tends to help, and who it does not
It is most likely to help a baby of about 2 to 6 months who still needs a night feed, feeds well while drowsy, and already falls asleep independently at bedtime. It is least likely to help an older baby who no longer needs night calories, a baby who will not feed while asleep or who wakes fully and stays up, and a baby who wakes every couple of hours.
That last group matters most. A dream feed addresses hunger. It does nothing for a baby who cannot link sleep cycles, which is the more common reason for frequent waking after 4 months. For those babies, a dream feed often just adds one more waking to the night. See why a 6 month old wakes every 2 hours.
Where it fits in a plan
This is why a dream feed works in one house and backfires in the next: it depends on your baby’s age, feeding needs and how they fall asleep. In the plans Dr. Sam writes at Actually Sleeping, a dream feed is used when it clearly earns its place for that baby and removed when it does not. The real work is teaching your baby to fall asleep on their own at bedtime, so the wakings between cycles stop needing you. Night feeds stay in the plan for as long as your pediatrician wants them.
Families get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins after it, so a feed that is not helping gets spotted in days, not weeks. See what families say in reviews from parents of 4 to 6 month olds.
Safety, if you do a late feed
Hold your baby in your arms, semi-upright, for the whole feed. Never prop a bottle and never feed a baby lying flat in the crib.
Afterwards, place your baby on their back in their own crib or bassinet.
Stay awake yourself. If you might doze off, feed sitting up in a lit room rather than in bed or on a sofa. The AAP lists sofas and armchairs among the most dangerous places to fall asleep with a baby.
If you are weighing up a dream feed because nights are long and broken, book a free consultation with Actually Sleeping and we will look at your baby’s feeds and sleep together.

# Is the pacifier helping or hurting my baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/pacifier-and-baby-sleep/

Is the pacifier helping or hurting my baby’s sleep?
It is helping if your baby takes it at bedtime and sleeps; the AAP recommends offering a pacifier at sleep onset because it is associated with a lower risk of SIDS. It is hurting if you are up several times a night replacing it. That is a sleep association, and the right fix depends on your baby’s age, so it belongs in a plan.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the AAP says
Offer a pacifier when placing your baby down for naps and at night. The protective association holds even if it falls out after the baby is asleep.
You do not need to put it back in once your baby is asleep, and you should not force it if your baby refuses.
If you are breastfeeding, wait until feeding is well established before introducing one.
Nothing attached: do not hang a pacifier around the neck or attach it to clothing, blankets or stuffed toys during sleep. Those are strangulation, suffocation and choking hazards.
Helping or hurting
HelpingHurting
Baby takes it at sleep onset, it falls out, baby stays asleepBaby wakes crying each time it falls out
Zero to one replacement per nightThree or more replacements a night, often every 45–120 minutes
Naps are a reasonable lengthNaps end at 30–40 minutes when the pacifier drops
The second column is a sleep association. Your baby fell asleep sucking, surfaced between cycles, and needs the same condition back to fall asleep again. It works exactly like feeding to sleep. The pacifier itself is not the problem; the fact that your baby cannot get back to sleep without it is.
A baby who needs the pacifier replaced all night is a solvable problem. Actually Sleeping fixes it with a plan written for your baby’s age, so the pacifier decision is made once, with your pediatrician’s input, not at 3 a.m.
Why there is no one right answer
Two things pull in different directions. The AAP links a pacifier at sleep onset with lower SIDS risk, and the NIH Safe to Sleep campaign says most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, and more than 90% before 6 months. At the same time, a baby who needs it replaced all night is not sleeping, and neither are you.
Age changes the picture. In practice, many babies have the hand control to find and replace a pacifier themselves from around 7 to 8 months; younger babies cannot. Some families keep it and work around it; others stop using it for sleep. That is a trade-off to weigh with your pediatrician for a baby under 6 months, not a decision to make alone at 3 a.m.
How Actually Sleeping handles it
When Actually Sleeping builds a plan for a pacifier baby, the decision to keep it, limit it or drop it is made with you and written into the plan, with your pediatrician’s view on the SIDS question for younger babies. Dr. Sam then sets how your baby will learn to settle without you replacing it, and you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins after that. Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own. You can hear from parents in reviews from families of 4 to 6 month olds.
Toddlers
Many families phase the pacifier out in the toddler years; ask your pediatrician or dentist about timing for your child. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, so a toddler’s pacifier can be part of the same plan.

Do I need to put the pacifier back in after my baby falls asleep?No. The AAP says it does not need to be reinserted once the baby is asleep, and the protective association holds even if it falls out. Do not force it if your baby refuses it.
At what age can a baby replace their own pacifier?In practice many babies manage it from around 7 to 8 months, once they have the hand control to pick it up and turn it around. There is no research-defined age, and younger babies cannot do it.

# When and how do I stop swaddling?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/swaddle-transition/

When and how do I stop swaddling?
Stop swaddling at the first signs your baby is trying to roll; that is the AAP’s guidance. Rolling usually happens around 3 to 4 months, but some babies start working on it as early as 2 months. Once rolling attempts have started, stop immediately and move to an arms-free wearable blanket. The unsettled sleep that often follows is the part a plan can fix.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why the timing is not flexible
Once a baby starts to roll, swaddling increases the risk of suffocation and strangulation; a swaddled baby who ends up on their stomach cannot use their arms to push up or turn. The AAP therefore says to stop when a baby looks like they are trying to roll, not once they have managed it.
Signs of rolling to watch for
Rolling to the side, or rocking side to side on the back.
Lifting head and shoulders high during tummy time, or pushing up on the arms.
Kicking the legs up and over, twisting the hips.
Regularly breaking out of the swaddle.
Any roll in either direction, even once, even by accident.
When you see any of these, the swaddle stops that night. Both arms out, in a regular, non-weighted wearable blanket (sleep sack).
The safety rule here is fixed. What happens to sleep afterwards is not, and that is the part Actually Sleeping fixes: a plan for your baby’s age that turns the end of the swaddle into the start of independent sleep.
Why sleep often falls apart afterwards
For many babies, the swaddle was doing a lot of the settling. It dampened the startle reflex, which starts to fade after about 2 months, and it gave a snug, familiar feeling at sleep onset. Take it away and some babies flail, startle and wake more for a few nights. Others keep waking for weeks, because the swaddle was one of the conditions they needed to fall asleep, and nothing has replaced it.
The timing makes it harder. Dropping the swaddle often lands near the 4-month sleep change, when sleep cycles mature and babies who rely on help to fall asleep start waking more often. Parents then change several things at once (more rocking, a later bedtime, a new product) and the baby ends up with more sleep associations, not fewer.
How Actually Sleeping uses this moment
The swaddle exit is a natural point to start putting your baby down awake, and in many Actually Sleeping plans it is the first step. Dr. Sam writes the plan around your baby’s age, feeds and how they currently fall asleep, you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins keep it on track. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage: foundations first, night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks. Parents who went through this exact change share their experience in reviews from families at the 4-month change.
What not to use
Weighted swaddles or weighted sleep sacks. The AAP advises against them; they can place too much pressure on a baby’s chest and lungs.
Positioners, wedges or rolled towels to keep a baby on their back. Nothing goes in the sleep space.
Any product that restrains the arms once rolling attempts have started. An arms-free sleep sack only.
Loose blankets as a substitute.
Keep placing your baby on their back for every sleep. Once your baby rolls both ways on their own, you do not have to turn them back over. More in safe sleep and sleep training.
If the swaddle is gone and sleep has not recovered, book a free consultation and we will look at what your baby needs now.

# Why does my baby wake 30–45 minutes after bedtime?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/false-starts-at-bedtime/

Why does my baby wake 30–45 minutes after bedtime?
A waking 30–45 minutes after bedtime is called a false start: your baby reached the end of the first sleep cycle and could not move into the next. The usual causes are falling asleep with help (feeding, rocking, a replaced pacifier), a last wake window that is too long or too short, or a bedtime early enough that the body treats it as a nap.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why it happens at exactly that time
A baby’s sleep cycle is typically about 50 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes in adults. At the end of the first one, every baby surfaces briefly. If conditions match what they were at sleep onset and sleep pressure is high, the baby slides back into deep sleep. If something has changed, or the drive to sleep is weak, they wake fully. How infant sleep cycles develop covers the mechanics.
The usual causes
CauseClues
Sleep associationBaby was fed, rocked or held to sleep; wakes crying and settles quickly with the same help
OvertiredFussy or wired before bed, asleep within a minute or two, wakes screaming
UndertiredTook 20+ minutes to fall asleep, or wakes happy and chatty
Bedtime treated as a napA very early bedtime, or a late nap that ended shortly before bed
DiscomfortGas, a burp, reflux symptoms, illness, a room that is too warm
EnvironmentEvening light, household noise, a sound machine that switches off
False starts are one of the most fixable patterns in baby sleep, and one of the most frustrating to troubleshoot, because several causes look alike. Actually Sleeping works out which ones apply to your baby and writes the plan around them.
Why guessing rarely fixes it
These causes overlap. An overtired baby who is also fed to sleep shows both sets of clues, and fixing one leaves the other. It is common to try moving bedtime, shortening a nap and adding a top-up feed all in the same week, and then be unable to tell which change did what. Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own. A schedule tweak also cannot fix a sleep association: if your baby needs a feed or a cuddle to fall asleep, they will ask for it again at the end of the first cycle whatever time bedtime is.
That is why false starts need a plan built for the individual baby: their age, feeding, temperament, how they currently fall asleep, and when your family’s evening actually happens.
How Actually Sleeping fixes false starts
False starts are usually among the first things to go in a Actually Sleeping plan, because the first skill taught is falling asleep independently at bedtime. Dr. Sam sets the last wake window and bedtime for your baby from your log, you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins adjust the timing as the pattern changes. Parents whose babies were fed or rocked to sleep describe the change in their video reviews.
We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. If it does not happen, you get a full refund.
When false starts mean something else
Under about 3–4 months, evening waking is common and developmental; at that age Actually Sleeping works on foundations rather than expecting long stretches. During a nap transition, the day reshuffles and false starts can come and go. And if your baby also snores, struggles to breathe or seems in pain lying down, that is a pediatrician question, not a schedule one.

# Why is my baby awake for hours in the middle of the night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/split-nights/

Why is my baby awake for hours in the middle of the night?
A baby who is wide awake and often cheerful for 1–3 hours in the middle of the night is having a split night. It usually means more time is being offered for sleep than your baby can fill: too much daytime sleep, a bedtime that is too early, or 13–14 hours in the crib for a baby who sleeps 11. The fix is a schedule matched to your baby’s real sleep need.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
How to recognize one
Awake for an hour or more, typically somewhere between midnight and 4 a.m.
Often calm: babbling, rolling around, practicing skills. Crying usually starts only once boredom sets in.
Feeding, rocking or holding does not bring sleep back quickly.
It happens most nights, at a similar time.
This is different from frequent brief wakings every 1.5–2 hours, which point to a sleep association instead. See waking every 2 hours.
Why it happens
Two systems keep a baby asleep: sleep pressure, which builds while awake and is spent in the first half of the night, and the body clock, which carries the second half. When a baby has slept a lot by day or gone to bed very early, pressure runs out before the clock takes over. The gap is the split.
Split nights are fixable. The answer is a schedule built for your baby’s real sleep need, not a chart, and that is what Dr. Sam sets in a Actually Sleeping plan and adjusts from your log every day.
The arithmetic behind it
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12–16 hours per 24 for babies 4–12 months and 11–14 hours for ages 1–2, naps included. Individual babies sit at different points in that range, and that is the catch. A schedule that is perfect for a baby who needs 15 hours leaves a baby who needs 13.5 with two hours to spare, and those hours turn up at 2 a.m.
ExampleOfferedActually sleepsResult
9-month-old, 3.5 h of naps, bed 6:30 p.m. to 7 a.m.16 hAbout 13.5 h2+ hours awake overnight
Same baby, 3 h of naps, bed 7:30 p.m. to 6:45 a.m.14.25 hAbout 13.5 hNight fills in
Why sample schedules make it worse
Most published schedules are built for an average baby. Followed closely, they can offer more sleep than your baby needs, and the usual response to a split night (sleeping in, an extra nap, an earlier bedtime “to catch up”) feeds the split. Other triggers pile on top:
Nap transitions. Hanging onto a nap your baby has outgrown is a classic cause. See nap transitions.
New motor skills. Crawling and standing get rehearsed at 2 a.m.
Jet lag or a clock change, which shift the body clock directly.
Catch-up sleep after illness, when long recovery naps linger after the illness is over.
Night feeds that anchor the waking in an older baby whose pediatrician has said they are optional.
How Actually Sleeping fixes split nights
Split nights are a schedule puzzle more than a behavior problem, and the answer is different for every baby. In a Actually Sleeping plan, Dr. Sam sets your baby’s schedule from their real sleep totals, then reviews the daily log each morning during the 1:1 check-ins and adjusts the timings as the pattern changes. Naps are coached until they are solid, so daytime sleep stops borrowing from the night. You also get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night. Parents of older babies talk about the change in reviews from families of 7 to 9 month olds.
If your baby is up for hours most nights, book a free consultation and bring a few days of sleep times with you.

Is a split night the same as a sleep regression?No. A regression is a burst of waking around a developmental change. A split night is one long wakeful period caused by more sleep opportunity than the baby needs, and it continues until the schedule changes.
Should I get my baby up and play during a split night?No. Treating it as daytime tends to teach the body clock to expect it. The lasting fix is the daytime schedule and bedtime, not what you do at 2 a.m., which is why a plan focuses there.
How long does it take to fix split nights?In practice, often 1–2 weeks once the schedule matches your baby’s actual sleep need. In a Actually Sleeping plan, Dr. Sam adjusts the timings daily from your log so that it gets there without guesswork.

# My baby will only sleep on me, not in the crib or bassinet. What do I do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib-or-bassinet/

My baby will only sleep on me, not in the crib or bassinet. What do I do?
This is normal in the first weeks. Whoever holds the baby must be fully awake; if you might doze, put your baby on their back in the crib or bassinet. After the newborn weeks it usually becomes a sleep association: a baby who falls asleep on you and wakes somewhere else protests the transfer. Teaching your baby to fall asleep in the crib itself is what ends it.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Safety first
Holding a sleeping baby while you are awake and alert is fine. The danger is you falling asleep. The AAP’s parent site says the risk is up to 67 times higher when infants sleep with someone on a couch, soft armchair or cushion. If you feel yourself fading, put the baby down on their back in the crib or bassinet, even if they cry, or hand them to another adult. A crying baby in a safe space is safe.
Do not solve the problem with inclined sleepers, loungers, nests, positioners, wedges, weighted sacks, or a swing for sleep. None is a safe sleep surface. The surface should be firm, flat and empty.
Why your baby objects to the crib
You are warm, moving and familiar; the crib is still, flat and cool. That contrast is biggest in the first 8–12 weeks.
The transfer wakes them. Newborns fall asleep through light, active (REM-like) sleep until about 3 months, so a put-down soon after they drift off often fails.
From about 4 months, it is a sleep association. Your baby fell asleep in your arms, surfaced between cycles, found the conditions changed and called for you.
A baby who only sleeps on you is a very fixable problem once the newborn weeks are past. Actually Sleeping teaches your baby to fall asleep in the crib itself, with a plan written for your baby and bootcamp-style coaching before the first night.
Why transfer tricks stop working
Waiting for deep sleep, warming the sheet, lowering feet first: these can buy a nap or two. They do not change the underlying pattern. Your baby still falls asleep in one place and wakes in another, so every sleep cycle is a fresh chance to notice. As sleep cycles mature around 4 months, the wakings usually get more frequent, not less. Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own.
The lasting fix is a baby who falls asleep in the crib itself, so there is no transfer at all. How to get there depends on your baby’s age, feeds, temperament and what they rely on now, which is why a plan has to be written for the individual baby.

# Why does my overtired baby fight sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/overtired-baby-fights-sleep/

Why does my overtired baby fight sleep?
When a baby stays awake well past the point their body was ready for sleep, many become more wired and harder to settle, not sleepier. The result looks backwards: the more tired the baby, the harder they fight. Overtiredness feeds itself through short naps and broken nights, and the lasting fix is a schedule and bedtime set for your baby’s age and actual sleep.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What “overtired” means
Sleep pressure builds the longer a baby is awake. Past a certain point, many babies get a second wind instead of settling. For parents the practical version is simple: a tired baby settles; an overtired one is wired, frantic and hard to console.
Tired versus overtired
TiredOvertired
Staring into space, quieter, less interested in toysCrying that escalates quickly, arching, stiffening
First yawn, slower movementsFrantic or jerky movements; pulling ears, rubbing eyes hard
Turning away from stimulationA burst of giddy energy in an older baby or toddler
Falls asleep in 5–15 minutesFights the put-down, or crashes in under 2 minutes and wakes 30–45 minutes later
From about 4–5 months, many babies skip the early cues entirely, so by the time you see a yawn the window has often passed.
Overtiredness is a symptom, and the cause differs from baby to baby. Actually Sleeping works out what is driving it for yours and sets a schedule and bedtime for them, instead of a one-size wake-window chart.
Why it becomes a cycle
Overtired babies take short naps, which leave them overtired for the next stretch. See 30-minute naps.
They often wake soon after bedtime. See false starts.
They wake more at night and earlier in the morning. See early morning waking.
Each bad stretch sets up the next one. Parents respond by rescuing naps with rocking, feeding or the car, which is reasonable on a hard day but means the baby never practises falling asleep alone. A few weeks in, the family has an overtired baby and a sleep association, and fixing one without the other does not hold.
When it is not overtiredness
“Overtired” gets blamed for nearly everything, which is one reason generic advice so often misses:
Undertired. A baby put down too soon also fights sleep, but is usually happy about it: playing, babbling, rolling.
Sleep association. If your baby only fights when put down awake and sleeps easily when fed or rocked, the issue is how they fall asleep, at any level of tiredness.
Evening fussiness in the first months. Fussing that typically peaks at about 3 hours a day around 6 weeks and declines by 3–4 months is common and not caused by the schedule. Long, inconsolable crying deserves a pediatrician’s opinion.
Pain or illness. A sudden change in a baby who normally settles well.
How Actually Sleeping breaks the cycle
Sorting out which of these is in play is most of the intake work at Actually Sleeping. Dr. Sam then sets the schedule for your baby’s age and actual sleep totals, not a chart’s average, and teaches your baby to fall asleep independently so naps can lengthen. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins to adjust timings, and naps are coached until they are solid. # How do I handle daycare naps when sleep training?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/daycare-naps-and-sleep-training/

How do I handle daycare naps when sleep training?
Daycare does not undo sleep training. Babies learn that different places have different rules, and nights carry the most weight. What matters is a home plan built around the daycare’s real routine, a bedtime that flexes with the day’s naps, and a center that follows safe-sleep rules. Actually Sleeping builds plans around daycare schedules from the start.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why daycare does not undo your work
In practice, babies distinguish settings well. A baby who is rocked by a caregiver at daycare can still fall asleep independently at home, as long as home stays consistent. Nights carry the most weight; get those solid and imperfect daycare naps are workable.
Why daycare naps are different
The room is busy. Light, noise and other babies make it harder to link sleep cycles, so naps are often shorter than at home.
Caregivers look after several babies at once. They cannot run a one-to-one plan, and a reasonable request is followed far more often than a long protocol.
Schedules are set for the room. Infant rooms are often flexible; toddler rooms usually run one group nap around midday, sometimes before a child is ready for one nap.
The car ride home can turn into a late nap that pushes bedtime back.
Weekends look different. Many daycare babies nap longer at home on Saturday and Sunday, so Monday’s schedule starts from a different place than Friday’s.
The result is that every day’s total sleep is a little different, and the evening has to absorb it. A fixed bedtime from a sample schedule does not; a bedtime set from that day’s actual naps does.
Daycare is not a reason to put off fixing sleep. Actually Sleeping builds the home plan around your center’s real schedule, so nights get solid even when daycare naps are imperfect.
Safe sleep at daycare is not negotiable
Ask every center about its safe-sleep policy. Every nap should be on the back, on a firm, flat surface in a crib or play yard, with nothing but a fitted sheet. Safe sleep guidance says sitting devices such as swings, bouncers and car seats are not for routine sleep; if a baby falls asleep in one, they should be moved to a flat sleep space.
Why generic advice falls short here
Advice written for a baby at home all day does not account for a center’s routine, a two-parent commute, short weekday naps and long weekend ones. The plan has to start from your actual week: when your baby is dropped off, when the room naps, how long naps really are, and when you get home. Starting sleep training and daycare in the same week also makes it hard to know what is working.

# How do I keep my baby sleeping while traveling or changing time zones?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-travel-and-time-zones/

How do I keep my baby sleeping while traveling or changing time zones?
Keep sleep safe first: a crib or play yard, your baby on their back, nothing else in it, and never an adult bed or sofa. Across time zones, adult data suggest the body clock shifts about 1 hour a day after flying east and a little faster after flying west. A baby who already falls asleep independently usually copes with travel far better.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Safe sleep away from home
Same rules as home: on the back, on a firm, flat surface, alone, nothing else in the sleep space.
Bring or request a crib or play yard that meets current safety standards. Inspect a hotel or rental crib: firm, snug-fitting mattress, no broken or missing parts, no added padding. Use a play yard as the manufacturer supplied it, with no extra mattress or padding added.
Not an adult bed, sofa, or cushion nest, even for one night. Couches and armchairs are never safe places for babies to sleep.
Car seats and strollers are for travel. Sleeping in a car seat while riding is expected; when you arrive, move your baby to a firm, flat sleep surface as soon as you can.
Scan the room: blind cords, loose cables, anything a baby can reach from the crib. Never drape a cover over the crib.
If your baby already struggles to sleep at home, travel tends to make it louder. Actually Sleeping fixes the underlying sleep, so a trip becomes a few off nights rather than a new problem to unpick.
What travel does to sleep
Travel removes the cues your baby relies on: their room, their light, their routine, often their schedule. A baby who falls asleep on their own in their crib usually carries that skill to a play yard in a hotel. A baby who needs feeding, rocking or holding to fall asleep needs the same help in a strange room, more often, and that help easily becomes the new normal by the end of the trip.
Time zones
The body clock does not reset when the plane lands. Light, meals and activity move it a little each day. Adult data from the CDC suggest the clock shifts about 1 hour a day after flying east and about 1.5 hours a day after flying west. Eastward travel (bedtime arrives before the body is ready) is usually harder than westward (early mornings for a few days), because the body clock shifts later more easily than earlier. Morning light helps after flying east. There is little research in babies, so expect variation.
Whether to stay on home time or switch to local time depends on the size of the change, the length of the trip, and your baby. A short trip across one or two zones is a different problem from two weeks across six.
In transit
On planes and long drives, sleep happens where it can: feeding, holding and motion are all fine while traveling. Sedating medicines are not a travel tool; see over-the-counter medicines and infant sleep.
How Actually Sleeping families handle trips
Families working with Actually Sleeping plan upcoming trips with their coach: when to travel relative to the start of the plan, which time to keep, and how to get back to baseline at home. Where there is a choice, a plan usually leaves about two weeks between the start of sleep training and a trip. Because Dr. Sam writes the plan for your baby and check-ins are daily and 1:1, the plan can flex around the trip rather than being thrown out by it. Parents talk about life after coaching in our client video reviews.

# How do I adjust my baby’s sleep for daylight saving time?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/daylight-saving-time-baby-sleep/

How do I adjust my baby’s sleep for daylight saving time?
The clock change moves your baby’s schedule by an hour that their body clock has not moved. In spring, bedtime arrives before your baby feels tired; in fall, your baby is tired early and wakes an hour early. Light is the main thing that moves the body clock, and a baby who already falls asleep independently adjusts with far less fuss.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the clock change does
Your baby’s body clock does not read the wall clock. After the spring change, a 7 p.m. bedtime feels like 6 p.m. to the body, so falling asleep is harder and mornings run later. After the fall change, 7 p.m. feels like 8 p.m., so your baby is tired early and up an hour early. Fall is the one parents dread, because nobody wants a 5 a.m. start.
What moves the body clock
Light is the strongest signal. The CDC notes that morning light shifts the body clock earlier and evening light shifts it later. Meals and activity are timing cues too. That is why the clock change interacts with everything else in your baby’s day: a bright evening in spring pushes the clock later just when you want bedtime earlier, and a dark fall morning does little to stop a 5 a.m. wake-up.
A baby who can fall asleep on their own usually takes a clock change in stride. If every schedule change knocks your baby off course, that is the problem Actually Sleeping fixes, with a plan written for your baby.
Why some babies struggle more than others
Babies who need help to fall asleep. A harder bedtime means more rocking or feeding, and those habits can outlast the clock change.
Early risers. In fall, a baby who already wakes at 6 can lock in a 5 a.m. start. See early morning waking.
Families with fixed daycare times, where the day cannot shift with the baby.
Babies in a nap transition, where the schedule is already unsettled.
Generic shift charts assume a baby who falls asleep easily and has a predictable day. For a baby who does not, the clock change is often just the trigger for a problem that was already there.
How Actually Sleeping handles the clock change
Families in a Actually Sleeping plan get the clock change worked into their baby’s schedule by Dr. Sam, with timings adjusted in the daily 1:1 check-ins rather than guessed from a chart. The deeper fix is the one Actually Sleeping teaches first: a baby who can fall asleep independently handles a one-hour shift with far less fuss, because the only thing that changed is the time. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night of any plan. You can hear from families in our 129 client video reviews.
What to expect
In practice most babies settle within 3–7 days after a clock change. Naps may be a little off during that week, and bedtimes may take longer. A baby whose sleep was already fragile may take longer, and new habits started during the adjustment week, such as extra rocking or a feed back to sleep at 5 a.m., can stick. If sleep has not settled after a couple of weeks, the clock change is rarely the real cause; it has simply exposed how your baby falls asleep.

# My baby’s sleep fell apart after being sick. How do I get back on track?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-after-illness/

My baby’s sleep fell apart after being sick. How do I get back on track?
While your baby is sick, comfort comes first: hold, feed and respond as much as needed, and follow your pediatrician’s advice. Once your baby is fever-free (a day without fever is a common rule of thumb), eating and drinking normally and back to themselves by day, sleep can return to normal. The habits that crept in during the illness are the part that needs a plan.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
During the illness
Respond freely. Extra feeds, cuddles and night checks are appropriate. Sick babies need fluids and may eat less by day and more at night.
Go to them rather than bringing them to you. If you want to be close, sleep on a mattress in your baby’s room instead of bringing a sick baby into an adult bed.
Keep sleep safe. Congested babies still sleep flat on their back in an empty crib. Inclined or tilted sleep surfaces are not safe, so do not prop the mattress, use a wedge or pillow, or let your baby sleep in a car seat or swing. Saline drops and gentle suction with a bulb syringe, plus a humidifier if the air is dry, are the usual comfort measures.
Medicines: fever and pain relievers only as your pediatrician directs for your baby’s age and weight. The AAP does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children under 4. More in over-the-counter medicines and infant sleep.
Let them sleep more. Extra and longer naps are part of recovery.
Comfort comes first while your baby is sick, and nothing on this page changes that. Once your baby is well, getting sleep back is the part Actually Sleeping helps with, through a plan for your baby and daily check-ins.
Call the pediatrician
Call right away for a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby 3 months or younger, even with no other symptoms. Also call for trouble breathing or fast, labored breathing; refusing feeds or far fewer wet diapers; a baby who is hard to wake or unusually limp; ear pulling with fever; or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better. Ear infections often cause pain and trouble sleeping, and only an examination can confirm one.
How to know your baby is well enough
ReadyNot yet
No fever for about a day without fever medicine (a common rule of thumb; ask your pediatrician)Fever within the last day
Eating and drinking close to normalPoor intake or fewer wet diapers
Playing and alert during the dayClingy, listless or clearly uncomfortable
A lingering mild cough or runny nose onlyBreathing that looks like work; untreated ear infection
If you are unsure, ask the pediatrician: “Is there any medical reason not to go back to our normal sleep routine?”
Why sleep does not bounce back on its own
A week of illness changes a lot: night feeds come back, naps get long, and your baby gets used to being held or fed back to sleep. Those were the right responses while your baby was sick. Once they are well, the body has relearned a new pattern, and it tends to continue. Parents then try to undo it gradually, which often drags the disruption out for weeks.
If your baby never slept independently before the illness, there is nothing to go back to. The illness simply made an existing problem louder, and that is a first plan, not a reset.
How Actually Sleeping handles illness
Families in an active Actually Sleeping plan pause during illness and pick up the same plan when the baby is well, with Dr. Sam confirming the restart in the daily 1:1 check-in. For families starting fresh, Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby once they are healthy, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and night feeds kept as long as your pediatrician wants. In the first daycare winter, colds can arrive every few weeks, and the plan is built to restart after each one. Families describe the experience in our client video reviews.

# How do I handle separation anxiety at bedtime?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/separation-anxiety-at-bedtime/

How do I handle separation anxiety at bedtime?
Separation anxiety is a normal stage that usually starts between 8 and 12 months, peaks between 10 and 18 months, and tapers off in the second half of the second year. Bedtime is the longest separation of the day, so that is where it shows. A predictable, confident response lowers distress; a response that changes from night to night tends to keep it going.

Why it shows up at bedtime
Somewhere between 8 and 12 months, babies grasp that you still exist when you are out of sight, but not yet when, or whether, you will come back. Bedtime is the longest separation of the day, so that is where the protest lands. It is a sign of healthy attachment, not a sleep problem in itself.
AgeWhat it often looks like
8–12 months (onset)Crying when you leave the room, clinging at put-down, new night waking
Up to about 18 months (peak window)Loud protest, standing and calling, wanting you to stay
2–3 yearsStalling, fears, leaving the room if in a bed
Separation anxiety is not a reason to wait, and it does not have to mean months of hard bedtimes. Actually Sleeping builds a plan around this stage, with a parent close by at first and a predictable response every night.
How a normal stage turns into a sleep problem
The anxiety itself passes. What tends to stay are the responses that grew up around it:
Staying until your child is asleep, or lying down with them, as a new nightly habit.
Night feeds or rocking that had already ended coming back.
Bed-sharing as a response, which the AAP advises against for infants.
Responding differently each night, so your child keeps testing which version they will get.
Moving to a bed, which removes the containment of a crib at the very stage a child is most unsettled.
Each of these is understandable at 11 p.m. with a crying baby. Together they teach a child that bedtime is uncertain, which is exactly what separation anxiety feeds on. That is why separation anxiety lasts months in some families and a few weeks in others.
A comfort object can help some children, but only after 12 months. The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations cover the first year, and until then the crib stays empty.
Is this a reason to delay sleep training?
No. If your baby does not yet fall asleep independently, a plan built around this stage, with a parent close by at first and predictable returns, tends to lower bedtime distress because your child learns exactly what happens next. At Actually Sleeping the approach is “not cry it out, not wait it out.” Dr. Sam writes a custom plan that fits your child’s age and temperament, you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins adjust how close you stay and for how long. Parents of babies this age describe it in reviews from families of 10 to 12 month olds. Related: the 8–10 month regression and the 18 month regression.
Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, so the same approach covers a toddler whose separation protests have turned into long bedtimes.
When to talk to the pediatrician
If the anxiety is extreme throughout the day, lasts many weeks without easing, follows a major upheaval, or comes with signs of illness or pain at night.

# When should I move my toddler from a crib to a bed?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/crib-to-toddler-bed-when/

When should I move my toddler from a crib to a bed?
As late as you safely can: ideally close to age 3, when a child can understand and follow a “stay in bed” rule. Move sooner only if your toddler keeps climbing out despite a lowered mattress and a bare crib, or has outgrown the crib’s height limit. A new sibling, an 18-month or 2-year regression, or bedtime resistance are not reasons to switch, and usually get worse in a bed.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why waiting helps
A crib does the job of impulse control for a child who does not yet have it. In practice, many children under about 2.5–3 cannot reliably stay in an open bed because they have been told to, however well they understand the words. Families who switch at 18–24 months often trade one problem for a bigger one: see my toddler won’t stay in bed.
Good reasons and poor reasons
Good reasons to movePoor reasons to move
Repeatedly climbing out despite the safety steps belowA new baby needs the crib (use a second crib or a bassinet for the newborn)
Taller than the limit in the crib’s manual, or about 35 inches (89 cm), the height by which MedlinePlus says children should no longer use a cribTurning 2
Close to 3, asking for a bed, following simple rules by dayFighting bedtime or waking at night
Night toilet training that requires getting to the bathroomA regression, a move or a new daycare in the same month
Many families consider a bed because bedtime has become a battle. That battle can be fixed in the crib, and Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, so it is worth fixing the sleep before changing the bed.
If your toddler is climbing out
Lower the mattress to its lowest setting.
A regular sleep sack limits how high a leg can lift. Not a weighted one.
Remove footholds: bumpers, large toys, anything inside or beside the crib that works as a step.
Do not use crib tents or homemade covers. The CPSC has recalled crib tents over strangulation and entrapment hazards and told parents to stop using them.
If your child still gets out, the crib is no longer safe, and a bed or a mattress on the floor is the safer choice.
Make the room the crib
Once a child can leave the bed, the whole bedroom has to be safe to be in alone:
Anchor dressers, shelves and televisions to the wall.
Secure blind cords and electrical cords; cover outlets.
Remove small objects, medicines, toiletries and anything climbable.
Put a gate at the bedroom door or the top of the stairs; lock windows or fit guards.
Choose a low bed or toddler bed, with guardrails made for the purpose, away from windows.
Why the switch so often goes wrong
Many toddlers stay put for the first few nights, then discover they can get up, and bedtime turns into a game of returns. Parents who moved to fix bedtime resistance find the resistance now has legs. The bed did not cause the problem; it removed the one thing containing it. What actually settles bedtime is a child who can fall asleep on their own and a limit both parents hold the same way.
How Actually Sleeping handles beds and cribs
Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, in cribs and in beds. Where a family has a choice, the plan Dr. Sam writes usually keeps the crib until sleep is solid, and builds the move to a bed in later if it is needed. For a toddler already in a bed, the plan covers getting out of bed as well as falling asleep, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Parents of toddlers share their experience in reviews from families of children 12 months and older.

Frequently asked
What is the best age to switch from a crib to a bed?For most children, close to 3. Earlier only for safety reasons such as climbing out despite a lowered mattress, or outgrowing the crib’s height limit.
Should I move my toddler to a bed before the new baby arrives?Preferably not for that reason. If the move is truly needed, do it at least 2–3 months before the birth, or wait until a few months after. A second crib or a bassinet avoids rushing.
Is a toddler bed or a twin bed better?Either works. What matters is that it is low, has appropriate guardrails and sits in a fully childproofed room, with furniture anchored to the wall.

# Can I sleep train a premature baby or NICU graduate?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-a-premature-or-nicu-baby/

Can I sleep train a premature baby or NICU graduate?
Yes, in most cases, once your pediatrician confirms your baby is ready. Use corrected age (counted from the due date, not the birth date): gentle habit-shaping can begin around 10–12 weeks corrected, and fuller sleep training around 4–6 months corrected, provided weight gain is steady and any medical issues are stable. Night feeds stay until your pediatrician says they can go, which is often later for babies born early.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist. Readiness, feeding and any medical question for a baby born early belong to your pediatrician or neonatal follow-up team.
Corrected age, and why it matters
Corrected (adjusted) age is your baby’s age from birth minus the weeks they arrived early (40 minus the gestational age at birth). A baby born 8 weeks early who is 6 months old is about 4 months corrected. The AAP recommends using corrected age during the first 2 years to judge development, so it makes sense to use it for wake windows, nap counts and sleep expectations too.
Corrected ageWhat is realistic
Before the due date to about 10 weeksFeed on your team’s schedule, safe sleep, day–night cues. No training.
10–16 weeksConsistent routine, practice putting down awake, feeds kept as directed
4–6 monthsIndependent sleep onset; night feeds per pediatrician
6 months and beyondFull sleep training; night weaning when cleared
Questions for your pediatrician first
Is weight gain on track on my baby’s own growth curve?
How many night feeds does my baby still need, and may I stop waking them to feed?
Is fortified milk or a special formula schedule a factor overnight?
Are reflux, breathing or oxygen needs, or apnea history stable enough for a sleep plan?
Is there any reason my baby should not be given a few minutes to settle?
Babies born early can learn to sleep well. Actually Sleeping builds plans on corrected age and around your pediatrician’s feeding instructions, so the plan fits your baby rather than a term-born average.
What is different for NICU graduates
Feeding comes first, longer. Some preemies need scheduled feeds, including overnight, well past the point a term baby would. Never stretch or drop a feed without clearance.
Home sleep is on the back. Babies are sometimes placed on their stomach or side in the NICU under continuous monitoring. At home, NIH safe sleep guidance says all babies, including those born preterm, sleep on their backs until 1 year: firm and flat, nothing in the crib, no positioners or nests, no inclines.
Medical equipment. A baby discharged on oxygen or a prescribed monitor needs a plan built with the medical team. The AAP and NIH advise against using heart, breathing or motion monitors as a way to reduce SIDS risk; they do not replace safe sleep.
Light and noise. After weeks in a bright, alarm-filled unit, some babies sleep through anything and others startle easily.
Reflux questions are common. Babies with reflux still sleep on their backs. See sleep training a baby with reflux.
Parents carry the NICU with them. Being hyper-alert to every sound is a reasonable response to what you lived through. A plan with defined check-ins lets you respond on purpose rather than on adrenaline.
Why a generic plan does not fit
Most sleep advice is written by birth age, for babies born at term. Followed as written, it can push a preemie too early, or stretch feeds a pediatrician wants kept. A baby born early needs a plan built on corrected age, around the pediatrician’s feeding instructions, and paced to their growth.
How Actually Sleeping builds a plan for a baby born early

Dr. Sam writes each NICU graduate’s plan around the pediatrician’s feeding instructions: schedules run on corrected age, night feeds are written in at the times your pediatrician wants, the approach starts with more parental presence and smaller steps, and the plan pauses for illness or a slowdown in growth. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins after it. Parents of young babies describe the experience in reviews from families of newborns to 3 month olds. Twins born early have their own notes in sleep training twins.
When the plan waits
Faltering weight gain, a recent hospital readmission, unstable breathing, an upcoming procedure, or a pediatrician who says not yet. In those cases the medical team’s timing comes first.
If you are ready to work on sleep with a baby born early, book a free consultation and bring your pediatrician’s feeding instructions.

# Is there a 2 year old sleep regression?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/2-year-old-sleep-regression/

Is there a 2 year old sleep regression?
Yes. Around age 2, many toddlers who slept well start fighting bedtime, refusing the nap, waking at night or rising early. It is driven by development (independence, language, imagination and new fears) and often by a change such as a new sibling, toilet training or a move to a bed. Nearly all 2-year-olds still need their nap, and habits started during the regression often outlast it.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What it looks like
Bedtime stretches from 20 minutes to an hour of requests: water, another book, a different blanket.
Nap refusal: playing or shouting through the whole nap period.
Night waking with calling out, or appearing at your bedside if in a bed.
New fear of the dark, shadows or being alone.
Waking for the day at 5 a.m.
Why now
DriverWhat is going on
Independence and limit-testingYour child is learning that words and protest can change what happens
Imagination and first fearsYour child can now picture things that are not there, and the dark is where they do it
Second molars (about 23–31 months for the lower and 25–33 months for the upper, per the ADA)A few uncomfortable days around eruption; pain relief only as your pediatrician directs
Big changes: sibling, toilet training, new room, new daycareSleep is where a toddler’s stress often shows first
Crib-to-bed moveThe bed removes the containment a crib provided. See when to move to a bed
Schedule driftA nap that runs too late or too long, or a bedtime that no longer matches sleep need
Toddlers at this age respond to clear, consistent limits, which makes the 2-year stage a good time to work on sleep. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on and writes those limits for your child.
The nap is not finished
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 11–14 hours of sleep per 24 for ages 1–2 and 10–13 hours for ages 3–5, naps included. A large review found fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2, while 94% have stopped by 5. A 2-year-old refusing the nap for a week or two is on strike, not finished. Dropping the nap too early usually makes evenings and nights harder, not easier.
Why it sticks
The development behind the regression settles. What lasts is what grew up around it: lying with your child until they fall asleep, extra books every night, a later bedtime, a nap that was dropped. If it has gone on longer than six weeks, it has usually stopped being a regression and become the new routine. Bedtime “scripts” and charts from the internet often fail here because they assume an average toddler, and because two tired parents rarely hold them the same way.
How Actually Sleeping handles the 2-year-old stage
Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, and a plan at this age is mostly about clear, kind limits that both parents hold the same way, set for your child’s temperament, nap and bedtime. Dr. Sam writes the plan, you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins keep both parents consistent while it settles. More than 700 families have been coached, and parents of toddlers share their experience in reviews from families of children 12 months and older.

Regression or something else?
Ask your pediatrician about regular snoring, mouth breathing or pauses in breathing, restless sleep with sweating, pain, or a sleep change alongside loss of skills. Night terrors (screaming while still asleep, no memory in the morning) are different from nightmares and are worth mentioning too. Related: the 18 month regression.

Frequently asked
How long does the 2 year sleep regression last?There is no research-defined length. It lasts longer when new habits, such as lying with the child until asleep, begin during it. Once it has gone on for more than a few weeks it has usually become the new routine, and that is what a Actually Sleeping plan addresses.
Is my 2 year old ready to stop napping?Probably not. In a large review, fewer than 2.5% of children had stopped napping before 2; most stop during the preschool years. A week or two of refusal is usually a nap strike, not the end of the nap.
Should I move my 2 year old to a bed during the regression?No, unless there is a safety reason such as climbing out despite a lowered mattress. Changing beds in the middle of a regression usually makes both harder.
Why is my 2 year old suddenly scared at bedtime?Imagination develops quickly around this age and fears come with it. Take the fear seriously and keep the response calm and predictable. If fears are intense or show up during the day too, mention them to your pediatrician.

# What does a baby sleep consultant actually do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/what-does-a-baby-sleep-consultant-do/

What does a baby sleep consultant actually do?
A baby sleep consultant assesses how your baby falls asleep, wakes and naps, writes a plan to change the behavioral parts, and supports you while you carry it out. Good consultants screen for medical red flags and refer you to your pediatrician when they find them. They do not diagnose, prescribe, or make feeding decisions that belong to your pediatrician.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The usual sequence
Intake. A questionnaire or call covering age (and corrected age if your baby was born early), how your baby falls asleep, what happens at each waking, feeding, naps, the sleep space, health history and what you have already tried.
Assessment. The consultant looks for the drivers: a sleep association, a schedule mismatch, an overtired or undertired baby, early morning light, or something that needs a doctor rather than a plan.
The plan. A written document covering the routine, the schedule, how you respond to wakings, how night feeds are handled (with your pediatrician’s input), and how naps will be approached.
Support while you do it. This is where consultants differ most, and where results are won or lost.
Adjustment. Babies rarely follow a script exactly. The consultant reads your notes and changes timing or responses as needed.
Wrap-up. Guidance for what comes next: nap transitions, illness, travel, a new sibling.
At Actually Sleeping, Dr. Sam does every one of these steps personally. The plan is written from scratch for your baby, you get bootcamp-style coaching before night one, and daily 1:1 check-ins continue until nights and naps are solid.
What a consultant brings that a book does not
Pattern recognition. Someone who has worked with many babies can often tell from a short description whether an early waking is a schedule problem or a light problem, or whether a setback on night 4 is normal. The value is less in knowing the method and more in knowing which detail to change for your baby, today.
What a consultant should not do
Diagnose. Snoring, breathing pauses, poor weight gain, reflux symptoms and suspected allergies belong with your pediatrician. See sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist.
Recommend medication or supplements for sleep. Questions about medicines go to your pediatrician or pharmacist.
Override your pediatrician on feeding. Whether your baby still needs night feeds is a growth and health question.
Bend safe sleep rules. The AAP advises a firm, flat, non-inclined surface, on the back, without soft bedding, and says weighted swaddles and weighted objects on or near the baby are not safe. A plan should never work around these.
What it is like for you
You still do the nights. A consultant does not usually come to your home and put your baby down; you do it, following the plan, and report what happened. That is deliberate. Your baby is learning to fall asleep with you as the parent in the room, and you are learning what to do the next time sleep goes sideways. A short daily log is what lets a consultant adjust the plan instead of guessing.

# How do I choose a baby sleep consultant? Questions to ask before you hire
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-choose-a-baby-sleep-consultant/

How do I choose a baby sleep consultant? Questions to ask before you hire
Ask every consultant the same questions and compare the answers in writing: Is there a written guarantee and exactly what does it say? Who writes the plan? What are their credentials? How much coaching, and for how long? What method, and how much crying? What ages do they work with? How are their reviews verified? Vague answers are an answer.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The questions
1. Is there a written guarantee, and what exactly does it say?
Ask to see the wording. A useful guarantee names a measurable outcome (for example, hours of night sleep), a time frame, what you have to do to qualify, and what happens if it is not met. “We guarantee you’ll be happy” or “support until it works” are not outcome guarantees. Without an outcome guarantee, the risk that the plan does not work sits entirely with you. More detail: what a sleep-training guarantee should say.
2. Who writes the plan?
A named person reading your intake, or an age-based template with your baby’s name added? Ask: “If two families with 6-month-olds came to you this week, how different would their plans be?”
3. What are their credentials?
Sleep consulting has no required license. Ask which training they completed, whether they hold any licensed health care credential, and what that credential does and does not cover. See what credentials a sleep consultant should have.
4. How much coaching, and for how long?
How thoroughly do they prepare you before the first night?
How often do they check in after that: daily, every few days, weekly?
Through what channel, and how fast do they reply?
Does support end on a fixed date, or when sleep is solid? Are naps included?
5. What approach do they use, and is crying involved?
Ask them to describe night one in plain words: where you are and what you do when your baby cries. Most changes to sleep involve some protest, because your baby is learning something new. The honest answer describes how much, and what you do about it. Be wary of “no tears, ever” and of an approach that does not fit your limits. See do sleep consultants use cry it out.
6. What ages do they work with?
Ask what they do with a newborn (foundations, not training), with a 4-month-old, and with a toddler in a big bed. A consultant who works across ages should explain how the plan changes with each.
7. How are their reviews verified?
Testimonials on a website are chosen by the business. Ask whether reviews are from real, identifiable clients (video reviews help), whether any are collected by an independent service that confirms each reviewer was a paying client, and how recent they are.

Four more questions worth asking
What does your intake ask about health? Look for questions on growth, feeding, reflux, prematurity, snoring and breathing.
How do you handle night feeds? The right answer defers to your pediatrician.
Do your plans follow AAP safe sleep guidance? Back to sleep, firm flat surface, nothing soft or weighted in the sleep space.
Have you ever told a family you could not help them? A consultant who screens is a consultant who expects to deliver.
What should decide it

# Sleep course vs app vs 1:1 sleep consultant: which is right for my family?

Sleep course vs app vs 1:1 sleep consultant: which is right for my family?
Pick by how much personalization, coaching and accountability you want. Books and self-paced courses give you a method to apply yourself. Apps track sleep and suggest timing. Group programs add shared questions and answers. A 1:1 consultant writes a plan for your baby and adjusts it daily. A night nurse is overnight newborn care, not sleep teaching.

Where the self-directed options fall short
Books, courses and apps all hand the hardest part back to you. They describe a method for an age band, and you decide what to do when your baby does something the method did not describe. That usually happens on the second or third night, at 2 a.m., when you are least able to judge it. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried one or more of these. What was missing was not information. It was a plan that fit their baby, coaching that prepared them for those moments, and someone to adjust it every day.
What only 1:1 coaching gives you
A plan written for your baby, from age, feeding, temperament, how your baby falls asleep now and your family’s schedule.
Someone on the first night, when plans most often wobble.
Daily adjustment, so a detail that is not working is changed the next day instead of after a week of guessing.
Help with complicating factors: reflux under treatment, prematurity, twins, room sharing, a toddler out of the crib, daycare naps.
Accountability for the result. With a written guarantee, the outcome is the coach’s responsibility as well as yours.
Where overnight newborn care fits
A night nurse or overnight newborn carer gives you rest in the first weeks, which can be invaluable after a difficult birth or with multiples. It does not change how your baby falls asleep. Many families use overnight care early and add a sleep consultant for foundations or for changing sleep later. See consultant vs night nurse vs doula.
The evidence behind every category
The behavioral methods behind all of these are well studied. A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found 94% reported behavioral interventions effective. The difference between formats is how reliably a family gets the method right for their baby and stays consistent long enough for it to work.
