# What are the red flags when hiring a baby sleep consultant?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-red-flags/

What are the red flags when hiring a baby sleep consultant?
Walk away from a consultant who bends AAP safe sleep rules, suggests medication or supplements for sleep, tells you to drop night feeds without your pediatrician, diagnoses medical problems, promises results without written terms, will not describe how much crying is involved, or pressures you to sign before you understand what is included.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Safety red flags (disqualifying)
Anything that conflicts with safe sleep. The AAP advises that babies sleep on their back, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface, without soft toys, pillows, blankets or other bedding. It says weighted swaddles, weighted clothing and weighted objects on or near the baby are not safe, and that there is no evidence that commercial devices marketed to reduce the risk of SIDS do so. A plan that uses any of these, or that props or inclines a baby, is not a plan to follow.
Medication or supplement suggestions for sleep. Melatonin, antihistamines and “natural” sleep products are not a coaching tool. Questions about medicines go to your pediatrician or pharmacist. See is melatonin safe for babies.
Dropping night feeds on the consultant’s say-so. Whether a baby still needs to eat at night depends on age and growth, and that is your pediatrician’s call.
Diagnosing. “It’s silent reflux,” “it’s a tongue tie,” “it’s sleep apnea.” A consultant who hears snoring, breathing pauses or poor weight gain should send you to your pediatrician, not name a condition.
Sleep training a newborn. Newborn work should be foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine. Not leaving a newborn to cry and not stretching feeds.
Honesty red flags
“Guaranteed” in the ads, nothing in writing. If a result is promised, the exact words should be in the agreement you sign.
Medical-sounding titles that are not medical. “Sleep doctor” or “pediatric sleep specialist” from someone who is not a physician or a sleep-medicine clinician. Ask what the credential is and who issued it.
“No tears, ever.” Most babies protest when something about bedtime changes. An honest consultant tells you how much to expect and what you will do about it.
Vague about the approach. If they cannot describe night one in plain words, you will be guessing when it arrives.
Reviews you cannot check. Only first names, no dates, no way to tell whether the reviewer was a client.
Claims that sound like research but have no source. Ask where a number came from.
Process red flags
No health questions at intake. A good intake asks about growth, feeding, reflux, prematurity and breathing.
The same plan for every baby of the same age. Then you are paying for a template, not a consultant.
Support that disappears after day one. Ask how often they check in, through what channel, and until when.
Pressure. “Only two spots left today” or a discount that expires in an hour. You should be able to read the agreement and sleep on it.
Telling you to stop asking your pediatrician. A consultant works alongside your pediatrician, not instead of them.
The green flags that matter
A plan written for your baby by a named person.
Intensive, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily check-ins after it.
A measurable result guaranteed in writing, with a refund if it is not met.
An intake with real health questions and a willingness to say “check with your pediatrician first.”
A plain description of how crying is handled, matched to your limits.
Reviews from identifiable families, with dates.

# Do sleep consultants use cry it out?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/do-sleep-consultants-use-cry-it-out/

Do sleep consultants use cry it out?
Some do, many do not. Approaches run from full extinction (cry it out) to graduated checks, staying in the room, and bedtime fading. Research supports several of these, not only cry it out. Ask any consultant to describe night one in plain words, including how much crying to expect and what you will do. Actually Sleeping does not use cry it out.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The main approaches
ApproachIn one lineCrying
Extinction (“cry it out”)Baby down awake; parent does not return until morning or a planned feedMost intense
Graduated extinction (timed checks)Brief parent checks at lengthening intervalsStill some crying; less intense for many parents
Parent in the room (chair or camping out)Parent stays near the crib and withdraws graduallyUsually some protest; lasts longer overall
Bedtime fadingBedtime matched to real sleepiness, then brought earlierOften less; slower
Pick up, put downLift until calm, return to the crib, repeatVaries; can overstimulate some babies
More on each: cry it out, timed checks, the chair method, bedtime fading, gentle methods compared.
What the research says
A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found the strongest support for unmodified extinction and preventive parent education, with further support for graduated extinction and bedtime fading with positive routines. A randomized trial of 43 infants aged 6 to 16 months compared graduated extinction and bedtime fading with a sleep-education control. Both methods improved how quickly babies fell asleep. Infant cortisol and maternal stress showed small-to-moderate declines in the method groups, and at 12 months there were no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or in parent-child attachment.
So the evidence does not require cry it out. Approaches with less crying also work. What they need is a good fit with the baby and consistency.
That is the Actually Sleeping approach: not cry it out, and not wait it out either. Dr. Sam writes a plan around your baby and your limits, and you are coached bootcamp-style before night one, so you go in knowing exactly what to do instead of standing at the door with a timer.
Why “no crying at all” is rarely realistic
When you change how your baby falls asleep, your baby notices and protests. That protest is communication, and it usually fades as the new pattern becomes familiar. A consultant who promises zero tears is either describing a baby who was nearly ready anyway or setting you up to feel you failed. A better promise is a clear plan for how you will respond, and coaching thorough enough that you carry it out with confidence.
What to ask any consultant
“Describe night one for my baby. Where am I, and what do I do when my baby cries?”
“How will you prepare me before night one, and how often will you check in after it?”
“Can you adjust the approach if it is too much for us?”
“What is different for a younger baby versus a toddler?”
Why fit matters more than the method name
The best approach is one that suits your baby’s temperament and that you will carry out the same way every night. Some babies settle better with a parent nearby; others are wound up by it. Some parents cannot listen to crying from outside the door; others find in-between approaches confusing. A consultant should work this out before writing the plan, not after night one. Families who wanted an alternative to cry it out describe their experience on our video reviews page.

# When is the right time to hire a baby sleep consultant?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/when-to-hire-a-sleep-consultant/

When is the right time to hire a baby sleep consultant?
There are two good moments. In the newborn weeks, for foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine and realistic expectations, with no crying-based training and no stretching of feeds. And later, as soon as sleep has become a problem that is not passing on its own. You do not need to wait until you are exhausted.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Newborn: foundations, not training
A newborn should not be sleep trained. That does not mean nothing can be done. The newborn weeks are when habits form, and a foundations plan shapes them gently. It covers:
Safe sleep from night one. Back to sleep, a firm flat surface, nothing soft or weighted in the crib or bassinet, and room sharing without bed sharing, as the AAP recommends.
Feeding on cue, day and night, with your pediatrician guiding growth.
Day and night cues, and a short, repeatable wind-down that becomes your baby’s signal for sleep.
Realistic expectations for what newborn sleep looks like, so you can tell normal from a problem.
Research supports this kind of early guidance. A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found its strongest support for preventive parent education, alongside unmodified extinction. Actually Sleeping works with families from newborn, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at your baby’s 10-week birthday. Parents of newborns describe it on these video reviews.
Later: when a problem has settled in
Good signs it is time:
Sleep has been hard for more than two weeks, and it is not explained by illness, travel or a new tooth.
Your baby wakes at about the same times every night and needs the same help each time.
You have tried things and sleep is still broken.
Sleep loss is affecting your health, work, relationship or mood.
A transition is coming: return to work, daycare, a new sibling, a move.
Picking the start date
You can book the consultation any time. When it comes to night one, a few things affect the date:
Illness. Start once your baby is well; see sleep after illness.
Medical questions. If your pediatrician is looking into weight gain, breathing or reflux, start once you have the all-clear.
Travel. Choose a stretch of about two weeks at home without travel, visitors or big schedule changes.
Support at home. It helps when both parents, or a supportive second adult, can be around for the first few nights.
Dr. Sam plans the start date with you on the consultation so the plan is ready before night one, not rushed.
Is it ever too late?
No. Older babies and toddlers respond well to behavioral plans; they tend to have more established habits and more opinions. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on. See sleep consultants for toddlers.
Hiring help is not a sign you failed
Parents often wait until they are exhausted because asking for help feels like giving up. It is not. Most families who get stuck have done many things right and are missing one or two details, or need someone to hold the line with them for a couple of weeks. Getting help earlier means fewer broken nights for everyone. For age-specific context, see the best age to sleep train.

# Can a sleep consultant help with a toddler, or is it too late?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-for-toddlers/

Can a sleep consultant help with a toddler, or is it too late?
It is not too late. Behavioral sleep methods have been studied in toddlers and young children as well as babies, and they work. Toddler plans look different: more talking, clear limits, a predictable routine, a plan for leaving the bed, and often a cue for morning. Expect more negotiation than with a baby; progress is often quick once every adult responds the same way.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the research covers
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine review of 52 studies covered bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children, not only babies. A randomized trial that enrolled 264 mothers of children aged 6 to 36 months found faster sleep onset and fewer, shorter night wakings, with improvements seen by one week and more by week two. Toddlers can and do change their sleep.
How toddler sleep problems differ
BabyToddler
Wakes needing a feed, rock or pacifierWakes needing you, a drink, another story, your bed
Protests by cryingProtests by negotiating, stalling, calling out, climbing out
Cannot understand rulesCan understand simple rules and rewards
Schedule is about wake windowsSchedule is often about dropping or shortening the nap
Generic toddler advice tends to fail because toddlers find the gaps. If one adult gives in, or the rule changes on a tired night, a toddler learns that pushing works. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, and Dr. Sam writes toddler plans around your child, your room and bed setup, and every adult who does bedtime.
What a toddler plan has to account for
The routine. Short and fixed, so the order is not up for debate.
Curtain calls. The extra drink, hug and question, and how every adult responds to them.
Leaving the bed or climbing out. See toddler won’t stay in bed.
Mornings. A toddler who does not know when morning starts will test it at 5 a.m.
Nap and bedtime timing. Many toddler bedtime battles are a toddler who is not tired yet. See the 2-year-old schedule.
Every caregiver. Grandparents, sitters and both parents need the same plan.
Common toddler situations
Bed sharing that worked for a while and now does not.
A move from crib to bed that came too early. See when to move to a toddler bed.
Bedtimes that stretch past an hour.
A new sibling, and an older child who suddenly wakes at night.
Separation anxiety at bedtime. See separation anxiety at bedtime.
Night waking that started with an illness and never stopped.
What is harder, and what is easier
Habits are older, so the first few nights can be louder, and toddlers test whether the new rule is real. The upside is that toddlers understand explanations, respond to praise, and can see their own progress. Many families find toddlers change faster than they feared once every adult responds the same way, which is exactly what daily support helps you hold.

Loud snoring most nights, pauses in breathing, mouth breathing, very restless sleep, or daytime sleepiness that seems unusual. These can point to a medical cause. See sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist.

# What should a sleep-training guarantee actually say?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-guarantee-what-it-should-say/

What should a sleep-training guarantee actually say?
A real guarantee is written in the agreement, not only in marketing. It names a measurable result (such as hours of night sleep), a time frame, when that time frame starts, what you must do to qualify, and what you get if the result is not met. If any of those five parts is missing, you have a slogan, not a guarantee.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The five parts of a guarantee worth having
A measurable outcome. Something you can count: hours of night sleep, number of wakings, nights in a row. “Better sleep” and “a happier family” cannot be measured.
A time frame. Within how many days or nights.
A start point. When the clock starts. The first night of the plan, or a certain age. This matters most for young babies.
Your side of it. What counts as following the plan, and how that is shown. Daily check-ins are a fair way to show it; vague terms that can always be read against you are not.
The remedy. What happens if the outcome is not met: a full refund, a partial refund, extra sessions, or continued support. Know which one before you pay.
Why a guarantee matters
A written outcome guarantee changes who carries the risk. Without one, if the plan does not work, you have lost the time, the nights and the fee. With one, the consultant has to stand behind the plan they wrote. It also tells you something about the consultant: someone who guarantees a measurable result in writing expects to deliver it.
Actually Sleeping puts this in its Terms of Service: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
Common wording and what it really means
WordingWhat it really means
“Satisfaction guaranteed”No defined outcome. Ask what happens if you are not satisfied.
“We’ll support you until it works”More support, not money back. It is not a refund.
“Results guaranteed” with no detailAsk for the written terms. If there are none, there is no guarantee.
“Most babies sleep through in a week”A claim, not a guarantee. Ask where the figure comes from.
Specific hours, specific days, refund namedA real outcome guarantee. Now read the conditions.
Fair conditions versus unfair ones
Every outcome guarantee has conditions, and that is reasonable. A consultant cannot be responsible for a plan that was not followed. Fair conditions:
Following the written plan consistently.
Reporting each day what happened, so the plan can be adjusted.
A minimum age, because young babies still need to feed at night.
Conditions that make a guarantee hollow:
Terms that can never be checked, such as “perfect compliance” with no way to show it.
Exclusions so broad that any normal event (a cold, a tooth) cancels it.
A remedy you only learn about after you ask for it.
Questions to ask
“Can I read the exact guarantee wording before I sign?”
“What does ‘through the night’ mean, in hours?”
“When does the clock start for my baby?”
“How is following the plan measured?”
“If it is not met, what do I receive?”
Get it before you pay
Read the full wording before you pay, not after. Save a copy. If something is unclear, ask for it to be clarified in writing. You can read ours on the guarantee page, and hear from families who were coached under it on our video reviews page.

# Is online sleep coaching as effective as in-person?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/online-vs-in-person-sleep-coaching/

Is online sleep coaching as effective as in-person?
There is no trial comparing remote and in-person sleep coaching head to head that we are aware of. A randomized trial of an online program improved sleep in children 6 to 36 months, with changes seen by one week, without anyone visiting the home. Because you do the nights either way, the quality of the plan and the support matters more than whether the coach is in the room.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the evidence shows
A randomized trial of 264 mothers and children aged 6 to 36 months tested an online program that gave personalized recommendations from an algorithm, with no live coach. Compared with a control group, children in the program fell asleep faster and had fewer and shorter night wakings. Mothers’ sleep, mood and confidence improved. Improvements were seen by one week, with additional benefits by week two.
That does not prove remote coaching beats in-person coaching. It does show that behavioral sleep help works without anyone in your home. Remote coaching with a real person, who reads what happened and adjusts the plan each day, adds what an algorithm cannot: judgment about your baby.
Why remote works so well
You do the nights anyway. In both formats, your baby needs to learn to fall asleep with you, not with a visitor.
Preparation that travels. Video coaching before night one and daily 1:1 messaging work anywhere, so night two, when most plans wobble, is something you are already prepared for.
Your baby behaves normally. A stranger in the room can change how a baby or toddler acts at bedtime.
Daily adjustment. A remote coach reading your notes every day can change the plan as often as an in-person one.
Access. You choose by quality and fit, not by who lives nearby.
Actually Sleeping is built this way. Dr. Sam writes your baby’s plan, coaches you bootcamp-style before night one, and checks in with you every day, wherever you live.
What to check in any remote service
Response time. How quickly do they reply to your daily check-ins in the first week?
Preparation for night one. How thoroughly do they coach you before you start?
Daily review. Who reads your log, and how often?
Room check. Do they ask for a photo or video of the sleep space to check it against AAP safe sleep guidance: firm, flat, non-inclined, nothing soft or weighted?
A named person. Do you know who writes your plan and who answers your messages?
Getting the most from remote coaching
Keep your phone nearby but on silent during the first nights, so you can message without waking the house.
Write short notes as you go: times, what happened, what you did. Your coach can only adjust what they can see.
Send a quick video of the room and of bedtime if your coach asks. It replaces much of what an in-person visit would show.
Ask questions as they come up rather than saving them for a weekly call.
Self-paced online versus coached online
“Online” covers very different things. A self-paced course or app gives you material and leaves the adjusting to you. Coached remote support gives you a person who reads what happened and changes the plan. When you want a result on a timeline, the person is what makes the difference. # What credentials should a baby sleep consultant have?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-credentials/

What credentials should a baby sleep consultant have?
Sleep consulting has no required license. Certifications come from private training programs that set their own standards, so the letters after a name vary in meaning. Ask what training they completed, whether they hold a licensed health care credential, what that credential covers, and how they screen for medical issues. Judge the answers alongside their process, support and written commitments.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the title does and does not mean
Anyone can call themselves a sleep consultant or sleep coach. There is no single standard credential. A 2018 survey of 142 practicing sleep coaches in 17 countries found education ranging from high school diplomas to doctoral degrees. Only 20% were or had been licensed health care providers, and 38% carried malpractice insurance. Most respondents named a formal sleep coach training program as the most important qualification. The authors suggested their findings could inform future guidelines for training and credentialing.
None of this means consultants are unqualified. It means you have to ask.
Types of background you will see
BackgroundWhat it can addWhat it does not make them
Private sleep consultant certificationStructured training in behavioral methods and schedulesA licensed health care provider
Licensed nurseClinical training, infant care, recognizing when to referA sleep-medicine specialist
Licensed pharmacistMedication and supplement knowledge; see belowA physician or a sleep-medicine specialist
Psychologist in behavioral sleep medicineClinical expertise in behavioral treatment of sleep problemsA physician
Physician in sleep medicineDiagnosis and treatment of sleep disordersUsually not a day-to-day coach
Experience as a parent or caregiver onlyEmpathy and practical tipsTrained in screening or methods
What a pharmacist’s training adds
Dr. Sam, who founded Actually Sleeping, is Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, PharmD, a Doctor of Pharmacy and Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist. A Doctor of Pharmacy is a professional doctorate centered on medications: how they work, how they interact, and how they are used safely. For a family, that background is useful in specific ways:
Clear answers on why melatonin, antihistamines and “natural” sleep products are not a fix for a baby’s sleep, and when to take a medication question to the pediatrician.
Understanding how a parent’s own medications or caffeine relate to breastfeeding, and where to look it up.
Context on reflux medicines and other treatments a baby may already be on, without changing them.
A licensed professional’s accountability.
What it does not add: a pharmacist is not a physician, does not diagnose sleep disorders, and is not your baby’s doctor. Behavioral sleep coaching is a different skill, built through training and experience with many families. Dr. Sam has coached more than 700 families.

How long does it take to see results with a sleep consultant?
Many families see the first changes within the first week, with more by the second, when the plan is followed consistently. Naps usually take longer than nights. What the research shows

Improvements were seen by one week, with additional benefits by week two. A review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that improvements from behavioral interventions were maintained for 3 to 6 months.
A typical shape
Before night one: intake, plan, and any changes to the room or schedule.
The first few nights: often the hardest. Protest is normal while your baby learns a new way to fall asleep. This is when thorough preparation beforehand matters most.
End of the first week: many families see shorter settling and fewer wakings.
Second week: nights usually consolidate. A short bump is common and does not mean the plan failed.
Naps: usually lag behind nights. Daytime sleep pressure is lower, so naps take longer to become reliable.

A plan fitted to your baby’s actual schedule and sleep drivers.
Every adult responding the same way, every time.
Daily review of what happened and quick adjustments.
A healthy baby and two calm weeks at home.
What slows them down
Changing approach mid-way. Each switch resets the learning.
Giving in on a hard night after holding steady on easier ones. Your baby learns to protest longer.
Illness, travel, daylight saving time or starting daycare in the middle.
A schedule that leaves your baby overtired or not tired enough at bedtime.
Night feeds that are still needed. That is fine; your pediatrician decides them, and they stay in the plan.

# Sleep consultant vs night nurse vs postpartum doula: what’s the difference?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-vs-night-nurse-vs-postpartum-doula/

Sleep consultant vs night nurse vs postpartum doula: what’s the difference?
A night nurse cares for your baby overnight so you can sleep. A postpartum doula supports you and your household in the weeks after birth. A sleep consultant writes a plan and coaches you to change how your baby sleeps, while you do the nights. The first two give you rest now; a sleep consultant changes how your baby sleeps for good.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Side by side
Night nurse or overnight newborn carePostpartum doulaSleep consultant
Main focusYour baby, overnightYou and your householdYour baby’s sleep habits
Who does the nightsThey doVaries; some offer overnight shiftsYou do, with support
Typical timingNewborn weeks and monthsLate pregnancy and the weeks after birthNewborn foundations through toddler years

GoalRest for you nowRecovery, confidence, practical helpIndependent sleep that lasts
What it does not doTeach your baby to sleep without help, unless that is agreedSleep training, as a ruleCare for your baby overnight
Night nurse or overnight newborn care
Someone comes to your home in the evening and cares for your baby until morning: bringing the baby to you for breastfeeds or giving bottles, changing, settling and putting the baby back down. Some are licensed nurses; many are experienced newborn care providers without a nursing license. The title is used loosely, so ask what training and licenses they hold. It gives you rest while it lasts. When it ends, your baby’s sleep is usually where it was.
Postpartum doula
A postpartum doula supports the parent in the weeks after birth. That can include feeding support and referrals, newborn care teaching, emotional support, light household help, and time for you to rest or shower. Some offer overnight shifts. The focus is your recovery, not your baby’s sleep habits.
Sleep consultant
A consultant assesses how your baby sleeps, writes a plan, and supports you while you carry it out. With a newborn the work is foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine. Later it is teaching your baby to fall asleep independently, so nights stay good after the help ends. See what a sleep consultant does.

# Does Benadryl (diphenhydramine) help a baby or toddler sleep, and is it safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/benadryl-diphenhydramine-for-baby-sleep/

Does Benadryl (diphenhydramine) help a baby or toddler sleep, and is it safe?
No. Diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy. In a randomized trial of babies 6 to 15 months old who woke at night, it worked no better than a placebo. It can cause excitement instead of drowsiness in children, and too much can cause seizures or heart problems. Use it only for a reason your child’s pediatrician agrees with.

A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Diphenhydramine is an older antihistamine. In adults it causes drowsiness, which is why it appears in many “PM” and nighttime products. Children are not small adults. The same medicine that makes a parent sleepy can make a toddler wired, and the trial evidence in babies shows it does not fix night waking.
Parents who reach for Benadryl at bedtime are usually past exhausted. Actually Sleeping exists for that point. The practice is led by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist, so a question about an antihistamine is taken seriously, and anything medical goes back to your pediatrician. The waking itself gets a plan written for your child.
What the evidence and the regulators say
The label position. The National Library of Medicine’s drug page states that diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy. It also says not to use it in children 2 to 5 years old unless a doctor directs it, and lists excitement, especially in children, as a side effect.
The trial. The TIRED study randomized babies 6 to 15 months old who woke two or more times a night to diphenhydramine or placebo. Its safety board stopped the trial early because the medicine was no more effective than placebo. Only 1 of 22 babies on the medicine improved, compared with 3 of 22 on placebo.
Overdose risk. The FDA warns that taking more than the recommended amount can lead to serious heart problems, seizures, coma or death. It asks families to store medicines out of children’s reach and sight, and to check labels, because many combination products also contain diphenhydramine.
Travel. CDC travel guidance for clinicians says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1, and that antihistamines and decongestants have not been shown to help ear pain on flights.
Why it so often backfires
When an antihistamine does sedate, it changes how a child falls asleep for one night. It does not change how the child falls asleep the next night, or what happens between sleep cycles. If your child wakes at 1 and 4 a.m. because they fall asleep being fed or rocked at bedtime, a sedating medicine leaves that pattern untouched. Paradoxical excitement adds a wired, overtired child to the same problem.
Hidden diphenhydramine
Read the active ingredients on every allergy, cold, “nighttime” and itch product in the house. Giving two products that both contain diphenhydramine is one of the ways children get too much. Keep all of them locked up and out of sight.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is there a medical reason my child is not sleeping, such as allergies, eczema itch, ear pain or snoring?”
“If my child needs an allergy medicine, which one fits their age, and is it one that affects sleep?”
“Is my child’s sleep within the normal range for their age, or is this something to evaluate?”
Medicine is not the answer to a sleep problem
A sedating medicine changes one night at best. The pattern underneath, how your child falls asleep and what they need at each waking, is still there the next night. The AAP calls good sleep habits the best medicine, and that pattern is fixable. It just needs a plan built for your child: age, feeds, temperament, how they fall asleep now and your family’s schedule. Generic tips rarely fit all of those at once.

# Is magnesium safe for toddler sleep, and does it work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/magnesium-for-toddler-sleep/

Is magnesium safe for toddler sleep, and does it work?
There is very little research on magnesium for sleep, and almost none in toddlers. NIH notes conflicting results even in adults. Magnesium from food is safe, but supplements above the upper limit can cause diarrhea, nausea and cramping, and extremely high amounts can affect the heart. Ask your child’s pediatrician before giving any magnesium supplement, spray or powder.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Magnesium is an essential mineral, and toddlers need it. That does not make a supplement a sleep aid. The research that exists is small, mostly in adults, and inconsistent. For a healthy toddler eating a varied diet, a magnesium supplement is not a sensible first step for bedtime battles or night waking.
Families often try magnesium after other things have not worked. Actually Sleeping works on the cause instead: Dr. Sam, a pharmacist, writes a sleep plan for your toddler, takes the supplement question seriously and sends anything medical to your pediatrician.
What the evidence says
Very little research. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH) states that there is very little research on magnesium for insomnia, and that a 2022 review found conflicting results and called for larger, longer studies.
Food is the main source. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements lists legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains, leafy greens such as spinach, fortified cereals, and milk and yogurt as sources. It states that magnesium naturally present in food and drinks is not harmful.
Supplements have upper limits. NIH sets upper limits for magnesium from supplements and medicines for children, and says not to go above them unless a health care provider recommends it.
Too much causes problems. Excess magnesium from supplements or medicines can cause diarrhea, nausea and abdominal cramping. Extremely high intakes can cause an irregular heartbeat.
Interactions. Magnesium can interfere with some antibiotics if taken too close together in time. If your child takes any regular medicine, ask your pharmacist about spacing.
Sprays, lotions, bath flakes and gummies
The NIH evidence summaries cover magnesium taken by mouth. They do not show that magnesium sprays, lotions or bath products improve a child’s sleep. Gummies add another problem: they look like candy. Any supplement in the house should be stored up high and out of sight, because NIH notes that supplement labels do not always match what is in the bottle and that many supplements have not been tested in children.
Why magnesium often seems to work
Parents usually start a supplement on a bad week. Sleep regressions, illnesses and schedule changes often settle on their own within days or weeks. A new bedtime ritual, such as a warm bath with a lotion, can also help simply because it is calm and predictable. The routine may be doing the work, not the mineral.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Does my child’s diet give enough magnesium, or is there a reason to test or supplement?”
“Could restless sleep be linked to iron, snoring or something else worth checking?”
“Does a supplement interact with any medicine my child takes?”
The sleep problem is the fixable part
Toddler bedtime battles and night waking are rarely about a mineral. They are about routine, limits, naps and how the child falls asleep, and every toddler’s mix is different. A spray or a powder cannot sort that out. A plan built for your toddler can.
Actually Sleeping writes that plan around your child’s age, temperament, naps and evenings, gives you bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and checks in 1:1 every day while it settles. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. Toddler families describe how it went in the over-12-months video reviews. Related reading: toddler won’t stay in bed and the 2 year old sleep regression.

# Does gripe water help a baby sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/gripe-water-and-baby-sleep/

Does gripe water help a baby sleep?
There is no good evidence that it does. Gripe water is usually sold as a dietary supplement, not a tested medicine, so ingredients and quality vary. A study of 335 mothers found babies given gripe water were no less likely to have colic. Fussy evening crying usually peaks around 6 weeks and eases by 3 to 4 months. Ask your pediatrician before using it.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Gripe water is a traditional remedy for gas, colic and fussiness. Ingredients vary from product to product, so “gripe water” does not describe one thing. What the products share is a lack of evidence that they help a baby sleep or cry less.
Fussy evenings are hard, and it is natural to look for something in a bottle. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn weeks. Because the practice is led by a pharmacist, remedy questions are taken seriously and medical ones go to your pediatrician, while the plan focuses on sleep foundations that never restrict feeds.
What the evidence and the regulators say
Study evidence. A cross-sectional study of 335 mothers of babies 1 to 6 months old found that about 64% had given gripe water. Colic was actually more common in the babies who received it, as was constipation. The authors concluded that gripe water does not prevent excessive crying from colic. A study like this shows an association, not cause and effect, but it gives no support for a benefit.
Regulation. Many gripe water products are labeled as dietary supplements. NIH notes that the federal rules for supplements are less strict than those for medicines, that many supplements have not been tested in children, and that “natural” does not necessarily mean safe.
Quality problems have happened. In 2007 the FDA warned parents about a gripe water product after lab testing found Cryptosporidium, a parasite, and the product was linked to illness in a 6-week-old baby.
Why gripe water seems to work
Colic follows a predictable curve. The AAP describes fussing that typically peaks around 6 weeks and drops off by 3 to 4 months. Anything started at the peak will appear to work as the curve comes down. That is not the same as better sleep.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is this crying normal colic, or could there be a medical cause?” The AAP advises checking with your pediatrician before trying remedies.
“Is my baby feeding and gaining well?”
“If I am breastfeeding, is it worth trying to remove a food from my diet? If formula feeding, should we consider a different formula?”
“Is anything my baby takes, including supplements, safe at this age?”
What actually helps a fussy baby
The AAP’s colic tips are practical and drug-free: walking with your baby in a carrier, rocking, white noise, a pacifier, a tummy-down hold across your knees with a back rub while your baby is awake, and avoiding overfeeding. Take turns with another adult; even an hour or two away helps you stay steady. If your baby falls asleep while held, place them in the crib on their back. If you feel overwhelmed and no one can take over, it is okay to lay your baby on their back in the crib and step out for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.
When the crying eases and the sleep does not
Many families find that colic fades but the nights stay broken. During the hard weeks the baby learned to fall asleep being held, rocked or fed, which was exactly right at the time. Once the crying passes, that way of falling asleep is what keeps the baby waking. A remedy does not change it. A plan built for that baby does.

# Are natural or homeopathic baby sleep drops and teething tablets safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/homeopathic-and-natural-baby-sleep-remedies/

Are natural or homeopathic baby sleep drops and teething tablets safe?
Not reliably. The FDA has approved no homeopathic product and has not reviewed them for safety or effectiveness. FDA testing of homeopathic teething tablets found belladonna levels that sometimes far exceeded the label, a risk the agency called unnecessary for children under 2. Herbal “sleep” products have weak evidence. Check with your child’s pediatrician before using any of them.

This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. The short answer
“Natural” and “homeopathic” are marketing and regulatory categories. They do not mean tested, gentle or safe for babies. Some of these products contain plant extracts that are poisonous in larger amounts, and manufacturing control has been a documented problem.
Parents usually look at drops and tablets because they want something gentler than medicine. The gentler route is fixing the sleep pattern itself. What the FDA says about homeopathic products
No approvals. The FDA states that there are no FDA-approved products labeled as homeopathic, and that homeopathic products have not been reviewed by the FDA for safety and effectiveness.
Risky ingredients. The FDA warns that homeopathic makers use sources that include known poisons or toxins, and that poor manufacturing controls can produce products that exceed their labeled strength. Some are marketed for infants and children.

Cough and cold. The FDA advises against giving homeopathic cough and cold medicine to children younger than 4.
Herbal and supplement “sleep drops”
Chamomile: NIH says there is no conclusive evidence from clinical trials on whether it helps sleep. People allergic to ragweed or related plants can react to it.
Valerian: clinical trials have had inconsistent results, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s 2017 guideline recommended against valerian for chronic insomnia in adults.
Labels you cannot fully trust: the AAP notes that some sleep supplements have been found to contain other substances, such as CBD or serotonin. Read every ingredient. See is melatonin safe for babies.
Supplements in general: NIH notes that many have not been tested in children, may contain contaminants, and sometimes do not match their labels.

# Can low iron (ferritin) cause restless sleep in a toddler?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/iron-deficiency-and-restless-toddler-sleep/

Can low iron (ferritin) cause restless sleep in a toddler?
It can play a part. Restless legs that disturb sleep are listed by the AAP as a sign of more significant iron-deficiency anemia, and sleep guidelines ask clinicians to check ferritin in children with restless legs. Iron deficiency in infancy has also been linked to altered sleep patterns later. Never start iron on your own; ask your child’s pediatrician about testing.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Iron matters for the brain, and low iron has real links to sleep. But restless sleep in toddlers has many possible causes, and iron supplements are dangerous in an accidental overdose. The right step is a conversation with the pediatrician and, if they think it fits, a blood test. Not a supplement from the store.
Restless nights are often a mix of a medical piece and a sleep-habit piece. Actually Sleeping handles the second, with a plan written by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist, around whatever your pediatrician decides about the first.
What the evidence says
Signs of iron deficiency. The AAP lists pale skin, irritability, fatigue or needing more naps, and cravings for non-food items such as ice or dirt. In more severe anemia it lists restless leg syndrome that interferes with healthy sleep.
Long-term sleep effects. A study of 4-year-olds followed from infancy found that children who had iron-deficiency anemia as babies had differences in how their sleep stages were organized across the night on overnight sleep studies, compared with children who had not.
Restless legs in children. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s 2025 guideline says clinicians should check iron studies, including ferritin, in patients with clinically significant restless legs syndrome, and it suggests iron treatment for children with restless legs when ferritin is below a set level. Which test, which product and how long are clinical decisions.
Restless sleep disorder. Sleep experts have defined a separate “restless sleep disorder” with criteria that include a sleep study, but they note the current evidence applies to ages 6 to 18. In toddlers, restless sleep is a symptom to evaluate, not a diagnosis to assume.
Who is at higher risk
Too much cow’s milk. The AAP advises no cow’s milk before 12 months, and after age one no more than 24 ounces a day, because milk is low in iron and fills children up.
Breastfed babies after 4 months without iron-rich foods yet. The AAP recommends iron supplementation for partially or fully breastfed babies starting at 4 months until iron-containing foods are eaten; ask your pediatrician how this applies to your baby.
Babies born early or small, whom the AAP flags for earlier iron support.
The AAP calls for iron screening around the first birthday, with timing that depends partly on how your baby is fed.
Why not just try an iron supplement
Federal rules require this warning on iron products: “Accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.” Iron given without a test can also mask the real cause of a sleep problem. If your child ever swallows iron pills or chewables, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately.
What to ask the pediatrician
“My toddler is restless, kicks or seems uncomfortable at night. Should we check iron and ferritin?”
“How much milk should my child drink each day?”
“Could snoring, mouth breathing or pauses in breathing be part of this?”
Once the medical side is checked
Iron is a medical question, and the answer belongs to your pediatrician. Whatever that answer is, many restless toddlers also have a sleep pattern that keeps the nights broken: a late or uneven schedule, short naps, or a way of falling asleep that needs a parent at every waking. That part is fixable, and it needs a plan built for your child rather than a list of tips.
Actually Sleeping writes that plan around your pediatrician’s advice, never instead of it. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, daily 1:1 check-ins and naps coached until solid. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. Families with toddlers describe it in the over-12-months video reviews.

# Is it safe to give a baby or toddler melatonin for a flight or jet lag?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/melatonin-for-flights-and-jet-lag-toddler/

Is it safe to give a baby or toddler melatonin for a flight or jet lag?
Not without your pediatrician’s direction. The AAP says melatonin should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician. It is sold as a supplement, product strength varies widely, and child poisonings rose sharply over the past decade. Light, meals and naps on local time shift a young child’s body clock without a supplement.

A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
A one-off dose for travel can sound harmless. The problems are the same as with nightly use: you cannot be sure how much is in the product, there is little research in babies and toddlers, and travel bags are where curious toddlers find gummies. For a young child, planning the trip around light and schedule avoids those problems.
Families planning a trip often ask Actually Sleeping about melatonin first. Because the practice is led by a pharmacist, the question is taken seriously and the medical part goes to your pediatrician. The sleep part is planned for your child, travel included.
What the evidence and the regulators say
Pediatrician first. The AAP says melatonin should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises parents to talk with a health care professional before giving melatonin or any supplement to children.
Unregulated strength. Melatonin is sold as a dietary supplement. The AASM cites a study in which melatonin content ranged from less than half to more than four times the amount on the label, with chewables varying most. CDC travel guidance also notes melatonin is not regulated by the FDA.
Poisonings. A CDC report found pediatric melatonin ingestions rose about 530% from 2012 to 2021. Children 5 and younger made up most reports, and two children under 2 died.
Jet lag benefit does not settle safety. NIH notes melatonin may help with jet lag, but its long-term safety has not been established.
No help for ears. CDC guidance says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1 and have not been shown to help ear pain on flights; swallowing does. Let babies nurse or suck a bottle or pacifier on descent.
How the body clock actually shifts
CDC travel guidance gives an average adaptation of about 1.5 hours a day after flying west and 1 hour a day after flying east. Bright morning light helps the clock move earlier; evening light pushes it later. CDC also notes jet lag disturbs children’s sleep just as it does adults’. So the tools are the same for a toddler: light, meals and sleep timing.
Why trips undo sleep, and how to stop that
Jet lag is temporary. What lasts is what changes during the trip: a baby who fell asleep in a carrier every night of the holiday, a toddler who moved into the parents’ bed in the hotel. Those changes come home with the luggage. The tools that move a body clock (light, meals and sleep timing) are well known; using them for one particular child, on one particular itinerary, is the hard part. More background is in keeping your baby sleeping while traveling.
Packing safety
If an adult in the family takes melatonin, pack it in a locked or zipped compartment and never leave it on a hotel nightstand. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 if a child swallows any.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is there any reason my child should not fly right now, such as an ear infection?”
“Is melatonin appropriate for my child at all? If so, which product and timing?”
“Which medicines should I pack for illness on the trip?”
Medicine is not the answer to travel sleep
A child who falls asleep on their own at home brings that skill on vacation. That skill is the real protection against a ruined trip, and it is fixable whatever age your child is. # Can I give cough and cold medicine at bedtime to a baby or toddler?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/cough-and-cold-medicine-at-bedtime-toddler/

Can I give cough and cold medicine at bedtime to a baby or toddler?
For young children, generally no. The FDA does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children under 2, product labels say not to use them under 4, and the AAP says to use them at 4 to 6 only if your child’s doctor recommends it. Saline, suction, a cool-mist humidifier and, after age 1, honey are the usual night-time helpers.

A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
A coughing, stuffy child at 10 p.m. is hard on everyone, and the medicine aisle looks like the answer. For babies and young toddlers it is not. These products do not shorten a cold, and combination products make it easy to double up on an ingredient.
Colds pass. What often lasts is the sleep that slipped during them. Actually Sleeping helps families with that part, with a plan written by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist who takes medicine questions seriously and sends medical ones to your pediatrician.
What the regulators say
FDA: does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children younger than 2. Manufacturers label them “do not use in children under 4 years of age.” The FDA also advises not to give homeopathic cough and cold medicine to children younger than 4.
FDA: cough or cold medicine “will not change the natural course of a cold or make it go away faster.”
AAP: over-the-counter cough and cold medicine is not recommended under 4; from 4 to 6, use only if your child’s doctor recommends it.
AAP: many children with a cough or stuffy nose are happy, play normally and sleep well. Treat symptoms when they cause discomfort or trouble sleeping.
Night-time comfort that is recommended
Saline: plain saline drops or spray to loosen mucus, followed by gentle suction for babies. Squeeze the bulb before placing it in the nostril. Suctioning before feeds and sleep helps.
Cool-mist humidifier near the sleep space but out of reach, cleaned as directed. The FDA advises against warm-mist humidifiers.
Fluids through the day, which thin mucus.
Honey for children 1 year and older. The AAP says research shows honey is better than store-bought cough syrups at reducing how often and how badly children cough at night. Never give honey to a baby under 12 months; CDC warns it can cause botulism.
Mentholated chest rub only for children 2 and older, per the AAP, and stored out of reach.
Safe sleep stays the same when your baby is sick
The AAP says babies should always sleep flat on their backs on a firm surface, and that propping a baby on towels or pillows or inclining the mattress is not safe, even with congestion. Swings, car seats and carriers are not safe for sleep.
When to call
The FDA lists a fever of 100.4°F or higher in a baby 2 months or younger, or 102°F or higher at any age, as reasons to call.
The AAP says call 911 for a baby struggling for each breath or with bluish lips, and call the doctor for breathing much faster than normal or coughing that stops your baby from sleeping, eating or playing.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is this a cold, or could it be an ear infection, croup or asthma?”
“Which fever or pain reliever, if any, is right for my child’s age and weight?”
“Is honey okay for my child, and how much?”
Why sleep stays broken after the cold is gone
A sick child deserves comfort, freely given. The trouble is that comfort often changes how a child falls asleep: extra feeds, rocking, a parent’s bed. After a week of that, the child expects it at every waking, and the nights stay broken long after the cough is gone. More background is in getting sleep back on track after illness.

# Do vitamin D drops or probiotics affect a baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/vitamin-d-probiotics-and-baby-sleep/

Do vitamin D drops or probiotics affect a baby’s sleep?
Not in any proven way. The AAP recommends vitamin D for most babies for bone health, not sleep, and a randomized trial found a higher vitamin D dose gave no sleep benefit over the standard dose. Probiotic trials for colic have mixed results, and the FDA has approved no probiotic as a drug for infants. Ask your pediatrician before changing either.

A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Vitamin D drops are a routine part of infant care for many babies, and you should keep giving them as your pediatrician advised. They are not a sleep treatment, and giving more will not improve sleep. Probiotics are a different story: optional, variable products with mixed evidence for colic and no proven effect on sleep.
When a supplement question is really a sleep question, Actually Sleeping can help. The practice is led by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist, so supplement questions are taken seriously and medical ones go to your pediatrician, while the plan works on how your baby sleeps.
Vitamin D: what the evidence says
Why babies get it. The AAP recommends that all infants receive a vitamin D supplement, except babies drinking enough vitamin D-fortified formula. Breastfed babies specifically need it. Your pediatrician will tell you which product and how much.
Sleep. In the VIDI randomized trial, infants given a higher daily vitamin D dose had no sleep benefit up to age 2 compared with the standard dose. The researchers saw an association between higher vitamin D blood levels and better sleep, but an association does not show that vitamin D causes better sleep.
More is not better. The AAP notes that fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the body and at very high levels could make a child sick. Use the measuring device that comes with the product and never double up.
Probiotics: what the evidence says
Colic trials are mixed. Trials of one probiotic strain found benefits in breastfed babies with colic, while a later trial that included formula-fed babies found no benefit. Less crying, where it happened, is not the same as longer sleep.
Regulation. The FDA states it has not approved any probiotic product for use as a drug or biological product in infants of any age. Probiotics are commonly sold as foods or dietary supplements.
Preterm babies. In 2023 the FDA warned that probiotic products given to hospitalized preterm infants had contributed to serious infections, including one infant death. If your baby was born early, do not start a probiotic without your pediatrician.
Why parents notice a change
Babies change fast. A new supplement often starts in the same weeks as a growth spurt, a shift in naps or the natural easing of colic around 3 to 4 months. It is easy to credit the drops with a change the calendar made.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Does my baby need vitamin D drops, given how they are fed?”
“Is a probiotic reasonable for my baby’s crying, and which one, if any?”
“My baby was born early. Is any supplement unsafe for them?”
Medicine is not the answer to a sleep problem
Keep giving vitamin D as your pediatrician advised. For sleep, look somewhere else: at the schedule, the routine and how your baby falls asleep. Those are different for every baby, which is why age charts such as wake windows by age are only a starting point.

# Do allergy medicines affect a toddler’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/allergy-medicine-and-toddler-sleep/

Do allergy medicines affect a toddler’s sleep?
They can, in both directions. Older antihistamines can cause drowsiness or, in some children, excitement, and should never be used just to make a child sleep. Newer ones can cause mild sleepiness. Decongestants can make it harder to fall asleep. Treated nasal allergies, on the other hand, can improve sleep. Choose with your child’s pediatrician.

A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Untreated nasal allergies disturb sleep, and the right treatment can help. The wrong product, or the right one used for the wrong reason, can make nights worse. The goal is to treat the allergy, not to sedate the child.
Allergies are your pediatrician’s territory. The sleep habits that grow up around a stuffy, uncomfortable child are where Actually Sleeping comes in, with a plan written by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist who takes medication questions seriously.
How each type of medicine relates to sleep
Older (first-generation) antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine, can cause drowsiness, the AAP notes. They can also cause excitement in children, and the drug label says diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy. CDC guidance says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1. More in Benadryl and baby sleep.
Newer antihistamines are described by the AAP as non-drowsy, though they may cause mild sleepiness, especially after the first dose. Ask your child’s doctor whether one suits your child.
Cetirizine and levocetirizine. In 2025 the FDA added a warning about rare but severe itching after stopping long-term use, usually after months or years of daily use. If your child takes one daily, ask the pediatrician how long to continue and how to stop.
Oral decongestants can make children act hyper, feel anxious or have a racing heart, the AAP warns, and some can make it harder to fall asleep. Ask before using them.
Steroid nasal sprays are called the most effective treatment for nasal allergy by the AAP, which says they can help a child breathe more easily and may improve sleep.
Montelukast carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events. Listed effects include bad or vivid dreams, sleepwalking and trouble sleeping. The FDA says it should be reserved for allergies that other medicines have not controlled, and to stop it and contact a health care professional right away if mood or behavior changes.
How allergies themselves affect sleep
The AAP notes that a blocked nose makes it hard to sleep, and that poor sleep leads to daytime drowsiness and low energy. Saline rinses and sprays are a drug-free daily option the AAP mentions. Tracking whether night symptoms follow a season, a pet or dust exposure gives your pediatrician useful information.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Are these allergies, a run of colds or something else, such as enlarged adenoids?”
“Which treatment fits my child’s age, and is it sedating or stimulating?”
“How long should my child take a daily antihistamine, and how do we stop?”
“My child snores or breathes through the mouth at night. Should that be checked?”
The AAP advises using over-the-counter allergy products only with your child’s doctor’s advice. Bring a list of everything your child takes, including supplements.
When the allergy is treated and the nights are not
The right allergy treatment removes one reason to wake. It does not change how your child falls asleep, and that decides how well they resettle between sleep cycles. Children who spent months uncomfortable at night often learned to need a parent at every waking. Medicine is not the answer to that; a plan is.

# Are essential oils, lavender products or sleep sprays safe for babies?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/essential-oils-lavender-and-baby-sleep/

Are essential oils, lavender products or sleep sprays safe for babies?
Use caution. There is no good evidence they improve a baby’s sleep, and NIH says aromatherapy research needs larger, better studies. Undiluted oils can irritate skin, several oils are poisonous if swallowed, and repeated skin use of lavender and tea tree oils has been linked to breast growth in young boys. Keep oils out of the crib and out of reach, and ask your pediatrician first.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
A calming scent can be a pleasant part of an adult’s evening. For a baby, the potential harms are concrete and the sleep benefit is unproven.
A scent is usually a hope that something simple will calm bedtime. What calms bedtime is a routine and a way of falling asleep that fit your baby. That is the work Actually Sleeping does, with a plan written by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist.
What the evidence and the regulators say
Weak evidence for sleep. NIH reports that a 2021 review suggested aromatherapy may improve sleep quality, but the researchers said larger and more rigorous studies are needed. These studies were not in babies.
Skin. The AAP notes that some people develop skin irritation when pure, undiluted oils are applied directly to the skin.
Hormone-like effects. A report in the New England Journal of Medicine described three young boys who developed breast growth after repeated use of products containing lavender or tea tree oil. It resolved after the products were stopped, and lab tests showed the oils had weak estrogen-like and anti-androgen effects. The authors concluded the oils probably caused it; NIH notes it is unclear whether the oil was responsible. Either way, it is a reason for caution with daily use on young children.
Poisoning. The CPSC requires child-resistant packaging for wintergreen oil because it contains methyl salicylate, and warns of serious injury or death if young children swallow it. It also requires child-resistant packaging for thin, oily products such as some baby, bath and massage oils, because children under 5 who swallow and inhale them can develop chemical pneumonia.
Chest rubs. The AAP lists mentholated chest rubs for children 2 years and older only.
Diffusers and pillow sprays
There is no good evidence that diffusing oils or spraying bedding improves a baby’s sleep. Sprays put product on the sleep surface, and diffusers put a hot or wet device with a bottle of concentrated oil within reach as babies start to move. Keep the AAP’s safe sleep rule simple: the crib holds only the baby, on the back, on a firm, flat surface, with no soft bedding or other objects.
If you use oils at home
Store every bottle locked and out of sight. Child-resistant is not child-proof.
Do not apply essential oils to a baby’s skin, diluted or not, unless the pediatrician has said to, and keep them away from the face and hands.
Read “sleep” and “calming” product labels for melatonin or other active ingredients.
Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away if a child swallows any oil.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is any scented product safe on my baby’s skin, given eczema or sensitive skin?”
“My child has asthma or wheezes. Should we avoid scents and diffusers at home?”
“What is safe for congestion at my baby’s age?”
No product is the answer to a sleep problem
Babies calm to predictability, not to a smell. The routine, the timing and how a baby falls asleep are what decide the night, and each of them has to fit the baby in front of you. Generic advice on all three is everywhere; getting it right for one baby is the hard part.

# Can asthma or ADHD medicines affect a young child’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/asthma-and-adhd-medicines-and-toddler-sleep/

Can asthma or ADHD medicines affect a young child’s sleep?
Yes, some can. Montelukast carries an FDA boxed warning that includes vivid dreams, sleepwalking and trouble sleeping. Oral steroids can change behavior and appetite. Stimulants for ADHD commonly cause trouble falling or staying asleep, though AAP ADHD guidance starts at age 4 with parent training first. Apart from the FDA’s montelukast advice, do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; talk to your child’s pediatrician.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a licensed pharmacist, not a physician. This page explains in general terms how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep; it does not replace your child’s pediatrician. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer
Asthma, ADHD and the medicines for both can change sleep. The fix is almost never to stop the medicine at home. It is to tell the prescriber exactly what you are seeing, so they can adjust the plan.
Once the medical side is in hand, many families find the sleep is still hard. Actually Sleeping works on that part, with a plan written by Dr. Sam, a pharmacist who takes medication questions seriously and plans around your child’s treatment.
Asthma: the condition affects sleep too
The AAP uses nighttime flare-ups as one way to grade asthma: rare night symptoms fit milder asthma, while flare-ups more than once a week fit moderate asthma, and severe asthma can disrupt sleep often. The AAP stresses that overall control matters most. A child who coughs or wheezes at night may need a better controller plan, not a sleep fix.
Asthma medicines and sleep
Montelukast. The FDA requires a boxed warning about serious neuropsychiatric events. Listed effects include bad or vivid dreams, sleepwalking, trouble sleeping, agitation and anxiety. It is approved for asthma from age 1. The FDA says to stop it and contact a health care professional right away if mood or behavior changes.
Oral steroids for flare-ups. The AAP lists behavior change and increased appetite among short-term side effects, which go away after the course ends.
Inhaled steroids. The AAP says side effects are few, such as a mouth yeast infection or hoarseness. A spacer and rinsing the mouth lower the risk.
Albuterol. The National Library of Medicine lists shaking and nervousness among common side effects. If your child seems wound up after a bedtime treatment, mention it, but do not skip a rescue medicine your child needs to breathe.
ADHD medicines in young children
Age. The AAP’s ADHD guideline covers children aged 4 to 18. Toddlers are outside it.
First-line care for preschoolers is parent training in behavior management, not medicine, per the AAP.
Stimulants and sleep. The National Library of Medicine lists difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep among common side effects of methylphenidate, and advises asking your doctor or pharmacist how late in the day a missed dose can be taken.
If behavior is a concern in a young child, ask your pediatrician to look at sleep as part of the picture.
What to ask the pediatrician
“My child’s sleep changed after starting this medicine. Is that a known effect, and what are our options?”
“Is my child’s asthma well controlled if they wake with coughing?”
“Could snoring or breathing pauses be part of the problem?”
“Is there a better time of day to give this medicine?” Your pharmacist can help with timing questions too.
Medicine is not the answer to a sleep problem
Follow your child’s asthma action plan and the prescriber’s advice. Beyond that, sleep in a child with a medical condition is shaped by the same things as in any child: schedule, routine and how they fall asleep. Children with medical conditions still learn to fall asleep independently. They just need a plan that accounts for their treatment, and that rarely comes from a general list of tips.
