# Newborn sleep in the first 4 weeks: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/newborn-sleep-0-to-4-weeks/

Newborn sleep in the first 4 weeks: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the pediatrician
In the first 4 weeks, sleep comes in short pieces spread across day and night. HealthyChildren says newborns sleep about 16 to 17 hours a day, often only 1 or 2 hours at a time, and healthy babies vary widely. There is no official sleep target at this age. Feed on cue, keep every sleep safe, and call the pediatrician for fever, poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is normal in the first month
A newborn has no working body clock yet. The AAP notes that babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months, so sleep lands evenly across 24 hours and night is not yet different from day.
Newborn sleep is about half active (REM) sleep, according to the AAP. Grunting, twitching, eye movements and short cries during sleep are common and do not always mean your baby is awake. The AAP also describes periodic breathing: pauses of 5 to 10 seconds followed by a burst of faster breathing. It is generally considered normal and is outgrown by about the middle of the first year.
MeasureWhat the sources say
Official hours targetNone. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) makes no recommendation under 4 months because normal sleep varies so widely and evidence on health outcomes is insufficient.
Total sleepAbout 16 to 17 hours a day (HealthyChildren). A review of observational studies found an average of 14.6 hours at 0 to 2 months, with a normal spread of about 9 to 20 hours.
Length of a stretchOften only 1 or 2 hours at a time (HealthyChildren).
PatternNone yet. Day sleep and night sleep look the same.
These first weeks are about feeding, safety and recovery, not schedules. Many parents still want someone in their corner from the start. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage: Dr. Sam writes a plan around your baby’s feeds and your household, foundations first, with every feed your pediatrician wants left in place.
What parents find hardest
Day–night mix-up. With no body clock yet, night is not different from day. The AAP describes the contrast babies need: normal, bright days and dark, quiet nights with contact limited to basic care.
Sleeping only on you. Very common now. Contact naps are fine while you are awake and alert. When you get drowsy, move your baby to their own flat, empty sleep space.
Evening fussiness. The AAP says about one in five babies develop colic, usually between the second and fourth weeks, and the fussy period tends to fall between 6 p.m. and midnight.
Your own exhaustion. This is where the riskiest sleep happens. The AAP warns that sleeping with a baby on a couch or armchair raises the risk of a sleep-related death up to 67 times. If you think you might doze while feeding, do not sit on the sofa.
Safe sleep from the first night
On the back for every sleep, naps included. The AAP says the side position is just as dangerous as the stomach.
A firm, flat surface with a fitted sheet and nothing else. Crib bumpers and inclined sleepers (more than 10 degrees) have been banned products under federal law since November 12, 2022.
Share a room, not a bed. The AAP says sharing a sleep surface raises risk 5 to 10 times when a baby is under 4 months.
If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing or carrier, move them to a flat sleep surface on their back as soon as you can.
If you swaddle, always place your baby on the back, keep the hips loose, avoid overheating, and never use weighted swaddles. No hat indoors once you are home.
Night feeds
Newborns eat around the clock. How often to feed, whether to wake a sleepy baby to eat, and when a longer stretch is fine are decisions for your pediatrician, based on your baby’s weight gain. Nothing on this page is a reason to cut a feed.
When to call the pediatrician
A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby 3 months or younger. The AAP says to call immediately, even without other symptoms.
Your baby is hard to wake for feeds, feeds poorly, or seems floppy or unusually sleepy.
Breathing that stops for more than 20 seconds: the AAP says call 911.
Crying that seems like pain or illness, or you feel low and unable to cope. The AAP asks parents to tell their doctor about both.
What you can start now
Foundations can start now. What they should look like depends on your baby’s feeding, temperament and how your nights actually run, which is why Actually Sleeping builds them into a plan written for your baby rather than a generic checklist, with daily 1:1 check-ins while it settles. Night feeds are never forced out, and feeding decisions stay with your pediatrician. How many hours should a newborn sleep?There is no official target. The AASM makes no recommendation under 4 months because normal sleep varies so widely. HealthyChildren says newborns sleep about 16 to 17 hours a day, and a review of studies found healthy babies at 0 to 2 months anywhere from about 9 to 20 hours.
Is it normal for my newborn to grunt and twitch while asleep?Yes. About half of newborn sleep is active sleep, when grunts, twitches and brief cries are common. Short breathing pauses of 5 to 10 seconds followed by faster breathing are also described as normal by the AAP. Pauses longer than 20 seconds need a 911 call.
Can my newborn sleep in the swing or car seat?Not for routine sleep. The AAP says sitting devices such as car seats, swings and strollers are not recommended for routine sleep, especially under 4 months. # Sleep at 1 month: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-1-month/

Sleep at 1 month: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 1 month, sleep is still scattered and short, and evening crying often builds. The AAP says fussing usually peaks at about 3 hours a day by 6 weeks, then eases. There is no official sleep target before 4 months. This is also the start of the highest-risk window for SIDS, so safe sleep for every sleep matters most now.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing in weeks 4 to 8
Your baby is waking up to the world. By 2 months, the CDC lists milestones such as calming down when spoken to or picked up, looking at your face, and smiling when you talk or smile. Those first social smiles make evenings more fun and also more stimulating, which is part of why the late-day stretch gets harder.
The body clock is still forming. Night and day begin to separate a little, but long, predictable night sleep is not expected yet. Tummy time also matters this month: the AAP suggests building up to 15 to 30 minutes a day, in short sessions, by 7 weeks. Awake, supervised tummy time is the counterweight to back sleeping.

Weeks 4 to 8 are often the hardest stretch for parents: crying builds, nights are still broken, and the advice online contradicts itself. Actually Sleeping works with families from this stage. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby that starts with foundations and leaves night feeds exactly as your pediatrician wants them.
What parents find hardest
The evening witching hours. Cluster feeding and crying from late afternoon are typical, and the AAP says colicky fussing tends to fall between 6 p.m. and midnight.
Catnaps that last one cycle. Short daytime sleeps are expected at this age. They are not a sign you are doing something wrong.
Waking when put down. Many babies startle awake on the transfer to the bassinet. It is one of the most common reasons parents end up holding every nap.
Sleep debt in parents. Weeks of broken nights add up. If you think you might doze while holding your baby, put your baby down in their own flat, empty sleep space first.
Safe sleep matters most right now
The NICHD Safe to Sleep campaign reports that most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months of age, and that 72% occur in months 1 to 4. Everything below applies to every nap and every night.
Back to sleep, on a firm, flat surface, with nothing in the sleep space. The AAP says the side is just as risky as the stomach.
Room-share without bed-sharing. Never sleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair.
Pacifiers reduce SIDS risk even if they fall out after your baby is asleep. If you breastfeed, the AAP suggests waiting until breastfeeding is established.
If you swaddle, stop as soon as your baby shows any sign of trying to roll. The AAP notes some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months.
Night feeds
Feeding on cue at night is still normal at this age. How often to feed, and whether a longer stretch is fine, is your pediatrician’s decision based on growth. Do not stretch or drop feeds on your own.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Any rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher: the AAP says call immediately for babies 3 months or younger.
Crying that changes in sound, comes with vomiting, fever or poor feeding, or feels like pain. The AAP advises checking with your pediatrician first to rule out a medical cause.
Noisy, laboured breathing in sleep, or pauses longer than 20 seconds (call 911).
You feel depressed or unable to cope. The AAP asks parents to tell their own doctor, who can suggest help.

Sleep at 2 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
At 2 months, many babies begin to show one slightly longer stretch, but sleep is still irregular and night feeds are normal. There is no AASM sleep target until 4 months. The big safety change is rolling: the AAP says some babies start working on it as early as 2 months, and swaddling must stop at the first sign.

What is changing at 2 months
By 2 months, the CDC lists milestones such as holding the head up during tummy time, moving both arms and legs, making sounds other than crying, and smiling back at you. More control and more awareness mean your baby is now easier to engage and easier to overstimulate.
Studies show a longest stretch that varies enormously. A review of observational studies found the longest sleep period in babies 0 to 5 months averaged 5.7 hours, with a normal spread from about 2 to nearly 10 hours. Some 2 month olds give you a 5 hour block. Many do not yet. Both are normal.

Those figures come from parent reports pooled across many studies, so treat them as a picture of normal variety, not targets. Daytime sleeps are a common pattern, not a rule.
What parents find hardest
The swaddle question. Many babies still settle best swaddled just as they start to wriggle onto their side. Watch closely for rolling attempts.
Relying on motion. Swings and car rides work, but the AAP says sitting devices are not recommended for routine sleep, especially under 4 months.
Late, unpredictable bedtimes. Bedtime often drifts late because the body clock is still forming.
Short naps. One sleep cycle and awake is common at this age, and it makes every day look different from the last.
Safe sleep at 2 months
Stop swaddling as soon as your baby shows any sign of trying to roll. The AAP says some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months, and every baby is different. A swaddled baby who rolls to the stomach cannot push up.
No weighted swaddles, weighted sleep sacks or weighted objects. The AAP says they are not safe.
Back to sleep for every sleep, on a firm, flat surface. Keep room-sharing without bed-sharing.
Most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, according to the NICHD. You are in the middle of that window.
Night feeds
Night feeds are expected. Whether your baby can go longer between feeds is your pediatrician’s call at the 2-month visit, based on growth. Use that visit to ask directly.
When to talk to the pediatrician
A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher: call immediately at this age.
Your baby does not yet smile back, react to loud sounds, or lift the head during tummy time. These are on the CDC’s 2-month list; raise any concern early.
Crying that is getting worse instead of better, or comes with poor feeding or vomiting.
Frequent snoring or breathing that sounds like a struggle during sleep.
Getting ready for the next stage
Foundations can start now. # Sleep at 3 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-3-months/

Sleep at 3 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 3 months, crying usually starts to ease and nights may get a little more organized, but there is still no AASM sleep target until 4 months. The main changes are physical: rolling attempts can start any time now (the AAP notes some babies begin as early as 2 months), so the swaddle has to go at the first sign, and the bassinet will soon be outgrown.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing at 3 months
Colic is on its way out for most families. The AAP says colicky fussing declines to 1 or 2 hours a day by 3 to 4 months and generally stops by then, though it can last until 6 months.
Your baby is getting stronger. By 4 months, the CDC lists pushing up onto elbows or forearms during tummy time, holding the head steady, and bringing hands to mouth. Hands to mouth is a real self-settling tool, and many babies begin sucking fingers in the crib now.
The body clock is maturing. The AAP says regular sleep cycles appear at about 4 months, so the next few weeks are a period of change rather than a settled state.

Your baby has now passed the 10-week birthday, which is when the Actually Sleeping guarantee clock starts. Three months is also when many parents notice that what worked as a newborn has stopped working. What parents find hardest
Leaving the swaddle. It has to go at the first sign of rolling, and many babies sleep worse for a while with free arms.
Naps that stay short. One cycle and awake is still common. Daytime sleeps averaged about 3 a day in studies of babies 0 to 5 months, with a lot of variation.
Newborn tricks stop working. Bouncing and rocking often lose their effect as your baby becomes more alert, just as sleep is about to change at 4 months.
Safe sleep at 3 months
Back to sleep for every sleep. Rolling is about to make positioning harder; the rule does not change until your baby can roll both ways.
No weighted products, no inclined surfaces over 10 degrees, no bumpers.
Keep room-sharing, ideally for at least the first 6 months, per the AAP. Bed-sharing risk is highest under 4 months.
Most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, according to the NICHD. Do not relax the basics yet.
Night feeds
Some babies naturally space out night feeds now; others do not. Either way, how many night feeds your baby needs is your pediatrician’s call, not a calendar’s.
When to talk to the pediatrician
A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby 3 months or younger: call immediately.
Crying that is increasing rather than settling, or continues past what you were told to expect.
Frequent snoring, struggling to breathe, or breathing pauses longer than 20 seconds (call 911).
Not yet bringing hands to mouth or lifting the head and chest on the tummy as 4 months approaches.

The AAP’s advice for babies 4 months and older is to put them to bed drowsy rather than asleep, so the weeks ahead matter. # Sleep at 4 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-4-months/

Sleep at 4 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
From 4 months, the AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours of sleep per 24 hours, including naps, and the AAP supports that range. Sleep cycles become more adult-like around now, so many babies start waking more between cycles. Rolling is common, teething may begin, and the AAP suggests putting babies 4 months and older to bed drowsy.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing at 4 months
The AAP says babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months. Once they do, there are more brief wake-ups between cycles. A baby who was rocked fully asleep may now need the same help several times a night. That is the change people call the 4-month regression; it is a developmental step that tends to stick.
By 4 months, the CDC lists pushing up onto elbows during tummy time, holding the head steady, bringing hands to mouth, chuckling, and moving or making sounds to keep your attention. Teething can also start: the AAP says it typically begins by about 4 to 7 months.
Measure at 4 monthsFigureSource
Recommended total sleep12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including napsAASM, supported by AAP
Average total in studies, from 3 months13.6 hoursGalland 2012
Daytime sleeps, 0 to 5 monthsAbout 3 on average, often 3 to 4Galland 2012
Night wakings, 3 to 6 months0.8 on average, 0 to 3 is within normalGalland 2012
This is the age when many families first look for help. A baby who needs feeding or rocking at bedtime tends to need it at every cycle. Actually Sleeping changes that with a plan Dr. Sam writes for your baby, bootcamp-style coaching before night one, and daily 1:1 check-ins. It is not cry it out and not wait it out.
The nap count is a common pattern, not a rule. Some 4 month olds take three long naps, others four or five short ones.
What parents find hardest
Frequent waking after months of better nights. Often a sleep-association problem appearing, not hunger. Ask the pediatrician before assuming either way.
Rolling in the crib. Babies roll onto their tummy and get annoyed, or practise rolling instead of sleeping.
Short naps. Naps of a single sleep cycle are very common at this age.
Distracted daytime feeds that shift calories into the night.
Safe sleep at 4 months
Still place your baby on the back for every sleep. The AAP says that once your baby rolls both ways, back to tummy and tummy to back, you do not need to keep turning them over, as long as the sleep space is empty.
No swaddle once rolling attempts begin. Arms-free sleep sacks only, and never weighted.
Keep room-sharing without bed-sharing, ideally for at least the first 6 months.
If you still use a bassinet, plan the move: the CPSC says they are not meant for use beyond about 5 months or once a baby can push up on hands and knees.
Night feeds
Some 4 month olds still need one or more night feeds and some do not. That decision belongs to your pediatrician, based on weight gain. The plan you choose should work around those feeds, not cut them.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Fever above 101°F (38.3°C). The AAP says teething does not cause a fever that high, so it needs a look.
Frequent snoring, laboured breathing, or daytime sleepiness that seems excessive.
Sudden frequent waking with fever, ear pulling, vomiting or poor feeding.
Not yet holding the head steady or pushing up on the forearms.
Where to go from here
The AAP’s advice for babies 4 months and older is to put them to bed drowsy rather than asleep. Getting a specific baby there, without tears you are not comfortable with and without cutting feeds, is the part generic advice leaves out. Actually Sleeping writes plans for this stage that keep any pediatrician-approved night feeds in place, and coaches naps until they are solid. Frequently asked
How many hours should a 4 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for babies 4 to 12 months, and the AAP supports that range. Healthy babies vary, so look at mood, feeding and growth along with the total.
Is the 4-month regression real?Something real does change. The AAP says regular sleep cycles appear around 4 months, which means more brief wakings between cycles. Babies who need feeding or rocking to fall asleep often need the same help each time they surface. That pattern is what Actually Sleeping coaches.
My 4 month old rolls onto their tummy in the crib. What do I do?Keep placing your baby on the back. The AAP says once your baby rolls comfortably both ways you do not need to keep turning them, provided there are no blankets, pillows, toys or bumpers in the crib. Make sure the swaddle is gone.
Is my 4 month old teething?Possibly. The AAP says teething typically starts by about 4 to 7 months. It can cause a slight rise in temperature, but not above 101°F (38.3°C). A higher fever is not from teething; call your pediatrician.

# Sleep at 5 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to the pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-5-months/

Sleep at 5 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to the pediatrician
At 5 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. This is mostly an equipment month: the CPSC says bassinets are not meant for use beyond about 5 months, the AAP says to remove mobiles by 5 months, and the crib mattress should be lowered before your baby can sit. Short naps and early waking are the common complaints.

What is changing at 5 months
Your baby is getting close to the CDC’s 6-month milestones: rolling from tummy to back, pushing up with straight arms, and leaning on the hands while sitting. More strength means more movement in the crib and more ways to get stuck awake.
Teething can be part of the picture. The AAP says teething typically starts by about 4 to 7 months and that timing varies a lot. Interest in the world also jumps, so feeds get distracted and short.
Equipment check at 5 monthsGuidanceSource
Bassinet or cradleNot intended for use beyond about 5 months, or once your baby can push up on hands and kneesCPSC

Five months is when short naps and broken nights that started at 4 months tend to settle into a pattern. The equipment changes are simple; the sleep pattern is not, because it depends on how your baby falls asleep. That is what Actually Sleeping works on, with a plan Dr. Sam writes for your baby.
What parents find hardest
Short naps. One sleep cycle and awake is common at this age, and it usually has the same root as night waking.
Very early waking. Light, bedtime and how the day is spaced can all drive early waking, and the cause differs from baby to baby.
The first nights in the crib. A new space can bring unsettled nights, especially for a baby used to being held to sleep.
Distracted daytime feeds. Calories can shift into the night, and only your pediatrician should decide what happens to night feeds.
Safe sleep at 5 months
Back to sleep for every sleep until the first birthday, even if your baby then rolls.
Room-share in a crib or play yard next to your bed, ideally until at least 6 months. No sleeping together on a couch or armchair.
The crib stays empty: no bumpers, pillows, blankets or soft toys. Crib bumpers are banned products under federal law.
No weighted sleep sacks or weighted blankets.
Night feeds
Some 5 month olds still feed once or twice at night, some more. Whether that should change is your pediatrician’s decision. Starting solids is also their call.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Fever above 101°F (38.3°C): the AAP says this is not teething.
Snoring on most nights, gasping, or breathing pauses during sleep.
A sudden change in sleep alongside feeding refusal, vomiting or fewer wet diapers.
Not rolling or pushing up with straight arms as 6 months approaches.

If nights have become a series of short wake-ups that need feeding or rocking, the cause is usually how your baby falls asleep, not a lack of sleep pressure. # Sleep at 6 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-6-months/

Sleep at 6 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 6 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. The AAP says it is normal for a 6 month old to wake briefly at night and go back to sleep within a few minutes. In studies, babies 6 to 11 months averaged about 2 daytime naps. The AAP recommends room-sharing for at least the first 6 months.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing at 6 months
By 6 months, the CDC lists rolling from tummy to back, leaning on the hands to support sitting, knowing familiar people, and laughing. Sitting and rolling give your baby new things to practise at 2 a.m.
Several things also wind down around now. The AAP says periodic breathing of infancy is generally outgrown by about the middle of the first year, and colicky crying, which can last until 6 months, is usually over. Separation anxiety can begin in the second half of the first year, and the AAP notes that nightmares can start as young as 6 months.

By 6 months many babies are physically able to sleep a long stretch, so a 6 month old who still needs a parent at every waking is usually showing a sleep habit rather than a need. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping at this age have already tried things on their own. What parents find hardest
Waking every 2 hours. Brief waking is normal; needing a full rescue every time usually points to how your baby falls asleep at bedtime.
Sitting up in the crib and not knowing how to lie back down.
The room-sharing decision. The AAP minimum is about to pass. Some families move the crib now, others later. Both are reasonable if the sleep space is safe.
New foods causing a few unsettled nights or changes in digestion.
Safe sleep at 6 months
Back to sleep until the first birthday. If your baby rolls both ways, you can leave them in the position they choose, with nothing else in the crib.
The NICHD reports more than 90% of SIDS deaths happen before 6 months, but it and the AAP both say safe sleep practices continue to age 1.
Lower the mattress before your baby can sit unassisted, and to the lowest setting before standing.
No bottle in bed. The AAP advises against putting a baby to bed with a bottle, as part of its tooth decay prevention advice.
Night feeds
Some healthy 6 month olds still take a night feed. Whether to keep it, reduce it or drop it is your pediatrician’s decision, and any change should follow their advice. A sleep plan is built around that decision, not the other way round.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Frequent snoring, gasping, or loud or heavy breathing in sleep. The AAP lists snoring and sleep apnea among common childhood sleep problems.
Fever above 101°F (38.3°C), or waking with ear pulling and fever.
Not rolling, or not reaching for toys, by 6 months.
Any question about starting solids or how your baby is eating.

Studies of babies 3 to 6 months recorded 0 to 3 wakings as within the normal range. Frequent wakings that each need a parent are what Actually Sleeping helps families change.
Should my 6 month old move to their own room?The AAP recommends room-sharing for at least the first 6 months. After that it is a family decision. Wherever your baby sleeps, keep them on the back on a firm, flat, empty surface until the first birthday.
How many naps should a 6 month old take?There is no rule. In a review of studies, babies 6 to 11 months averaged 2.2 daytime naps, with a normal spread from about 1 to 3.5. Many 6 month olds take 3 naps and move to 2 over the next couple of months.

# Sleep at 7 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-7-months/

Sleep at 7 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 7 months, the AASM range is still 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Night waking often creeps back: in studies, babies 7 to 11 months woke slightly more on average than babies 3 to 6 months. Sitting, early crawling and separation anxiety are common reasons. Many babies move from 3 naps to 2 around now, as a common pattern rather than a rule.

What is changing at 7 months
Your baby is working toward the CDC’s 9-month milestones: getting into a sitting position alone, sitting without support, and moving things from hand to hand. New motor skills tend to get practised in the crib.
The emotional side is shifting too. The AAP says separation anxiety can begin in the second half of the first year and can disrupt sleep for several months, with babies waking and crying anxiously for a parent.
A first tooth may also arrive. The AAP says teething typically starts by about 4 to 7 months and can cause a slight temperature rise, but not above 101°F (38.3°C). A higher fever is not teething.

What parents find hardest
New night wakings. Often tied to new skills or separation anxiety, and easy to turn into a habit when the response changes from night to night.
Sitting or rolling and getting stuck, which turns a brief waking into a long one.
Fighting the third nap. In studies, babies 6 to 11 months averaged about 2 naps a day. Many drop the late catnap around now, and the in-between weeks are often messy.
Early waking. Light leaks and a bedtime that is too late are frequent causes.
Safe sleep at 7 months
Back to sleep until the first birthday; if your baby rolls both ways, let them settle where they land, in an empty crib.
The mattress should already be lowered for sitting. Move it to the lowest setting before your baby can pull to stand.
Keep the crib away from windows, blind cords and anything climbable.
No pillows, blankets or soft toys yet. The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations run to age 1.
Night feeds
A 7 month old waking more is not automatically hungry, and is not automatically not hungry. Ask your pediatrician whether night feeds are still needed before you change anything.

Waking that comes with fever, ear pulling, vomiting, rash, or a cough that worsens lying down.
Snoring most nights or breathing that looks like hard work.
A fever above 101°F (38.3°C) blamed on teething: the AAP says teething does not cause that.
Your baby is not yet rolling or bearing weight on the hands while sitting.

# Sleep at 8 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the doctor
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-8-months/

Sleep at 8 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the doctor
At 8 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Clinginess and bedtime protest are very common because stranger and separation anxiety are emerging; the AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months. SIDS becomes less common after 8 months, but safe sleep rules still apply until the first birthday.

What is changing at 8 months
Your baby now knows exactly who you are, and minds when you leave. The AAP describes stranger anxiety as one of the first emotional milestones and says separation anxiety starts around the same time, usually peaking between 10 and 18 months. By 9 months, the CDC lists being shy, clingy or fearful around strangers and reacting when you leave by looking, reaching or crying.
Physically, many babies are pulling toward sitting, crawling and the first attempts to stand. The AAP and MedlinePlus say the crib mattress should be at its lowest setting before your baby can stand.

Practising crawling or standing in the crib instead of sleeping.

Your baby does not seem to know familiar people, or does not respond to their name by 9 months.
Anxiety so intense that daytime life is very hard, or that does not ease at all over months.

# Sleep at 9 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help

Sleep at 9 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 9 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and studies found an average of about 12.6 hours for babies from 9 months. Most babies take 2 naps as a common pattern. Bedtime protest is typical because babies now understand that you still exist when you leave, and the CDC lists clinginess with strangers as a 9-month milestone.

What is changing at 9 months
The CDC’s 9-month milestones explain a lot of what happens at bedtime. Each one has a sleep side.
CDC 9-month milestoneHow it can show up at night

Very loud, inconsolable screaming episodes early in the night. Usually harmless, but worth describing to the doctor if they recur.

Pulling up and cruising are the big sleep disruptors, and the AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months. Most babies still take 2 naps as a common pattern. What is changing at 10 months

Language is coming too. By 12 months, the CDC lists understanding “no” and calling a parent “mama” or “dada”. Babies who can call you, will.
Many babies can pull up long before they can get back down, which turns a brief waking into a long one. The mattress must already be at its lowest position before your baby learns to stand (AAP, MedlinePlus).

# Sleep at 11 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-11-months/

Sleep at 11 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
At 11 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Most babies still take 2 naps: a large review found the big shift to one nap happens between 12 and 18 months. Nap refusal at this age rarely means a baby is ready for one nap. Keep the crib empty and your baby on the back to start until the first birthday.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing at 11 months
Your baby is close to the CDC’s 1-year milestones: pulling up to stand, walking while holding furniture, waving bye-bye, understanding “no”, and playing games like pat-a-cake. That is a lot of new ability and a lot of new reasons to stay awake.
Separation anxiety is often near its peak; the AAP places the usual peak between 10 and 18 months.
Sleep need does not fall off a cliff at the birthday. A review of studies found babies from 9 months averaged 12.6 hours per 24 hours and babies from 12 months averaged 12.9 hours, so expect much the same total sleep for the next few months.

Nap strikes and early waking at 11 months often feed each other, and the fix that suits one baby makes another worse. Actually Sleeping works out which pattern your baby is in and writes a plan for it, with Dr. Sam checking in with you 1:1 every day.
The age row comes from a systematic review of napping studies. The other rows are a rule of thumb many families find useful, not a study finding.
What parents find hardest
Nap strikes. Babies who drop to one nap too early commonly start waking at night or very early in the morning.
Bedtime battles. More awareness, more protest.
Illness. Each cold can bring rough nights, and the extra help given while a baby is sick can outlast the illness.
Dreading the first birthday change in daycare rooms, which often move to one nap at a set age.
Safe sleep at 11 months
The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations cover babies up to 1 year. Keep the crib empty and start every sleep on the back until then.
No bottle in bed. The AAP advises against putting a baby to bed with a bottle, as part of its tooth decay prevention advice.
Mattress at the lowest setting. Check the rail height against your baby as they grow.
Keep the crib away from windows and blind cords, and anchor nearby furniture.
Night feeds
Ask your pediatrician at the 12-month check about night feeds and the move to whole milk; both are their call. Changes to night feeds should follow that advice, not a birthday.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness that seems excessive.
Night waking with fever, ear pulling, or crying that suggests pain.
Your baby is not yet pulling to stand, babbling, or using gestures like waving as 12 months approaches.

Sleep at 12 months: what’s normal at the first birthday and when to get help
At the first birthday, the AASM range shifts from 12 to 16 hours for babies to 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours for 1 to 2 year olds, including naps. Most 1 year olds still take 2 naps; the move to one usually happens between 12 and 18 months. The AAP’s infant safe sleep recommendations cover the first year.

What changes at the first birthday
By 1 year, the CDC lists pulling up to stand, walking while holding furniture, waving bye-bye, calling a parent “mama” or “dada”, and looking for things you hide. First steps may be close. Separation anxiety is often strong; the AAP says it usually peaks between 10 and 18 months.

What is normal
Two naps is still the most common pattern at 12 months. A systematic review found a dramatic drop in two-nap days between 12 and 18 months, and fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping altogether before age 2. Among babies under 12 months who napped, naps averaged about 3.1 hours a day in total; for 1 to 2 year olds the average was 2.3 hours.
What parents find hardest
The 12-month nap wobble. Many babies refuse one nap for a while, which makes it hard to tell a phase from real readiness.
Walking practice. Standing and cruising in the crib continue.
Daycare moving to one nap before your child is ready.
Milk changes. If your pediatrician moves your child from formula or changes feeds, expect some adjustment.
Safe sleep after the first birthday
The crib remains the safest place to sleep. Keep the mattress at its lowest setting.
The AAP advises against putting a child to bed with a bottle, as part of its tooth decay prevention advice.
Move to a bed when your child is 35 inches (89 cm) tall or the rail is below about three-quarters of their height, per the AAP and MedlinePlus. Most 1 year olds are nowhere near.
Ask your pediatrician before adding a pillow or blanket.
Night feeds
Whether a 1 year old still needs anything at night is a question for the 12-month visit. Your pediatrician decides; a sleep plan works around that decision.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping, or pauses in breathing. The AAP lists sleep apnea signs as frequent snoring, problems breathing at night, daytime sleepiness, attention difficulty and behavior problems.
Waking with pain or fever.
Your child is not yet pulling to stand, using gestures, or saying any special name for a parent.

If the year has ended with nights still broken, this is a very workable age to change it. What is changing at 15 months

# Sleep at 18 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help

Sleep at 18 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 18 months, the AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and most toddlers are on one nap. Climbing, separation worries and screen habits are the common sleep disruptors. The AAP says to avoid screens before 18 months, cap entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day from 18 months to age 5, and switch screens off an hour before bed.

What is changing at 18 months
By 18 months, the CDC lists walking without holding on, climbing on and off a couch or chair without help, trying to say three or more words, and moving away from you while checking you are still close. Climbing is the one that matters most at night.
The AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months and fades during the last half of the second year. Many toddlers are right at the top of that curve now.

Sleep at 21 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help

Most toddlers take one nap, and dropping it entirely is rare: a large review found fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2. Nap refusal, bedtime stalling and early waking are the usual complaints, and they are usually phases rather than signs your child has outgrown sleep.

What is changing at 21 months

Sleep at 2 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 2 years, the AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and nearly all 2 year olds still nap once a day. Bedtime stalling, the crib-to-bed question and early night terrors are common. The AAP says separation anxiety usually fades around the second birthday, and the time to leave the crib is at 35 inches tall or when your child can climb out.

What is changing at 2 years

Separation anxiety usually fades around the second birthday, according to the AAP. Night terrors, which the AAP says happen most often in toddlers and preschoolers, may start to appear.

At 2 the schedule is rarely the problem. Stalling, climbing and early starts come from a child who knows exactly how bedtime works in your house. Actually Sleeping works with families until age 3: Dr. Sam writes a plan for your child, and you get bootcamp-style coaching before night one and daily 1:1 check-ins.
If none of these apply, there is no medical reason to rush. Many families keep the crib until closer to 3, which is a common choice rather than a rule.
What is normal
In a review of studies, 2 to 3 year olds averaged 12.0 hours of sleep per 24 hours, with a normal spread of about 9.7 to 14.2 hours. Among those who napped, naps averaged about 1.9 hours at 2 to 3 years. Almost all children still nap at 2; by 3, about one in three have stopped.
What parents find hardest
Stalling. One more book, one more drink, one more question.
A new sibling or a new bed at the same time.
Night terrors. Screaming early in the night without really waking. The AAP says to stay calm and keep your child safe; most are much shorter than the 45-minute maximum it describes.
Climbing out of the crib once and then doing it every night.
Screens creeping into the evening. The AAP advises stopping screens 1 hour before bedtime and capping entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day from 18 months to age 5.
Night feeds
Most 2 year olds do not need to eat overnight, but your pediatrician decides that for your child. The AAP advises against a bottle in bed as part of its tooth decay prevention advice.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping, pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness and behavior changes that could signal sleep apnea.
Night terrors that keep happening, or any night event that looks like a seizure.
Fewer than two-word phrases, not running, or loss of skills your child had.

# Sleep at 2½ years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-30-months/

Sleep at 2½ years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 2½, the AASM range is still 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and most children still nap; about a third have stopped by age 3. Imagination is taking off, so fears, nightmares and night terrors become more common. Big-bed escapes are frequent, and the CDC lists turning doorknobs as a 30-month skill, so room safety matters.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing at 2½
By 30 months, the CDC lists saying about 50 words, using things to pretend, following simple routines when told, and using the hands to twist things, like turning doorknobs or unscrewing lids. Pretend play means a richer inner world, and with it new fears of the dark, monsters and dreams.
The AAP says nightmares can begin as early as 6 months and peak between 3 and 12 years. Night terrors are most common in toddlers and preschoolers. It helps to know the difference.
NightmareNight terror
WhenSecond half of the night, when dreaming is most intenseEarly in the night, often before parents go to bed
Your childWakes, is scared, wants comfort, may remember itScreams or thrashes but is not really awake
How longCalms once comfortedCan last up to 45 minutes; most are much shorter
What to doGo quickly, comfort, then encourage sleepStay calm, keep your child safe, do not try to wake them
At 2½, fears, big-bed escapes and long negotiations are normal development, and they are common reasons families reach out to Actually Sleeping. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your child that takes their fears seriously and gives every caregiver the same calm response, with daily 1:1 check-ins.
All rows come from the AAP’s HealthyChildren guidance.
What is normal
In a review of studies, 2 to 3 year olds averaged 12.0 hours per 24 hours. Among those who napped, naps averaged about 1.9 hours. About one in three children has stopped napping by age 3, so a 2½ year old who still naps is typical, and one who naps on some days is too. The AASM range for 1 to 2 year olds, 11 to 14 hours, still applies; its 3 to 5 year range of 10 to 13 hours starts at the third birthday.
What parents find hardest
Leaving the bed. Once in a big bed, many toddlers test it every night.
Fears at bedtime. Real to your child, and easy to turn into a nightly negotiation.
Naps that make bedtime late, while dropping the nap leaves an overtired evening.
Toilet training adding night trips and new reasons to call out.
Safe sleep at 2½
A doorknob-turner can leave the room. The AAP suggests a safety gate across the bedroom door and one at the top of the stairs.
Anchor dressers and shelves; latch or tape drawers so they cannot be used as steps (AAP).
Keep beds away from windows and use window guards above the first floor (AAP).
Night feeds
Night milk is rarely needed now, but your pediatrician decides. The AAP advises against a bottle in bed as part of its tooth decay prevention advice.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping or breathing pauses, or daytime sleepiness and behavior changes.
Night terrors that keep happening.
Fears that are severe, daily, and get in the way of daytime life.
Few words, no pretend play, or loss of skills.

Is my 2½ year old having nightmares or night terrors?Nightmares happen later in the night; your child wakes scared and wants comfort. # Sleep at 3 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-36-months/

Sleep at 3 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
From age 3, the AASM recommends 10 to 13 hours of sleep per 24 hours, including naps. About a third of children have stopped napping by their third birthday, and most of the rest stop over the next two years. Bedtime negotiation, fears and early waking are common. Regular snoring is worth raising with your pediatrician because sleep apnea affects an estimated 2% of children.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What is changing at 3
By 3 years, the CDC lists holding a conversation with at least two back-and-forth exchanges, asking who, what, where and why questions, joining other children to play, and calming down within 10 minutes after you leave, such as at a childcare drop-off. Your child can now argue about bedtime fluently.
The AASM range drops at the third birthday: 10 to 13 hours for 3 to 5 year olds, compared with 11 to 14 hours for 1 to 2 year olds. In a review of studies, children aged 2 to 3 averaged 12.0 hours per 24 hours. Night terrors remain common at this age, according to the AAP, and usually happen early in the night.
Napping at 3 and afterWhat the research shows (Staton 2020)
Stopped napping by age 3About 33%
Stopped by age 3 to 4About 57%
Stopped by age 4 to 5About 80%
Average nap, ages 3 to 4, among nappersAbout 1.7 hours
If your 3 year old still naps and falls asleep at a reasonable bedtime, there is no reason to stop. If the nap pushes bedtime late night after night, what to do about it depends on your child.
At 3, a plan works through rules your child can understand and predict, held the same way by every adult. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on: Dr. Sam writes the plan for your child, with bootcamp-style coaching before night one and daily 1:1 check-ins.
What parents find hardest
Negotiating. Requests, questions and “one more” at bedtime.
Coming out of the room, again and again.
Fears and nightmares. The AAP says nightmares peak between 3 and 12 years and happen in the second half of the night. Go quickly, comfort, and encourage sleep.
Dropping the nap. The in-between months, when some days need a nap and some do not, are often the hardest.
Sleep and safety at 3
Keep the bedroom safe for a child who wanders: anchored furniture, a gate at the top of the stairs, window guards above the first floor (AAP).
Stop screens 1 hour before bedtime and keep the bedroom media-free (AAP).
Cap entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day through age 5 (AAP).
Night waking and milk
Most 3 year olds do not need to eat at night, but if your child still wakes for milk, check with your pediatrician before changing it. Brush teeth after the last milk of the day.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Frequent snoring, problems breathing at night, daytime sleepiness, trouble paying attention or behavior problems. The AAP lists these as signs of sleep apnea and estimates it affects about 2% of children.
Night terrors that keep happening.
Sleep that is very short, very restless, or suddenly worse alongside other changes.
Your child is hard to understand most of the time or is not joining in play with other children.

# Baby and toddler sleep statistics: what the research actually shows
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-statistics/

Baby and toddler sleep statistics: what the research actually shows
The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep per 24 hours at 4–12 months, 11–14 hours at 1–2 years and 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, naps included, with no recommendation under 4 months. In one cohort of 388 babies, 27.9% to 57.0% of 6- and 12-month-olds did not sleep 6 or 8 hours straight. The CDC counted about 3,400 sudden unexpected infant deaths in 2024.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
35 findings, each one sentence long, each checked against the linked source on November 9, 2026. Numbers are given exactly as the source reports them. Where a study had a specific sample or definition, it is in the sentence, because a figure without its denominator is easy to misquote.
These figures describe large groups of children. They cannot tell you why one particular baby wakes at 2 a.m. or naps for 30 minutes. That is the question Actually Sleeping answers, one family at a time, with a sleep plan written for that baby and daily 1:1 support while it takes hold.
How much sleep: the official ranges
FindingYearSourceA 13-member American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) expert panel recommends 12–16 hours of sleep per 24 hours, naps included, for infants 4–12 months.2016sourceThe same AASM consensus recommends 11–14 hours per 24 hours, naps included, for children 1–2 years.2016sourceThe AASM recommends 10–13 hours per 24 hours, naps included, for children 3–5 years.2016sourceThe AASM makes no recommendation for babies under 4 months, citing the wide range of normal variation in sleep and too little evidence linking sleep to health outcomes at that age.2016source
What normal infant sleep looks like
FindingYearSourceA systematic review of 34 studies gave a mean infant sleep duration of 12.8 hours per 24 hours, with a reference range of 9.7 to 15.9 hours.2012sourceThe same review found reported night waking in babies 0–2 months ranged from 0 to 3.4 wakes per night.2012sourceIn a cohort of 388 infants, 27.9% to 57.0% of 6- and 12-month-olds did not sleep through the night, depending on whether that was defined as 6 or 8 hours of uninterrupted sleep.2018sourceIn that cohort, sleeping through the night was not significantly associated with mental development, psychomotor development or maternal mood.2018sourceA meta-analysis of napping found that fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2.2020sourceThe same meta-analysis found that 94% of children have stopped napping by age 5.2020source
How common parent-reported sleep problems are
FindingYearSourceIn a survey of parents of 2,154 children aged 0–3 years in Australia and New Zealand, 30.69% said their child had a sleep problem.2012sourceAcross 29,287 children aged 0–3 years in 17 countries and regions, the share of parents who said their child had a sleep problem ranged from 11% in Thailand to 76% in China.2010sourceIn 10,085 children aged 0–5 years across 13 countries and regions, more consistent bedtime routines were associated with better sleep outcomes in a dose-dependent way; the study was correlational.2015source
Prevalence figures depend heavily on who answers and how “problem” is defined. Most come from parent questionnaires, not clinical diagnosis.
Behavioral sleep interventions
FindingYearSourceAn AASM task force review of 52 treatment studies found 94% reported behavioral interventions effective, with over 80% of treated children showing clinically significant improvement maintained for 3 to 6 months.2006sourceThat review found strong support for unmodified extinction and for preventive parent education, plus support for graduated extinction, bedtime fading/positive routines and scheduled awakenings.2006sourceIn a cluster randomized trial of 328 mothers reporting an infant sleep problem at 7 months, sleep problems were less common with a behavioral intervention: 56% vs 68% at 10 months and 39% vs 55% at 12 months.2007sourceAt the 2-year follow-up of that trial, 15.4% of intervention mothers vs 26.4% of control mothers had depression symptoms above the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale community cut point.2008sourceIn a randomized trial of 43 infants aged 6–16 months, both graduated extinction and bedtime fading produced large decreases in time to fall asleep; graduated extinction also produced large decreases in night awakenings.2016sourceAt the 12-month follow-up of that trial there were no significant differences between groups in emotional and behavioral problems or in secure-insecure attachment.2016source
Parents’ sleep
FindingYearSourceIn a German panel of 2,541 women and 2,118 men, mothers’ sleep after a first child was at its lowest in the first 3 months, 62 minutes shorter than before pregnancy (fathers: 13 minutes), and did not fully recover for up to 6 years.2019source
Sleep-related infant deaths and safe sleep (United States)
FindingYearSourceAbout 3,400 sudden unexpected infant deaths (SUID) occurred in the United States in 2024.2024 datasourceOf those 2024 deaths, 1,351 were from SIDS, 1,099 from unknown causes and 947 from accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed.2024 datasourceThe U.S. average SUID rate for 2020–2024 was 106.6 per 100,000 live births.2020–2024 datasourceIn CDC case registry data on 4,861 SUIDs from 2020–2024, 66% of the infants were aged 0–3 months.2026sourceIn the same registry analysis, unsafe sleep factors were identified in at least 73% of cases.2026sourceMore than 90% of SIDS deaths occur before 6 months of age, and 72% occur in months 1–4.accessed 2026sourceIn 2015, 21.6% of mothers surveyed in 32 states and New York City reported placing their infant to sleep in a non-back (side or stomach) position.2018sourceIn the same 2015 survey data, 61.4% of respondents in 14 states reported any bed sharing, and 38.5% in 13 states and New York City reported using at least one type of soft bedding.2018sourceThe AAP recommends room sharing without bed sharing for at least the first 6 months and says it can decrease the risk of SIDS by as much as 50%.2026 (page update)source
SUID is the umbrella term for a sudden, unexpected death of a baby younger than 1 year; SIDS is one type of SUID. Definitions are in the sleep glossary.
Melatonin and young children
FindingYearSourceU.S. poison control centers received reports of 260,435 pediatric melatonin ingestions from 2012 to 2021; the annual number rose 530%, from 8,337 to 52,563.2022sourceIn that data, 94.3% of the ingestions were unintentional, 4,097 children were hospitalized, and two children died.2022sourceAn estimated 10,930 emergency department visits by children aged 5 and under were for unsupervised melatonin ingestion in 2019–2022, 7.1% of all such visits for unsupervised medication exposures; gummies were the most commonly documented form (47.3%).2024sourceLaboratory testing of 25 melatonin gummy products sold in the U.S. found actual melatonin content ranged from 74% to 347% of the labeled amount.2023sourceIn a 2023 parent survey (convenience sample), 5.6% of children aged 1–4 years had used melatonin in the past 30 days.2023source
The AAP’s parent site says over-the-counter melatonin is not regulated by the FDA for this use and should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician. See is melatonin safe for babies.
Sleep environment products
FindingYearSourceAll 14 infant sleep machines tested produced maximum sound levels above 50 A-weighted decibels at 30 cm, and three exceeded 85 decibels.2014source
How to read these numbers
Years. “Year” is the publication year of the source, or the data year where the source is a statistics page. “Accessed 2026” marks an undated web page.
Correlation is not cause. Survey and cohort findings (routines, sleeping through the night) show associations only. The trial rows are randomized.
Country. Death and melatonin figures are U.S. data. Prevalence studies are labelled with their countries.
Rule-of-thumb ranges are not here. Wake windows and nap lengths are practice conventions, not research findings, so they are on the wake window calculator, clearly labelled.
How to cite this page
Actually Sleeping. “Baby and toddler sleep statistics: what the research actually shows.” https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-statistics/ (checked November 9, 2026). For any single figure, please cite the original source linked in its row.

Frequently asked
How many babies sleep through the night at 6 months?It depends on the definition. In a 2018 Pediatrics cohort of 388 infants, 27.9% to 57.0% of 6- and 12-month-olds did not sleep through the night, using 6 or 8 hours of uninterrupted sleep as the cut-off. Not sleeping through was not linked to developmental delay or maternal mood.
How common are sleep problems in babies and toddlers?Parent surveys vary widely. 30.69% of parents of 2,154 Australian and New Zealand children aged 0–3 reported a sleep problem (2012). Across 17 countries and regions, the figure ranged from 11% in Thailand to 76% in China (2010).
Does sleep training work, according to research?An AASM task force review of 52 studies (2006) found 94% reported behavioral interventions effective, with over 80% of children improving for 3 to 6 months. A 2016 randomized trial found no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment at 12-month follow-up.
How many babies die of SIDS each year in the US?The CDC reports about 3,400 sudden unexpected infant deaths in 2024: 1,351 from SIDS, 1,099 from unknown causes and 947 from accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed. More than 90% of SIDS deaths happen before 6 months, according to the NICHD.
Has melatonin poisoning in children increased?Yes. CDC data show pediatric melatonin ingestions reported to U.S. poison control centers rose 530% from 2012 to 2021, to 52,563 a year. Most were unintentional. A 2024 CDC report estimated 10,930 emergency visits by children 5 and under in 2019–2022.

# Baby sleep glossary: 40 terms parents hear, in plain English
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-glossary/

Baby sleep glossary: 40 terms parents hear, in plain English
Most baby sleep jargon falls into three groups: timing (wake window, sleep pressure, circadian rhythm), how a baby falls asleep (sleep association, self-settling, drowsy but awake) and safety (SIDS, SUID, room sharing, safe sleep). Below, 40 terms are defined in one to three plain sentences, methods are described without endorsement, and safety facts link to AAP, CDC and NIH sources.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
40 terms, alphabetical, each in one to three sentences. Methods are described, not recommended. Safety and research statements are taken from the AAP, CDC, NIH and peer-reviewed sources listed at the bottom. Each term has its own link, for example /guides/baby-sleep-glossary/#wake-window.
Knowing the words is the first step. Knowing which of them explains your baby’s nights is harder, and that is what Actually Sleeping works out with each family: a sleep plan written for that baby, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins.
Jump to a term
Active sleep · Bed sharing · Bedtime fading · Camping out · Catnap · Chair method · Circadian rhythm · Cluster feeding · Contact nap · Corrected age · Dream feed · Drowsy but awake · Early rising · Extinction · False start · Graduated extinction · Melatonin · Nap transition · Night weaning · Overtired · Quiet time · REM sleep · Room sharing · Safe sleep · Self-settling · SIDS · Sleep association · Sleep cycle · Sleep debt · Sleep pressure · Sleep regression · Sleep sack · Split night · SUID · Swaddle · TOG · Undertired · Wake window · White noise · Witching hour
The terms
Active sleepThe newborn version of REM sleep: eyes may flicker, breathing is irregular and the baby twitches or grimaces. Newborns fall asleep through this stage rather than through quiet sleep, which is one reason they rouse so easily.Bed sharingA baby sleeping on the same bed, sofa or other surface as an adult or child. The AAP recommends avoiding bed sharing under any circumstances, including with twins and other multiples.Bedtime fadingA method that temporarily moves bedtime later, to when a child reliably falls asleep quickly, then moves it earlier in small steps. In a 2016 randomized trial it shortened the time infants took to fall asleep. More in bedtime fading.Camping outA parent-present method: the parent stays in the room while the child falls asleep and moves gradually farther away, and eventually out, over a series of nights. The term is often used interchangeably with the chair method.CatnapA short nap, often one sleep cycle or less. Parents also use it for the brief late-afternoon nap many younger babies take before bedtime.Chair methodA method in which a parent sits on a chair beside the crib at bedtime and moves the chair a little farther away every few nights until it is out of the room. See the chair method.Circadian rhythmThe body’s roughly 24-hour clock, which times sleepiness, alertness and hormones. In babies it develops at around 2 to 3 months, which is why newborn sleep is scattered across day and night.Cluster feedingA widely used term for a stretch of very frequent feeds close together, common in newborns and young infants, often in the evening hours.Contact napA nap a baby takes while being held or worn by an adult. If you might fall asleep, the AAP says to put the baby in their own sleep space first; it notes the risk of sleep-related death is up to 67 times higher when infants sleep with someone on a couch, soft armchair or cushion. See how to stop contact napping.Corrected ageFor a baby born early, age from birth minus the number of weeks born preterm (40 minus gestational age at birth). The AAP suggests using it during the first 2 years to judge when to expect developmental milestones.Dream feedA feed given to a sleeping baby, usually late in the evening before the parent goes to bed, without fully waking the baby. Some families use it to try to shift the baby’s longest stretch later. See does a dream feed work.Drowsy but awakePutting a baby into the crib relaxed and sleepy but still awake, so the final step of falling asleep happens in the crib. It is a common suggestion for helping a baby learn to fall asleep independently.Early risingWaking for the day earlier than the family wants and not going back to sleep. It is a parent-defined problem, not a medical diagnosis. See early morning waking.ExtinctionA method in which a parent puts the child to bed at a set time and does not return until morning, except for safety or illness. Researchers call it unmodified extinction; a 2006 AASM review found strong research support for it. See extinction explained.False startA waking soon after bedtime, often 30–45 minutes in, as if the first sleep cycle had been a nap. See false starts at bedtime.Graduated extinctionA method in which a parent leaves and returns for brief checks at intervals that lengthen over time. In a 2016 randomized trial it reduced time to fall asleep and night awakenings, with no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment at 12-month follow-up. See graduated extinction explained.MelatoninA hormone the body releases in darkness that signals nighttime; in babies a day-night melatonin rhythm appears by about 3 months. In the U.S. it is also sold as a supplement that the FDA does not regulate like medicines, and the AAP says to use it only after talking with your pediatrician.Nap transitionThe weeks during which a child drops from one number of naps to fewer, for example from 3 naps to 2 or 2 to 1. Days are often mixed during the switch. See nap transitions.Night weaningGradually or fully stopping feeds during the night. Whether and when a baby no longer needs night feeds is a decision for your pediatrician. See night weaning.OvertiredA parent term for a baby who has been awake too long for their age and becomes harder, not easier, to settle. It is a practical description rather than a medical diagnosis. See overtired baby.Quiet timeA rest period in a child’s room, usually after a toddler or preschooler stops napping, where the child plays quietly instead of sleeping.REM sleepRapid eye movement sleep, the lighter, dream-associated stage. In infants a full cycle of non-REM and REM sleep lasts about 50 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes in adults.Room sharingThe baby sleeps on their own safe surface in the parents’ bedroom. The AAP recommends it for at least the first 6 months and says it can decrease the risk of SIDS by as much as 50%.Safe sleepThe set of practices that reduce sleep-related infant death: back to sleep for every sleep, a firm flat surface, nothing soft in the sleep space, and room sharing without bed sharing. The AAP says any surface inclined more than 10 degrees is not safe for sleep. See safe sleep and sleep training.Self-settlingFalling asleep, or back to sleep after a waking, without an adult’s help. Also called self-soothing or independent sleep.SIDSSudden infant death syndrome: the sudden death of a baby younger than 1 year that has no known cause even after a full investigation. It is one type of SUID.Sleep associationSomething a child links with falling asleep, such as feeding, rocking, a pacifier or a parent’s presence. It matters most when the child needs it again to return to sleep after normal night wakings. See feed-to-sleep association.Sleep cycleOne round of non-REM and REM sleep. Infant cycles last about 50 minutes, and a brief partial waking between cycles is normal. See how infant sleep cycles develop.Sleep debtThe running shortfall between the sleep a person needs and the sleep they get. Parents use it loosely for a child who has had several short nights or short naps in a row.Sleep pressureThe drive to sleep that builds the longer someone is awake and eases during sleep. It is the idea behind wake windows: enough pressure helps a baby fall asleep, too little makes settling slow.Sleep regressionA popular term for a stretch, often around 4, 8–10, 12 or 18 months, when a child who was sleeping well starts waking more or fighting naps. It is not a medical diagnosis. See the 4-month regression.Sleep sackA wearable blanket. The AAP prefers infant sleep clothing over loose blankets, says sacks that do not swaddle and let the baby move freely can be used as long as you want, and says not to use weighted blankets, sleepers, swaddles or other weighted objects on or near your baby.Split nightA long stretch of wakefulness in the middle of the night, often 1–3 hours, with the child calm or playful rather than upset. See split nights.SUIDSudden unexpected infant death: a sudden, unexpected death of a baby younger than 1 year. It is the umbrella category that includes SIDS, accidental suffocation in a sleeping environment, and deaths from unknown causes.SwaddleWrapping a baby snugly in a thin blanket or swaddle product with the arms in. The AAP says to stop as soon as a baby shows signs of trying to roll, to leave room for the hips to move, to avoid overheating, and says there is no evidence to recommend swaddling as a way to reduce SIDS risk. See swaddle transition.TOGShort for thermal overall grade, a rating of how much warmth a fabric holds in. The higher the tog value, the more insulation; you will see it on some sleep sacks.UndertiredA parent term for a child put down before enough sleep pressure has built, who then plays, chats or takes a long time to fall asleep. Like overtired, it is a practical description, not a diagnosis.Wake windowThe stretch of time a baby is awake between one sleep and the next. Age-based wake window ranges are rules of thumb from practice, not research findings. See the wake window calculator.White noiseA steady, even sound used to mask household noise during sleep. In a 2014 study, all 14 infant sleep machines tested could exceed 50 decibels at 30 cm, so volume and distance from the crib matter.Witching hourA parent term for a regular period of evening fussiness in young babies. The AAP’s parent site notes fussy periods often fall between 6 p.m. and midnight.
Where the numbers come from
Figures in these definitions (cycle length, room-sharing guidance, the 10-degree incline limit, sound levels) are on the baby sleep statistics page or in the references below, each checked on the source page.

Frequently asked
What is the difference between SIDS and SUID?SUID, sudden unexpected infant death, is the umbrella term for any sudden, unexpected death of a baby under 1. SIDS is one type of SUID: a death with no known cause even after a full investigation. Accidental suffocation in a sleeping environment is another type.
Is a sleep regression a medical condition?No. It is a popular term for a period when a child who was sleeping well starts waking more or resisting naps, often around developmental changes. If sleep changes come with fever, pain or other symptoms, call your pediatrician.
What is the difference between extinction and graduated extinction?In extinction, the parent does not return after bedtime except for safety or illness. In graduated extinction, the parent returns for brief checks at intervals that lengthen over time. Both are behavioral methods studied in research; neither is required to improve a child’s sleep, and Actually Sleeping uses neither.
Are wake windows based on research?No. Age-based wake window ranges are practice conventions. The research recommendation is total sleep per 24 hours: the AASM gives 12–16 hours at 4–12 months and 11–14 hours at 1–2 years, and none under 4 months.

The calculator shows what a typical baby of that age does. Your baby may be nowhere near it, for reasons the chart cannot see: how they fall asleep, how they feed, their temperament, your family’s day. How the calculator works
Awake time is the typical range between one sleep and the next for that age. The first window of the day is usually the shortest and the last before bed the longest.
First nap is your wake-up time plus that range.
Bedtime is worked back from your wake-up time using typical overnight sleep for the age. Under about 3 months there is no derived bedtime, because night sleep is still broken by feeds.
Times are rounded to 5 minutes. Feeding on cue always comes before any clock time.

When the numbers do not fit your baby
A window that is too short and one that is too long can look the same: short naps, early waking, more night waking. And when the real cause is how a baby falls asleep, no change of timing fixes it. See why naps are only 30 minutes. Telling these apart from the outside is hard, which is why parents can spend weeks adjusting the clock without a better night.

Are wake windows evidence-based?No. Age-based wake windows are practice conventions, useful as a starting point. The research-based figure is total sleep: the AASM recommends 12–16 hours per 24 hours at 4–12 months and 11–14 hours at 1–2 years, naps included, with no recommendation under 4 months.
Should I wake my baby to keep to the calculator’s times?The times are an average, not a rule for your baby. Feeding on cue comes first for young babies, and your pediatrician’s advice comes before any chart. A plan from Actually Sleeping sets when to protect or cap a nap for your baby specifically.

# What time should my baby or toddler go to bed? Bedtime calculator by age
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-bedtime-calculator/

What time should my baby or toddler go to bed? Bedtime calculator by age
Work backward from wake-up time. The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep per 24 hours at 4–12 months, 11–14 hours at 1–2 years and 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, naps included, and makes no recommendation under 4 months. Subtract typical nap time to get night sleep, then subtract night sleep from wake-up time. The calculator does the math.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The calculator starts from research and works backward. The research part is the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) recommended total sleep per 24 hours for your child’s age. The rule-of-thumb part is how much of that sleep usually happens in naps. Night sleep is what is left, and bedtime is your wake-up time minus night sleep.
Child’s age
Under 4 months4 months5 months6 months7 months8 months9–11 months12–14 months15–23 months2 years3 years
Usual wake-up time

 Yes
 No
Work out bedtime
The calculator needs JavaScript. The same numbers are in the table below.
Keep in mind: a calculator gives an average. The hard part is getting your particular baby to follow it. That is what a custom plan and daily check-ins are for.
A bedtime on paper is the easy part. Many families already know roughly when their child should be asleep; the problem is that the child does not go to sleep then, or does not stay asleep. Actually Sleeping works on that part, with a plan written for your child and daily support while it settles.
The formula
Take the AASM range for the age: 12–16 hours at 4–12 months, 11–14 hours at 1–2 years, 10–13 hours at 3–5 years, naps included.
Subtract the middle of the typical nap total for the age (a rule of thumb). If your child no longer naps, subtract nothing.
The result is the night sleep that keeps the 24-hour total inside the AASM range.
Bedtime window = wake-up time minus that night sleep. The early end gives the most sleep; at the late end, total sleep only just reaches the AASM minimum.
Because the AASM ranges are 3–4 hours wide, the window is wide too. The last column of the table shows the narrower bedtime many families use in practice, which is a rule of thumb, not a research finding. That column describes time in bed, and children rarely sleep every minute of it, which is why it can start slightly earlier than the AASM-based window.
Under 4 months: no number
The AASM makes no recommendation for babies under 4 months, citing the wide range of normal variation and too little evidence linking sleep to health outcomes at that age. This page therefore shows no bedtime for that band. Newborn bedtimes are often late and drift earlier over the first few months.

Night sleep is calculated with the middle of the nap range. For a different wake-up time, move every bedtime by the same amount: a 6:30 a.m. riser’s window is 30 minutes earlier.
Children who have stopped napping
With no nap, all of the AASM total has to come at night, so the window moves earlier. A 2020 meta-analysis found fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2 and 94% have stopped by age 5, so a child under 2 who refuses naps for a few days is more likely going through a nap transition than finished with naps. See nap transitions.

Frequently asked
What time should a 1 year old go to bed?The AASM recommends 11–14 hours of sleep per 24 hours at 1–2 years. With about 2–2.5 hours of naps and a 7 a.m. wake-up, that gives an AASM-based window of about 7:15 to 10:15 p.m. In practice many families use 7–8 p.m., a rule of thumb.
Is a 6:30 p.m. bedtime too early?Not necessarily. For a baby 4–12 months who wakes around 6:30 a.m. and naps a typical amount, a 6:30 p.m. bedtime keeps total sleep within the AASM range of 12–16 hours. Use the calculator with your own wake-up time to check.
Why is there no bedtime for my newborn?The AASM makes no sleep-hours recommendation under 4 months because normal sleep varies widely and there is too little evidence linking sleep to health at that age. Any number would be invented, so the calculator shows none.
My toddler dropped their nap. How does bedtime change?Without a nap, all the AASM total has to come at night, so bedtime moves earlier. For ages 1–2 years and a 7 a.m. wake-up, 11–14 hours of night sleep means a bedtime between 5 and 8 p.m.; choose the earlier part during the transition.

# How long should my baby sleep in our room?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-long-should-baby-room-share/

How long should my baby sleep in our room?
The AAP recommends your baby sleep in your room, in their own crib or bassinet, for at least the first 6 months. After that, the choice is yours. Room sharing without bed sharing helps protect against SIDS. One large study linked room sharing at 4 and 9 months with less night sleep, so many families move their baby out after 6 months.
