What the AAP says
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that parents sleep in the same room as their baby, but not in the same bed, for at least the first 6 months. The baby sleeps on their back in their own crib, bassinet or play yard, close to your bed. The AAP’s parent site says room sharing can lower the risk of SIDS by as much as 50%, and that it is safer than bed sharing.
Six months is the minimum, not a deadline. Nothing in the guidance says you must move your baby at 6 months, and nothing says you must keep them in your room after it.
What happens to sleep after 6 months
A 2017 study in Pediatrics followed first-time mothers and their babies. At 9 months, babies who had their own room before 4 months slept 40 minutes more per night than babies still room sharing, and their longest stretch was 100 minutes longer. Room-sharing families also had about four times the odds of moving to overnight bed sharing at 4 and 9 months.
That study was observational. It shows an association, not proof that the room caused the difference, and it does not change the AAP’s advice to room share for at least the first 6 months. Still, the pattern matches what many parents notice: you hear every grunt, you respond to sounds a baby would have slept through, and your baby hears you come to bed.
Room sharing is a safety recommendation, and it can coexist with good sleep. When it does not, the fixable part is usually how your baby falls asleep, which is what Actually Sleeping works on, in whatever room your baby sleeps.
Signs room sharing is costing your family sleep
Your baby is past 6 months and you wake each other several times a night.
You go in at every noise, and your baby has learned to expect it.
Your baby wakes when you come to bed or turn over.
You find yourself bringing your baby into your bed in the early hours.
The room is rarely the whole problem
Moving a baby to their own room helps when the waking is caused by you: your noise, your movements, your quick response. It does not help a baby who wakes because they need to be fed, rocked or held back to sleep between sleep cycles. Those babies usually wake just as often in a new room, and parents end up walking further at 2 a.m. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried things on their own, often including a change of room.
The fixable part is how your baby falls asleep. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby that works in your actual setup, whether your baby is in your room, their own room or a shared one. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins after it. See sleep training while room sharing, and hear from families in our 129 client video reviews.
If your baby moves rooms
All the safe-sleep rules still apply in the new room until your baby’s first birthday: on the back, in a crib with a firm, flat mattress and only a fitted sheet, with no pillows, blankets, bumpers or soft toys. Keep monitor and lamp cords well away from the crib.

# Is bed-sharing with my baby safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/is-bed-sharing-safe/

Is bed-sharing with my baby safe?
The AAP does not support bed-sharing with a baby under any circumstances, including twins. Risk is highest for babies under 4 months, on sofas and armchairs, and when an adult has been drinking, smokes, or takes sedating medication. Room share instead: your baby sleeps on their back in their own crib or bassinet in your room, for at least the first 6 months.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the AAP says
The AAP’s 2022 safe-sleep recommendations say it “cannot support bed-sharing under any circumstances.” The AAP’s parent site adds that this includes twins and other multiples. It recommends room sharing without bed sharing for at least the first 6 months instead.
About 3,500 babies die from sleep-related causes in the United States each year, according to the AAP.
When the risk is highest
The AAP’s parent site gives these figures:
Bed-sharing risk is 5 to 10 times higher when a baby is younger than 4 months.
Risk is up to 67 times higher when a baby sleeps with someone on a sofa, soft armchair or cushion.
Risk is more than 10 times higher when a baby bed shares with someone who is very tired, has taken medications, or has used alcohol or drugs, and it is especially high with an adult who smokes or vapes.
The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign groups the situations like this:
Risk levelSituation
Very highA soft surface such as a waterbed, old mattress, sofa or armchair. An adult who is very tired, on drowsy-making medication, or using alcohol or other substances. An adult who smokes or uses tobacco, even outside the bed.
HighA baby younger than 4 months. A sleeping adult who is not the parent, such as a grandparent or a sibling.
Higher than normalA baby born preterm (before 37 weeks) or at low birth weight. Pillows or blankets in the sleep area.
Safe to Sleep also notes that the longer an adult shares a bed with a baby, the higher the baby’s risk. That matters for parents who plan to bed share only for the early hours: the guidance applies to those hours too, and to naps.
Many parents bed-share because their baby will not sleep any other way. That is the part Actually Sleeping fixes: a plan that gets your baby sleeping in their own safe space, without forcing night feeds to drop.
Why families end up bed sharing
Usually it is exhaustion, not a choice. A baby who wakes every hour and only settles next to a parent makes the bed feel like the only way anyone sleeps. Parents reach for bed-sharing because the baby is not sleeping, and the baby is not sleeping because they need a parent to fall back asleep between sleep cycles. That waking is the fixable part.
That is what Actually Sleeping does. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby that keeps them in their own safe sleep space and teaches them to fall asleep there, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. The plan never forces dropping night feeds; feeding decisions belong to your pediatrician. Families who moved from the family bed to the crib share their experience in reviews from families who were co-sleeping.
If you might fall asleep while feeding
This is the situation most parents actually face at 3 a.m. Plan for it instead of hoping it won’t happen.
Never feed on a sofa or armchair if you are drowsy. These are the most dangerous places to fall asleep with a baby.
If you feed in bed, clear pillows, blankets and soft items away from your side of the bed first, as Safe to Sleep advises.
If you fall asleep, put your baby back in their own sleep space as soon as you wake.
Set yourself up to stay awake: a light on low, sitting up, a phone timer, or a partner who takes the baby back to the bassinet.

# Are crib bumpers safe, including mesh bumpers?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/are-crib-bumpers-safe/

Are crib bumpers safe, including mesh bumpers?
No. Padded crib bumpers are banned from sale in the United States under the Safe Sleep for Babies Act, in effect since November 12, 2022, and the AAP says no bumper pads in your baby’s bed. The law does not cover non-padded mesh liners, but the CPSC’s advice is still “Bare is Best”: nothing but a fitted sheet in the crib.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the law says
The Safe Sleep for Babies Act was signed on May 16, 2022. Since November 12, 2022, crib bumpers are banned hazardous products in the United States, regardless of when they were made. They cannot be sold, made for sale, distributed or imported.
The law defines a crib bumper as any material meant to cover the sides of a crib to prevent injury. That includes:
Padded crib bumpers
Supported and unsupported vinyl bumper guards
Vertical crib slat covers
It does not include non-padded mesh crib liners. If you received a bumper as a gift or with a crib set, don’t pass it on to another family; the safest place for it is the trash.
What the AAP and CPSC recommend
The AAP’s parent site is direct: there should be no blankets, pillows, stuffed toys or bumper pads in your baby’s bed. Soft objects and loose bedding can increase the risk of entrapment, suffocation or strangulation. The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign says research links crib bumpers, and bedding other than a fitted sheet, to sleep-related deaths.
The CPSC’s rule of thumb is “Bare is Best”: nothing but a fitted sheet in a crib, bassinet or play yard. In its 2018 to 2020 data, the CPSC reported an annual average of 100 deaths, most associated with extra bedding such as pillows, blankets or comforters.
If you are looking at bumpers because your baby keeps waking in the crib, the waking is a separate problem with a safe fix. Actually Sleeping works on that, inside a bare crib.
What about mesh liners
Mesh liners are legal to sell because the law’s definition leaves them out. Legal to sell is not the same as recommended. The CPSC’s guidance is still a fitted sheet only, and the AAP lists nothing else that belongs in the crib. If you already have one, the safest choice is to take it out.
The worries bumpers were meant to solve
WorryThe safe answer
Head bumping the slatsBumps against the slats are usually just noisy. Check the crib instead: MedlinePlus advises slats no more than 2 3/8 inches apart, about the width of a soda can.
Arm or leg stuck between slatsAnnoying, and it wakes babies, but a stuck limb is easy to free. A sleep sack can make it less frequent. Never add padding or slat covers.
DraftsDress your baby in layers or a sleep sack rather than adding anything to the crib.
Noise of head bangingMove the crib a little away from the wall and tighten the bolts. See head banging and rocking at bedtime.
When the real worry is waking
Many parents look at bumpers because their baby keeps waking: a limb through the slats, a bump against the side, a baby who rolls into the corner and cries. Padding would not fix that, and it is not safe. A baby who wakes at every small disturbance and cannot get back to sleep alone usually needs help falling asleep between sleep cycles, and that is the part that can be fixed. Actually Sleeping works on exactly that, inside a bare crib: Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Hear from parents in our 129 client video reviews.
Older and second-hand cribs
If you are using a hand-me-down crib, check it against current standards: no drop sides, slats no more than 2 3/8 inches apart, no missing hardware, and a firm mattress that fits snugly. MedlinePlus states plainly that drop-rail cribs are not safe for babies. Remove any bumpers, positioners or padding that came with it.
Once your baby can stand, anything in the crib can also become a step. That is one more reason to keep it bare and to lower the mattress early; see when your baby stands up in the crib.

# Are baby loungers, inclined sleepers and sleep positioners safe for sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/inclined-sleepers-loungers-and-positioners/

Are baby loungers, inclined sleepers and sleep positioners safe for sleep?
No. Inclined sleepers with a sleep surface over 10 degrees are banned in the U.S. under the Safe Sleep for Babies Act. The CPSC says never to use infant support cushions, which include loungers and nursing-and-lounging pillows, for sleep or naps, and the FDA says never to use sleep positioners. Your baby should sleep flat on their back with only a fitted sheet.

Inclined sleepers
Under the Safe Sleep for Babies Act, an inclined sleeper is a product with a sleep surface inclined more than 10 degrees that is meant to provide sleep for a baby up to 1 year old. Since November 12, 2022, these are banned hazardous products in the United States.
The AAP’s parent site says any surface that inclines more than 10 degrees isn’t safe for a baby to sleep on. The CPSC tells parents not to let a baby sleep in any inclined product over 10 degrees, such as a rocker, bouncer, swing or glider. In its 2018 to 2020 data, the CPSC counted an average of 15 deaths a year associated with inclined infant products not intended for sleep.
Loungers and support cushions
The CPSC has approved a federal safety standard for infant support cushions. The products it covers include:
Infant loungers
Infant head positioner pillows
Infant sleep positioners and anti-rollover pillows
Multi-purpose pillows marketed for both nursing and lounging
The CPSC reports 79 infant deaths and 124 injuries associated with these cushions between 2010 and 2022. Its advice is clear: never use infant support cushions for infant sleep or naps. If your baby falls asleep on one, move them to a crib, bassinet or play yard.
Second-hand loungers and pillows are worth a second look too: older products were made before the new standard. A lounger is not a place to sleep even when you are in the room. Many of these products are used for supervised lounging during the day; the danger is a baby dozing off and being left there.
If your baby only sleeps propped up or in a lounger, the sleep problem underneath is fixable. Actually Sleeping gets babies sleeping flat on their backs in their own crib or bassinet, with a plan written for each baby.
Sleep positioners and wedges
The FDA tells parents to never use infant sleep positioners, the mats with raised side bolsters or wedges meant to hold a baby on their back or side. It warns that they can cause suffocation and death, and that it has never cleared a sleep positioner that claims to prevent or reduce the risk of SIDS. The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign adds that wedges, positioners and similar products do not meet federal guidelines for sleep safety.
What about reflux or a stuffy nose
These are the two most common medical reasons parents want to raise a baby’s head. The AAP’s answer is the same for both: propping a baby on towels or pillows, or inclining the mattress, is not safe. Babies should sleep flat on their backs on a firm, even surface. For reflux, see sleep and reflux; for congestion, see humidifiers and stuffy noses. If symptoms worry you, call your pediatrician rather than changing the sleep surface.

# Do I need a baby monitor, and what does the AAP say about wearable oxygen monitors?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-monitors-and-wearable-monitors/

Do I need a baby monitor, and what does the AAP say about wearable oxygen monitors?
A simple audio or video monitor is a convenience, not a safety device. The AAP says not to use home cardiorespiratory monitors as a way to reduce SIDS risk, and the NIH Safe to Sleep campaign says monitors that track heart rate, breathing or motion are not effective at detecting or preventing SIDS. Safe sleep practices are what lower risk.

What the AAP and NIH say
The AAP’s 2022 recommendations say: do not use home cardiorespiratory monitors as a strategy to reduce the risk of SIDS. Its parent site adds a warning that matters just as much: don’t let these devices give you a false sense of security. The AAP also advises against commercial devices that claim to reduce the risk of SIDS or other sleep-related deaths.
The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign says monitors that track a baby’s heart, breathing or motion are not effective at detecting or preventing SIDS, and are not recommended as a way to reduce that risk.

AudioLets you hear your baby from another roomConvenience only

Movement pad or clip-on motion sensorAlarms if it stops detecting movementNot a way to reduce SIDS risk, per NIH
Wearable sock or band with oxygen and heart rateReports readings to an app and alarms on certain valuesNot a way to reduce SIDS risk, per AAP and NIH
If you are shopping for a monitor because nights are hard, the monitor will not change the nights. Actually Sleeping works on why your baby wakes, with a plan written for your baby.
What research found on consumer oxygen monitors
A 2018 study in JAMA tested two consumer pulse-oximetry baby monitors against a hospital monitor in 30 infants aged 0 to 6 months who were in hospital. One monitor never detected low oxygen. The other detected low oxygen in every infant who had it, but also showed normal readings during some of those episodes. The monitor that missed low oxygen also falsely showed a low heart rate in 14 babies whose real heart rate was normal. The authors urged caution about using data from these monitors in medical decisions.
Products and software change, so those exact results may not apply to every model sold today. The core point stands: a reading on an app is not a diagnosis, and no monitor replaces a safe sleep space.
False alarms and parent stress
The AAP’s page on home apnea monitors notes that they cause many false alarms, that the noise can make parents worry too much and lose sleep, and that one study found parents of monitored infants felt more depressed. If a device is keeping you awake checking an app, it is costing your family sleep without lowering your baby’s risk.
When a doctor prescribes a monitor
In rare cases, a doctor recommends a home monitor for a specific medical reason, for example a baby who needs home oxygen or has serious breathing problems. That is a medical device used under a care plan. It is different from a consumer product bought for peace of mind. If your baby was in the NICU or has a breathing condition, ask your pediatrician whether monitoring is needed.
Keeping a regular monitor safe
Keep cords away from the crib. The CPSC says never place corded cameras within three feet of a crib; cords can strangle infants and toddlers. Mount the camera on the wall or a high shelf.
The basics do the protecting: back to sleep, a firm flat surface with only a fitted sheet, room sharing for at least the first 6 months, no smoking, and no bed sharing.
A monitor watches the waking; it does not change it
Many parents upgrade monitors when nights are hard, hoping more data will explain the waking. A monitor can tell you that your baby woke. It cannot tell you why, and it cannot teach your baby to fall back asleep. Babies who wake many times a night usually need help to get back to sleep between sleep cycles, and that is the fixable part. It is what Actually Sleeping works on: a plan written for your baby by Dr. Sam, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins. A video monitor can be useful during a plan, because you can see that your baby is safe and settling without opening the door. Parents describe the change in our 129 client video reviews.

# My baby only sleeps in the car seat, swing or stroller. Is that okay?

My baby only sleeps in the car seat, swing or stroller. Is that okay?
Dozing off in one is common, but staying asleep there is not safe. The AAP says sitting devices like car seats, strollers, swings and infant carriers are not recommended for routine sleep, especially under 4 months. If your baby falls asleep in one, move them to a firm, flat crib, bassinet or play yard, on their back, as soon as you can.

What the AAP and CPSC say
The AAP’s 2022 recommendations say sitting devices, such as car seats, strollers, swings, infant carriers and slings, are not recommended for routine sleep, particularly for babies under 4 months. If your baby falls asleep in one, the AAP’s parent site says to move them to a firm sleep surface on their back as soon as possible.
The CPSC tells parents not to let a baby sleep in any inclined product over 10 degrees, such as a rocker, bouncer, swing or glider, and to move a sleeping baby to a crib, bassinet or play yard. Its 2018 to 2020 data showed an average of 15 deaths a year associated with inclined infant products not intended for sleep.
In the car is different
A properly installed car seat is where your baby belongs in a moving car, asleep or awake. The concern is what happens after the trip: a sleeping baby left in the car seat on the floor, carried inside and parked by the sofa for a long nap. When you arrive, take your baby out and move them to their sleep space, even if it wakes them.
A baby who only sleeps in motion has a fixable sleep problem, not a stubborn personality. Actually Sleeping moves sleep into the crib with a plan written for your baby, and coaches naps until they are solid.
Carriers and slings
Babywearing is a lovely way to settle a fussy baby. The AAP lists carriers and slings among sitting devices not recommended for routine sleep. If your baby falls asleep in one, the AAP’s advice is the same as for any sitting device: move them to a firm, flat sleep surface, on their back, as soon as you can.
Why babies sleep so well in these places
Motion, a snug fit, constant noise and being upright all feel calming. Many babies also fall asleep in them at the right moment by accident: the walk or drive happens to line up with the end of a wake window. The crib then gets all the hard moments, overtired or not tired enough, and seems to be the problem.
Over time, motion becomes part of how your baby falls asleep. Every move to the crib wakes them, because the conditions they fell asleep in have changed. Parents end up driving laps, pacing with the stroller or running the swing for every nap, and the transfer fails as often as it works. Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own.
Why this needs a plan, not a trick
The lasting fix is a baby who falls asleep in the crib itself, so there is nothing to transfer. How to get there depends on your baby’s age, how much they rely on motion now, their feeds and temperament, and how many naps are on the move. That is why a plan built for the individual baby works where generic advice stalls.

# My baby rolls onto their tummy in their sleep. Should I flip them back?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-rolls-onto-tummy-while-sleeping/

My baby rolls onto their tummy in their sleep. Should I flip them back?
Always place your baby down on their back. If they can roll both ways, back to tummy and tummy to back, the AAP says you don’t need to keep turning them back over. If they roll onto their tummy but can’t yet roll back, gently return them to their back. Stop swaddling as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The AAP rule
Babies up to 1 year should always be placed on their back to sleep, for naps and at night. What happens after that depends on what your baby can do:
Your babyWhat to do
Rolls back to tummy, cannot roll tummy to backGently turn them onto their back.
Rolls comfortably both waysThe AAP says you don’t need to keep turning your baby back over. Keep placing them down on their back.
Is still swaddled and showing signs of rollingStop swaddling now. Arms need to be free to push up and roll back.
When rolling starts
The AAP’s parent site says rolling usually happens around 3 to 4 months, but it can happen earlier. That is also the reason to stop swaddling early: once a baby is trying to roll, a swaddle can stop them using their arms. See when and how to stop swaddling.
Rolling often arrives just as sleep falls apart. The safety rules stay exactly as they are; the broken sleep is the part Actually Sleeping fixes, with a plan that works inside them.
Why a bare crib matters more now
A baby who can roll can end up face down near anything in the crib. That is why the rules about a firm, flat mattress and nothing but a fitted sheet matter even more once rolling starts. No pillows, blankets, bumpers, stuffed toys, loungers or positioners. The FDA specifically warns parents never to use sleep positioners to hold a baby on their back or side; they can cause suffocation. Do not swaddle, wedge, or use any product meant to stop rolling.
Tummy time
Rolling is a motor skill that develops with awake floor time. The AAP says to always stay with your baby during tummy time and make sure they are awake.
Side sleeping
The side position is not a safe alternative to the back. Place your baby on their back every time. If they roll to their side or tummy on their own and can roll both ways, you can leave them there.
Sleep sacks and rolling
A sleep sack with arms out is the usual next step after the swaddle. It keeps your baby warm without loose bedding and leaves their arms free. Avoid any sleep sack or swaddle that is weighted; the AAP says weighted products are not safe on or near a baby.
Why rolling so often breaks sleep
Rolling tends to arrive alongside other changes around 4 months: the swaddle comes off, sleep cycles mature, and babies who rely on help to fall asleep start waking more. A baby who rolls, gets stuck and cries becomes a baby who is rocked or fed back to sleep several times a night. The rolling phase passes as the skill matures. The habits that grew around it often stay.

My baby stands up in the crib and can’t get back down. What do I do?
Lower the mattress to its lowest setting before your baby can stand; that is MedlinePlus safety advice. Pulling up to stand is a milestone the CDC lists by the first birthday, and early standers can have a short period of disrupted sleep. If standing has turned into weeks of night waking, the cause is usually how your baby falls asleep, not the skill.

Safety first: the mattress
MedlinePlus advises lowering the crib mattress before your baby can sit up on their own, and having it at its lowest level before your baby can stand. If your baby is already pulling up and the mattress is still high, lower it today.
Other crib checks at this stage:
Remove hanging crib toys and mobiles. MedlinePlus says to take them down when your baby first pushes up on hands and knees, because they can strangle a baby.
Keep the crib bare. Anything inside can become a step.
Move the crib away from windows, blind cords, curtains and furniture your baby could reach.
MedlinePlus says children should stop using a crib by the time they are 35 inches (89 cm) tall.
Some babies doze off sitting up or slumped at the rail. Once they are asleep, lay them down on their back.
Standing is a short phase. Weeks of broken nights afterwards are usually not about the skill, and that waking is what Actually Sleeping fixes.
Why it happens
The CDC lists “pulls up to stand” among the milestones most babies reach by 1 year. A small study that tracked babies with home sleep recordings found that, in babies who pulled to stand early, by 8 months, the new skill was linked in time with a period of disrupted sleep. Pulling up is easier to learn than getting down. So your baby stands, gets tired, and calls for help.
Why a short phase becomes weeks of waking
The skill itself settles. What often does not is the pattern that grew up around it. Parents lay the baby down twenty times, and standing becomes a game. Or they rock or feed the baby back to sleep after each stand, and soon the baby needs that help at every waking, standing or not. By the time the baby can get down easily, the night waking has a new reason to continue.
Often the milestone has passed, but the nights have not recovered. The fix is the same as for most night waking after 6 months: a baby who can fall asleep on their own at bedtime and get back to sleep between cycles. Schedules matter too. A baby who isn’t tired at bedtime has energy to practise, and getting the timing right for your baby is part of every plan.
Is it time for a bed
Standing is not a reason to leave the crib. Climbing out is a different matter. If your toddler is climbing out or has reached 35 inches, see when to move from a crib to a bed.

# Why is my baby’s sleep worse since they started crawling or walking?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/crawling-walking-and-baby-sleep/

Why is my baby’s sleep worse since they started crawling or walking?
New motor skills can disturb sleep for a while. One study found crawling babies had more bedtime difficulty and night waking than babies not yet crawling, and another linked early pulling-to-stand with a period of disrupted sleep. Make the crib safe for a mobile baby. If waking continues well after the skill is solid, the cause is usually a sleep habit rather than the milestone.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the research shows
A 2005 study of 107 healthy babies aged about 5 to 8 months found that babies who were already crawling had more bedtime difficulties and more night waking than babies who were not yet crawling. Among 7- and 8-month-olds, crawling predicted part of the difference in night waking even after accounting for age.
A later study followed 20 babies from 7 to about 12 months with home sleep recordings. In babies who pulled to stand early, by 8 months, the milestone was linked in time with a period of disrupted sleep.
Both studies are small, and neither proves the skill causes the waking. But they match what many parents see: a baby who crawls in the crib, sits up half asleep, or stands at 2 a.m. and can’t get back down.
Why new skills disturb sleep
Practice. Babies rehearse new movements, including at bedtime and between sleep cycles.
Getting stuck. Many babies learn to sit, crawl or stand before they learn to undo it.
Excitement and energy. A new way to move is thrilling, and a baby who spent the day on the move may also be more overtired by bedtime.
New skills come and go. If each one leaves weeks of broken nights behind, that pattern is fixable, and it is what Actually Sleeping works on.
Why the waking outlasts the skill
A milestone is temporary. What parents do to get through it often is not. Rocking, feeding or holding a baby back to sleep after every crawl or stand becomes the way that baby falls back asleep, and the waking continues long after the skill is solid. That is why some families find nights fall apart at every new skill, while others barely notice: the difference is usually whether the baby can fall asleep on their own.
That is the part Actually Sleeping fixes. Make the crib safe for a mobile baby
MedlinePlus advises lowering the mattress before your baby can sit up alone, and to its lowest level before they can stand.
Remove mobiles and hanging toys once your baby pushes up on hands and knees.
Keep the crib bare: a fitted sheet only, nothing to climb on.
Check that nothing within reach of the crib, such as cords or curtains, can be pulled in.
Put your baby down on their back as usual. If they move into another position on their own and can move back out of it, you don’t need to reposition them.
Walking
First steps usually come after pulling to stand and walking along furniture, which the CDC lists among milestones by 1 year. Many babies around this age are also moving toward one nap, which can unsettle nights for other reasons. See nap transitions.
When it is not the milestone
If the waking started with the new skill but is still going a month later, look elsewhere. The usual reason is that your baby needs help to fall asleep at bedtime, and needs the same help at every waking. See the 8 to 10 month regression and why a 12 month old starts waking. If your baby seems unwell, in pain, or is not reaching milestones, talk to your pediatrician.

# Is white noise safe for my baby, and how loud should it be?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/white-noise-machine-safety-and-volume/

Is white noise safe for my baby, and how loud should it be?
White noise can be used safely if it stays quiet and away from the crib. A 2014 study in Pediatrics tested 14 infant sleep machines at maximum volume: all were louder than the 50-decibel limit recommended for hospital nurseries when measured 30 cm away, and three went above 85 decibels. Use the lowest volume that works and place the machine across the room.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the research found
Researchers measured 14 infant sleep machines played at maximum volume, at 30, 100 and 200 cm from the machine, and adjusted for the size of a 6-month-old’s ear canal. Their findings, published in Pediatrics in 2014:
At 30 cm, every machine was louder than 50 A-weighted decibels, the recommended noise limit for infants in hospital nurseries.
Three machines produced more than 85 decibels, which exceeds occupational limits for accumulated noise exposure in adults.
The authors concluded that these machines can produce sound levels that may damage infant hearing, and that the loudest ones played for more than 8 hours could put hearing at risk.
The study measured machines at their loudest. The practical message is about volume and distance, not about avoiding sound altogether.
Parents often reach for white noise because the baby keeps waking. Used safely it can help, but it cannot fix waking that comes from how a baby falls asleep. That is what Actually Sleeping fixes.
How to use white noise safely
Distance. Place the machine across the room, not on the crib rail or inside the crib. Sound drops quickly with distance.
Volume. Use the lowest setting that masks household noise. If you have to raise your voice to talk over it next to the crib, it is too loud.
Check it. A sound-meter app on your phone, held where your baby’s head lies, gives a rough reading. Aim well below 50 decibels.
Cords. Keep the cord out of reach. The CPSC warns never to place corded baby cameras within three feet of a crib because of strangulation risk; treat any corded device the same way.
Nothing in the crib. Plush toys with built-in sound machines add a soft object to the sleep space. Keep the crib bare and the sound source on a shelf.
All night is fine at a low volume. The study’s concern was the loudest machines played for more than 8 hours, which is why distance and volume matter so much.
Why parents use it
Steady sound can mask the noises that wake a light sleeper: a dog, a sibling, traffic, a door. It is also a familiar cue that sleep is coming, at home or away. Many families find it especially helpful when siblings share a room or when naps happen during a noisy part of the day.
What white noise cannot do
Parents often turn white noise up, and up again, because the baby is still waking. That is usually a sign that noise is not what wakes the baby. A baby who wakes every hour or two in a quiet, dark room is usually surfacing between sleep cycles and needing help to fall back asleep: to be fed, rocked, held, or given a pacifier. No volume setting changes that, and a louder machine only adds risk.
That waking is the fixable part, and it is what Actually Sleeping does. White noise can stay in the plan as a helper, at a safe volume. Parents describe the change in our 129 client video reviews, and more than 700 families have been coached.

# What should my baby wear to sleep, and what TOG sleep sack do I need?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/what-should-baby-wear-to-sleep/

What should my baby wear to sleep, and what TOG sleep sack do I need?
Dress your baby in no more than one layer more than you would wear to be comfortable in the same room, which is the AAP’s rule. No hat indoors and no loose blankets. Watch for overheating: sweating, flushed skin, or a hot chest. TOG is a sleep-sack warmth rating; choose one that, with the clothes underneath, adds up to about one layer more than you.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The AAP’s rule of thumb
The AAP’s parent site says your baby only needs one more layer than you would wear in the same environment to be comfortable. Dressing your baby in layers is safer than using blankets, and the AAP advises keeping the room at a comfortable temperature.
Neither the AAP’s parent site nor the NIH Safe to Sleep campaign gives a specific room temperature. The guidance is about how your baby feels, not a number on the thermostat.
Signs your baby is too hot
The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign lists:
Sweating
Flushed, red or hot skin
A chest that feels hot to the touch
Check the back of the neck or the chest, not the hands and feet. If your baby is sweaty, remove a layer.
Hats and head covering
The AAP says not to put a hat on your baby indoors once you are home from the hospital; hats are for the first hours after birth or the NICU. Safe to Sleep adds that a baby’s head and face should stay uncovered during sleep.
If you are checking layers because your baby keeps waking, temperature is worth getting right, but it is rarely the whole story. The waking itself is what Actually Sleeping fixes.
What TOG means
TOG stands for thermal overall grade. It is a warmth rating that manufacturers put on sleep sacks and swaddles: a higher number means a warmer, thicker sack. TOG is not part of the AAP’s guidance, and brands differ in how they rate and what room temperatures they suggest. Use the maker’s chart as a starting point, then adjust to your baby.
Putting it together
Room feelsYou would wearA typical baby setup
WarmA T-shirtA short-sleeve bodysuit, or a bodysuit and a light sleep sack
ComfortableLight long sleevesA long-sleeve sleepsuit and a light-to-medium sleep sack
CoolA sweaterA long-sleeve sleepsuit and a warmer sleep sack
These are examples of the one-extra-layer rule, not fixed requirements. Your baby’s skin is the real guide. Hands and feet often feel cool even when a baby is warm enough, because they are small and exposed; go by the chest and neck.
Things to avoid
Loose blankets and quilts. Keep them out of the sleep space for the first year.
Weighted sleep sacks or swaddles. The AAP says weighted products on or near a baby are not safe. See weighted sleep sacks.
Swaddling a baby who is trying to roll. Stop swaddling at the first signs of rolling and move to an arms-out sleep sack.
Hoods, hats and thick fleece in a warm room.
Heaters or electric blankets near the crib.
When the question is really about waking
Many parents start comparing TOG ratings because their baby keeps waking, and wonder if the baby is cold or hot. A baby who is too warm or too cold may wake more, so it is worth getting right. But temperature is rarely the whole story. A baby who wakes several times a night in a comfortable room, correctly dressed, is usually waking between sleep cycles and needing help to fall back asleep.
That is the fixable part, and it is what Actually Sleeping does. What temperature should a baby’s room be?The AAP and NIH do not give a specific number. They advise a comfortable room temperature and dressing your baby in one layer more than you would wear, then checking for sweating, flushed skin, or a hot chest.
What TOG sleep sack should I use?TOG is a manufacturer’s warmth rating, not an AAP standard, and brands differ. Use the maker’s chart as a starting point, then choose clothing plus sack that adds up to about one layer more than you are wearing.

# When can my baby sleep with a blanket, pillow or stuffed animal?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/when-can-baby-sleep-with-blanket-pillow-or-lovey/

When can my baby sleep with a blanket, pillow or stuffed animal?
Not before 12 months. The AAP says to keep blankets, pillows, stuffed toys and bumpers out of your baby’s sleep space for the first year. Its parent site notes that research hasn’t shown exactly when these items become completely safe, but most experts agree they pose little risk to healthy babies after 12 months. After that, start small: one small lovey, then a light blanket.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The first year: nothing but a fitted sheet
For babies up to 1 year, the AAP’s parent site says there should be no blankets, pillows, stuffed toys or bumper pads in the bed. Soft objects and loose bedding can increase the risk of entrapment, suffocation or strangulation. The CPSC’s shorthand is “Bare is Best”: nothing but a fitted sheet.
A sleep sack keeps your baby warm in place of a blanket. Dressing your baby in layers is safer than using blankets.
After 12 months
The AAP’s parent site is honest about the evidence: research has not shown when it is 100% safe to have these objects in the crib. It adds that most experts agree they pose little risk to healthy babies after 12 months. If your child was born early or has a medical condition, ask your pediatrician what applies to them.
Choosing a lovey after 12 months
Small and simple. A small soft toy or a small cloth without long ribbons, strings, buttons or loose parts.
One, not a pile. A crib full of toys is something to climb on.
Many parents ask about a lovey or blanket hoping it will help their child sleep. The safety rules come first; the sleep problem behind the question is the part Actually Sleeping fixes.
Pacifier holders and plush pacifiers
The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign says not to attach a pacifier to clothing, stuffed toys, blankets or other items. That includes pacifiers sewn into plush animals, at least in the first year. After 12 months, if you use one, treat it like any other soft toy and keep it small.
Blankets for toddlers
Many toddlers kick blankets off, so a sleep sack often keeps working well into the second and third year. When you introduce a blanket, start with a thin, small one tucked no higher than the chest.
Pillows
The AAP’s safe-sleep guidance is written for the first year and doesn’t set an age for pillows. Toddlers don’t need one, and many families wait until the move to a bed. When you add one, choose a small, flat toddler pillow, not an adult pillow.

12 months and upA thin, small one if you likeOne small oneNot needed; small and flat if used

When a lovey is meant to fix sleep
Parents often ask about a lovey or blanket because their baby is not sleeping: waking at night, crying at bedtime, needing a parent to settle. The hope is that a comfort object will stand in for the parent. Before 12 months it cannot safely go in the crib at all. After 12 months it can comfort some toddlers, but it rarely changes a child who needs to be fed, rocked or held back to sleep several times a night.

# Should I use a humidifier in my baby’s room?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/humidifier-in-baby-room/

Should I use a humidifier in my baby’s room?
You don’t need one all the time, but a cool-mist humidifier can help a congested baby breathe more comfortably, and the AAP suggests one when the air is dry. Place it so the mist reaches the sleep space but your baby can’t reach the machine, change the water every day, and clean it as the manufacturer directs. Never prop up the mattress for a stuffy nose.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the AAP says
For a baby with a stuffy nose, the AAP’s parent site suggests a vaporizer or humidifier that fills the sleep space with a cool mist to help clear nasal passages. For colds more generally, it says that if the air in your home is dry, use a humidifier, because moist air keeps mucus from drying out.
A humidifier is a comfort measure. It does not treat an infection and it is not needed for healthy sleep.
Using one safely
Cool mist. The AAP’s advice for babies describes a cool mist.
Placement. Close enough that the mist reaches the sleep space, but out of your baby’s reach, as the AAP advises.
Cord. Keep the cord out of reach of the crib.
Fresh water daily. The AAP says to change the water every day and follow the manufacturer’s directions to keep mold and bacteria away.
Nothing added. Use plain water only. See essential oils and baby sleep.
Not too much. Damp walls, wet windows, or a musty smell mean the room is getting too humid. Turn it down or off. In humid climates or summer months, adding moisture can make a room feel stuffy and encourage mold.
A humidifier eases congestion. It does not fix sleep that was broken before the cold, or habits that grew during it. Once your baby is well, that sleep is the part Actually Sleeping fixes.
Other ways to ease a stuffy nose at night
The AAP suggests:
Saline drops to loosen congestion. Use plain saline with no medicine added.
Gentle suction with a bulb syringe or nasal aspirator. Squeeze the bulb before placing it in the nostril.
Feeding before sleep, once the nose is clearer, so your baby is not trying to feed through congestion.
Cough and cold medicines are a separate question for your pediatrician; see cough and cold medicine at bedtime.
What not to do
The AAP is clear that propping your baby up on towels or pillows, or inclining the mattress, is not safe, even with a cold. Inclined sleepers are banned. Babies sleep flat on their backs on a firm surface with nothing else in the crib. See inclined sleepers and loungers.
When to call the doctor
The AAP’s parent site says to call your pediatrician if:
Your baby’s breathing is much faster than normal
Their lips or face turn bluish when they cough
Nonstop coughing is keeping them from sleeping, eating or playing
Call 911 if your baby is struggling for each breath, can barely make sounds or cry, has bluish lips or face, or seems to have something caught in their throat.
When the cold is not the whole story
Parents often reach for a humidifier because the baby is not sleeping. During a cold, congestion really does wake babies. But a humidifier won’t fix night waking that started before the cold, and it won’t help a baby who has learned to need help falling back asleep. If your baby was waking often before they got sick, the cold may have made an existing pattern louder. Colds also leave a sleep hangover: extra night feeds and new habits from nights of comforting, which were the right response while your baby was ill.
Once your baby is well, that sleep is the fixable part, and it is what Actually Sleeping does. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your baby, you get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, and daily 1:1 check-ins pause the plan for illness and restart it when your baby is better. Night feeds stay in the plan until your pediatrician says otherwise. Hear from families in our 129 client video reviews. See also sleep after illness.

# Does my baby need blackout curtains or a night light, and what colour?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/blackout-curtains-and-night-lights/

Does my baby need blackout curtains or a night light, and what colour?
A dark room helps. In one study, bright light in the hour before bed cut young children’s melatonin by about 88%, and it stayed low after the light went off. Blackout curtains help with early sunrises and summer bedtimes. Babies don’t need a night light. If you use one for feeds or a toddler’s fears, keep it dim and out of direct view, whatever the colour.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why darkness matters
Melatonin, the hormone that signals night to the body, rises in the evening and is suppressed by light. A 2018 study measured this in 10 healthy children aged about 3 to 5. After a week on a steady sleep schedule, the children were exposed to bright light, about 1,000 lux, for one hour before bedtime. Their melatonin dropped by about 88% compared with dim light, and it stayed suppressed for at least 50 minutes after the light was turned off.
The study was small and in preschoolers, not babies, but it shows how sensitive young children’s body clocks are to evening light.
A dark room supports sleep. It does not teach a baby to fall back asleep between cycles, which is what Actually Sleeping works on.
Where light causes the most trouble
Early sunrises, especially in summer, when light reaches the room before your child’s wake-up time. See early morning waking.
Bedtime before dark, when the room is still bright as your child is trying to fall asleep.
Naps. A baby who wakes after one short sleep cycle often opens their eyes to a bright room, which makes drifting back off harder.
Streetlights or headlights shining in.
Screens in the evening. The AAP advises turning them off at least an hour before bed. See screens and toddler sleep.
Light by day matters too. Darkness at night works best alongside daylight in the morning, which helps set the body clock. If you add blinds or blackout covers, keep any cords well out of reach of the crib.
Night lights
Babies don’t need a night light. A dark room is fine, and many sleep better in it. You may want a little light for yourself during night feeds and diaper changes; keep it very dim, low and out of your baby’s line of sight.
On colour: the study above tested brightness, not colour. The safest approach is to keep any light as dim as possible, whatever colour you choose.
Toddlers and fear of the dark
Some toddlers start asking for a light. The AAP says you can leave a light on if it helps a child after a nightmare. A dim night light is a small, reasonable comfort. Lights that project moving images or change colour can keep a child watching instead of sleeping. See when your toddler is afraid of the dark.
What a dark room cannot do
Blackout curtains are one of the most common purchases parents make when sleep goes wrong, and they do help a body clock that is being pushed around by light. What they cannot do is change how a baby falls asleep. A baby who needs to be fed, rocked or held to sleep will still wake between sleep cycles, in a perfectly dark room, and ask for the same help. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried things on their own, and a darker room is often one of them.
That waking is the fixable part. # Do screens before bed affect my toddler’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/screen-time-and-toddler-sleep/

Do screens before bed affect my toddler’s sleep?
They can. The AAP advises turning screens off at least an hour before bedtime and keeping phones, tablets and TVs out of your child’s bedroom at night. The light from screens can disrupt melatonin, and exciting shows or games can leave a child more alert. Screens are often one part of a harder bedtime rather than the whole cause.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the AAP recommends
The AAP’s guidance on screens and sleep has three parts:
Stop screens at least an hour before bedtime.
Keep phones and screens out of your child’s bedroom at night.
Choose calm content. The AAP notes that an action-packed game or something intense can make children more alert and raise their heart rate, which makes falling asleep harder. It suggests relaxing or funny programs watched together instead.
The AAP also explains that the type of light given off by screens can disrupt the production of melatonin, the hormone that helps the body fall asleep.
Why young children are sensitive to evening light
A 2018 study exposed 10 healthy children aged about 3 to 5 to bright light for an hour before bed. Their melatonin fell by about 88% and stayed suppressed for at least 50 minutes after the light went off. A tablet held close to the face is not the same as a brightly lit room, but the study shows how responsive young children’s body clocks are to light at night.
Screens are often one piece of a harder bedtime. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on and fixes the whole evening, not just the last hour.
What it looks like at home
Parents often notice one of these patterns:
Bedtime battles start the moment the show ends.
Your toddler seems wired, not sleepy, at the time they should be winding down.
Falling asleep takes longer on nights with a show than without.
A show has become part of how your child falls asleep, and they ask for it again at night.
That last pattern is the one that matters most. When a screen becomes part of falling asleep, it works like any other sleep association: your child needs it to fall asleep, and asks for it, or for you, when they wake.
Why taking screens away often is not enough
Many families cut evening screens and find bedtime gets louder, not easier, for a while. The show was filling time, managing a tired toddler, and giving parents a break. Without something to replace it, and without a clear limit both parents hold, the protest moves to the routine. Babies are affected too: background TV in the room where a baby is falling asleep adds both light and noise.
Parents’ screens count as well, especially a phone lit up during night feeds or while sitting by the crib.

Mornings and daytime
The AAP’s sleep advice is about the evening. Daytime limits are a separate decision for your family and pediatrician. For sleep, the hour before bed and the bedroom matter most.

# What should a bedtime routine include, and when should I start one?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/bedtime-routine-for-babies-and-toddlers/

What should a bedtime routine include, and when should I start one?
Keep it short, calm and the same every night: for example a feed, bath or wash, pajamas, teeth, a book, a song, then into the crib awake. A study of more than 10,000 young children found that the more nights a week a routine happened, the better children slept, with earlier bedtimes and fewer night wakings. You can start one in the first months.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the research found
A 2015 study in the journal Sleep asked mothers of 10,085 children from birth to 5 years, across 13 countries and regions, how often their child had a bedtime routine. The more nights a week a routine happened, the better the sleep. Children with a consistent routine had:
Earlier bedtimes
Less time taken to fall asleep
Fewer and shorter night wakings
More total night sleep
The authors concluded that the earlier a routine starts, the better. The study was based on parent reports and shows an association, not proof of cause, but the pattern was strong and consistent.
The AAP’s simple version: Brush, Book, Bed
Brush: help your child brush their teeth every night.
Book: read a favorite book, or two.
Bed: get to bed at a regular time each night.
The AAP also warns against putting a baby to bed with a bottle of milk, formula, juice or any sugary drink.
A good routine is a foundation. When your baby still wakes through the night despite one, the missing piece is usually how they fall asleep, and that is what Actually Sleeping fixes.
Why routines work
A routine is a set of cues. When the same steps happen in the same order every night, a child learns that each step leads to sleep, and the body starts winding down before the lights go out. Predictability also lowers protest: a toddler who knows exactly what comes next has less to negotiate. The AAP’s parent site advises putting babies to bed when they are drowsy, not waiting until they are asleep, so they learn to fall asleep on their own.
Why a good routine is not always enough
Plenty of families have a lovely routine, bath, book and song in the right order every night, and a baby who still wakes every two hours. That is because a routine sets a child up to fall asleep well; it does not, on its own, change how they fall asleep. If the routine ends with your baby asleep on the breast, the bottle or your shoulder, they will need the same thing at every waking between sleep cycles.
Routines also drift. A feed creeps to the end. Two books become five. One parent does it one way and the other parent another. Each change is small and reasonable, and together they can turn a 20-minute routine into an hour.

The plan places feeds, sets the bedtime for your baby’s age and naps, and, most importantly, teaches your baby to fall asleep on their own at the end of it. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins, and naps are coached until they are solid. Frequently asked
When should I start a bedtime routine?You can start in the first weeks with something very simple, like a diaper change, feed, and song in a dim room. A large study of bedtime routines concluded that the earlier a routine starts, the better.
How long should a bedtime routine be?Most families find 20 to 30 minutes is plenty. The order and consistency matter more than the length. Long routines tend to invite stalling, especially with toddlers, so keep it short and predictable.
Should a bath be part of the routine every night?Not necessarily. A bath can be a calming cue, but a quick wash works just as well. What matters is doing the same steps in the same order most nights.
Is it okay to feed my baby to sleep as part of the routine?Feeding is a normal part of a routine. If your baby falls asleep feeding and then wakes often, the feed’s place in the routine is usually part of the reason. A Actually Sleeping plan reorganizes the routine around this and never forces night feeds to drop; those are your pediatrician’s call.

# My toddler stalls at bedtime with one more book, drink or hug. How do I stop it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-bedtime-stalling/

My toddler stalls at bedtime with one more book, drink or hug. How do I stop it?
Stalling is normal toddler behavior: your child is learning that words can change what happens, and bedtime means separation from you. It keeps going when the limits change from night to night, when requests get negotiated, or when bedtime comes before your toddler is tired. What ends it is a bedtime set for your child and a limit both parents hold the same way.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why toddlers stall
Stalling is normal toddler behavior. Your child is learning that words can change what happens, bedtime means separation from you, and every extra request is a chance to stay up a little longer. Sometimes there is a real need underneath, such as thirst, fear or a full bladder. Often there isn’t. And because the requests are so reasonable, one more hug, one more drink, they are hard to say no to.
A toddler who is not tired will fill the time
The AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours of sleep per 24 hours for children 1 to 2 years old, and 10 to 13 hours for 3 to 5 year olds, including naps. Those are wide ranges, and children sit at different points in them. A toddler with a long or late nap who is put down at a bedtime meant for a child who needs more sleep has an hour to spend, and they will spend it asking for things. No bedtime script works on a child who is not ready to sleep.
Stalling is fixable. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on and writes a bedtime and a response for your child that both parents can hold.
Why stalling grows
Negotiation teaches negotiation. When a request sometimes works, your toddler learns to keep asking. Long explanations tell them the door is still open.
The limit changes. Two books one night, four the next; one parent stays, the other leaves. Your child keeps testing which version they will get.
Real needs are met after lights out. If the last drink or potty trip happens after the goodnight, every night has a reason to call you back.
Your presence becomes part of falling asleep. “Lie with me” turns into a nightly requirement, and then into a request at every night waking too.
Expect stalling to get louder for a while whenever the rules change. That is normal, and it is the point where most families give in, which teaches the toddler that protest works.
Why generic scripts often fail
Charts, tickets and stock phrases from the internet are built for an average toddler. Whether they work for yours depends on your child’s age, temperament, nap, bedtime and, most of all, on two tired parents doing exactly the same thing every night. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried things on their own.

# My toddler says they’re scared of the dark. How do I help?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-afraid-of-the-dark/

My toddler says they’re scared of the dark. How do I help?
Fear of the dark is a normal stage as toddlers’ imaginations grow. Take it seriously: a dim night light is fine, and the AAP says you can leave a light on if it helps a child after a nightmare. If fears are severe, last for weeks, or show up during the day, talk with your pediatrician. When fear has become a nightly bedtime battle, that is a sleep problem a plan can fix.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Why it starts
As toddlers’ imaginations grow, so does their ability to picture things that aren’t there. Many children go through a stage of being afraid of the dark, monsters or noises at night. It is a normal part of development, not a sign that something is wrong.
It can be hard to tell real fear from stalling. A frightened child usually looks scared: clinging, crying, tense, and wanting you close. A stalling child tends to have a new request each time. Some children do both, and fear can become the most reliable way to get a parent back.
What the AAP says
Light. The AAP says you can leave a light on if it helps a child after a nightmare. A dim night light is a small, reasonable comfort; bright evening light can suppress melatonin in young children.
Comfort objects. For children over 12 months, the AAP’s parent site says most experts agree soft objects pose little risk to healthy babies.
Calm evenings. The AAP advises no screens in the hour before bed and choosing calm programs over intense ones. Scary books and shows close to bedtime can feed fears at night.
Fear of the dark deserves to be taken seriously, and the bedtime battles that grow around it can be fixed. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on.
What keeps fear going
Dismissing it. “There’s nothing to be scared of” can leave a child feeling unheard.
Elaborate rituals. Searching under the bed every night can suggest there is something to find.
Staying until they fall asleep every night, or bringing them into your bed. These help in a rough patch, but they quickly become what your child needs to fall asleep, and the fear becomes the way to ask for it.
A long bedtime. The longer the routine, the more time there is to think about the dark.
A response that changes from night to night, so your child cannot predict whether you will come back.
Why this needs a plan, not a trick
Night lights, monster sprays and reassurance scripts can all help a little. What they do not do is give a frightened child a predictable bedtime: knowing exactly what happens, when you will check on them, and that it will be the same tomorrow. Getting that right depends on your child’s age and temperament, whether they are in a crib or a bed, and how they fall asleep now.
Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your toddler that takes the fear seriously and builds a calm, predictable bedtime around it, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Hear from families in our 129 client video reviews.
Nightmares
If your child wakes up scared, remembers a bad dream, and wants comfort, that is a nightmare. The AAP advises comforting your child quickly, reassuring them they are safe, and reminding them that dreams aren’t real. Night terrors are different: your child is not really awake. See nightmares vs night terrors.
When to get help
Talk with your pediatrician if the fears are intense, last for weeks without improving, appear during the day too, or come with other changes such as trouble eating, frequent tantrums, or loss of skills. Sometimes a stressful event, such as a move or a new sibling, is behind a new fear; see a new sibling and moving house.

# Is my child having nightmares or night terrors, and what should I do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/nightmares-vs-night-terrors/

Is my child having nightmares or night terrors, and what should I do?
Nightmares usually happen in the second half of the night: your child wakes, is scared, remembers the dream and wants comfort. Night terrors happen in deep sleep, usually early in the night: your child may scream or thrash but isn’t really awake and won’t remember it. Comfort after a nightmare. During a night terror, stay calm, keep your child safe, and wait.

How to tell them apart
NightmareNight terror
WhenSecond half of the night, when dreaming is most intenseEarly in the night, during deep sleep
Your childWakes up and is scaredMay cry out or move around, but is not really awake
AwarenessAwake and wants comfortAsleep and unaware, so comfort may not register
Remembers itYes, can often describe the dreamNo

All of the timing and age information above comes from the AAP’s parent site.
What the AAP advises during a nightmare
Go to your child quickly and comfort them.
Reassure them they are safe.
Let them talk about the dream if they want to, and remind them that dreams aren’t real.
Leave a light on if it helps.
Night terrors and nightmares are a question for your pediatrician. Short, broken sleep, one of the listed triggers, is the part Actually Sleeping fixes.
What the AAP advises during a night terror
Stay calm. The AAP notes your child is asleep and unaware. It is upsetting to watch, but your child is not experiencing it the way you are.
Keep them safe. Move them away from anything they could hurt themselves on, and gently stop them if they try to get out of bed.
Stay nearby until it passes and your child settles back into sleep.
Don’t quiz them in the morning. They won’t remember it, and talking about it can make them worry.
Tell babysitters. The AAP suggests letting other caregivers know so they are not alarmed.

Not enough sleep
Stress
Travel and unfamiliar surroundings
Noise or light during sleep
Fever
Some medications
Sleep apnea
The AAP also advises no screens in the hour before bed, and scary stories and shows close to bedtime can feed nightmares.

Your child is very sleepy during the day.

# My toddler sleepwalks. Is it dangerous, and should I wake them?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-sleepwalking/

My toddler sleepwalks. Is it dangerous, and should I wake them?
Sleepwalking can start as soon as a child can walk. It usually happens in the first third of the night and tends to run in families. Don’t try to wake or hold your child down; gently lead them back to bed. The main risk is injury, so lock outside doors and windows, gate stairs and the bedroom doorway, and clear the floor.

What sleepwalking is
A sleepwalking child gets up and moves around while still asleep. They may sit up, walk around or talk. The AAP’s parent site says sleepwalkers usually return to bed on their own and often don’t remember it in the morning.
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) says:
Sleepwalking can start as soon as a child is able to walk.
Rates in children are as high as 17%, peaking around ages 8 to 12.
It most often happens in the first third of the night.
The AAP’s parent site adds that sleepwalking tends to run in families.
During an episode
Don’t try to wake them or hold them down. The AASM and AAP both advise gently leading your child back to bed instead.
Speak softly and keep it simple.
Guide, don’t pull. A light hand on the shoulder is enough.
Stay calm. Your child is not aware of what is happening.
Sleepwalking itself is a question for your pediatrician. Short or broken sleep, one of the listed triggers, is the part Actually Sleeping fixes.

Injury is the real risk. The AASM and AAP recommend:
HazardWhat to do
Getting outsideLock outside doors and windows at night.
StairsA safety gate at the top of the stairs and at the bedroom doorway.
TrippingKeep floors clear of toys and clutter.
Sharp or breakable itemsKeep them out of the bedroom.
Bunk bedsNo top bunk for a child who sleepwalks.

Not enough sleep

Travel and unfamiliar surroundings
Noise or light during sleep
Fever
Some medications

The next day
Your child won’t remember the episode. There is no need to tell them about it or ask them to explain. Treat it as a quiet, practical safety matter.

Night terrors often involve crying or screaming early in the night without waking. They share triggers with sleepwalking and some children have both. See nightmares vs night terrors.

Your child is very sleepy during the day.

# My toddler snores and breathes through their mouth at night. When should I see the pediatrician?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-snoring-and-mouth-breathing/

My toddler snores and breathes through their mouth at night. When should I see the pediatrician?
Occasional snoring with a cold is common. Snoring three or more nights a week is worth raising with your pediatrician, especially with labored breathing, pauses or gasps, bedwetting, daytime sleepiness, or learning or behavior problems. These can be signs of obstructive sleep apnea. The AAP guideline recommends a sleep study to diagnose it and removing the tonsils and adenoids as first-line treatment when they are enlarged.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: this guide is general information about sleep. Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist. Diagnosis and treatment decisions belong to your pediatrician.
What the AAP guideline says
The AAP’s clinical practice guideline on childhood obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) says pediatricians should ask whether a child snores as part of routine health visits. It notes that snoring is common in children and that almost all children with OSA snore. Based on the stronger studies it reviewed, OSA affects about 1.2% to 5.7% of children.
So most snoring children don’t have sleep apnea. But regular snoring is the signal that should start the conversation.
Signs to mention to your pediatrician
The guideline lists these among the things to ask about:
Frequent snoring, three or more nights a week
Labored breathing during sleep
Gasps, or pauses in breathing that you can see
Bedwetting
Sleeping in a seated position
A bluish color during sleep
Morning headaches
Daytime sleepiness
Attention, learning or behavior problems
The AAP’s parent site also lists sleepiness during the day, difficulty paying attention and behavior problems as signs.
What to bring to the appointment
A short video of your child sleeping on a typical night, with sound, especially if you see pauses or gasping.
A one- to two-week sleep diary: bedtime, wake time, naps, snoring nights, night waking, bedwetting.
Daytime notes: mood, attention, how hard mornings are, whether your child falls asleep in the car more than expected.
Breathing comes first: no sleep plan fixes it. Once your pediatrician has checked it, the sleep habits that built up around broken nights are the part Actually Sleeping fixes.
How it is diagnosed and treated
The guideline recommends an overnight sleep study, called polysomnography, for a snoring child with signs of OSA, or referral to a sleep specialist or ear, nose and throat specialist. During the study, sensors track breathing, oxygen levels and brain waves while your child sleeps.
If OSA is found and the tonsils and adenoids are enlarged, the guideline recommends removing them as the first-line treatment. The AAP’s parent site describes this as the most common and effective treatment, and notes follow-up matters because surgery is not always successful. If surgery doesn’t help or isn’t advised, a CPAP machine, which delivers steady air pressure through a mask, may be recommended.
Babies under 1 year
The AAP guideline specifically excludes infants younger than 1 year. That doesn’t mean snoring in a baby is unimportant: it means babies need individual assessment. Tell your pediatrician about regular snoring, noisy breathing, pauses, or struggling to breathe in a baby. Do not prop up the mattress or use positioners to ease breathing; the AAP says inclined sleep surfaces aren’t safe. See inclined sleepers and positioners.
Snoring during a cold
Snoring that starts with a cold and stops when it clears is usually congestion. The AAP suggests a cool-mist humidifier and saline drops for a stuffy nose; see humidifiers and stuffy noses. If snoring continues after the cold, mention it.
Why it matters for sleep
A child whose breathing is disrupted at night can still be tired the next day: the AAP lists daytime sleepiness as a sign. Sleep apnea is also one of the triggers the American Academy of Sleep Medicine lists for sleepwalking and sleep terrors. No behavioral sleep plan fixes a breathing problem. If your child snores regularly and sleeps poorly, rule out OSA with your pediatrician before working on sleep habits.
After the breathing question is answered

Is it normal for a toddler to snore?Occasional snoring, especially with a cold, is common. The AAP guideline says snoring is common in children and asks pediatricians to check for it at routine visits. Regular snoring, three or more nights a week, is worth raising with your pediatrician.
Does mouth breathing at night mean sleep apnea?Not on its own. A blocked nose from a cold can cause it too. Mention it to your pediatrician alongside snoring, pauses or gasps, restless sleep, bedwetting, or daytime sleepiness, which together may point to sleep apnea.

# Why does my baby bang their head or rock to fall asleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/head-banging-and-rocking-at-bedtime/

Why does my baby bang their head or rock to fall asleep?
Rhythmic movements like head banging, body rocking and head rolling are common in babies and toddlers as they fall asleep. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine reports that 59% of infants show one of them at nine months, dropping to 33% at 18 months and about 5% by age five. Typical cases rarely cause serious injury. See a doctor if it hurts your child or disrupts their sleep.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What it looks like
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) describes three main forms of sleep-related rhythmic movement:
Body rocking: rocking on hands and knees, or rocking the upper body while sitting. It usually starts around 6 months.
Head banging: repeated movement of the head into the mattress or crib. It usually starts around 9 months, and the AASM calls it the most disturbing form for parents.
Head rolling: rolling the head from side to side, usually while lying on the back.
It tends to happen while a child is drowsy, falling asleep, or drifting back to sleep after a waking.
How common it is
AgeChildren with a rhythmic movement (AASM)
9 months59%
18 months33%
5 yearsAbout 5%
The AASM says the behavior commonly fades by age two or three.
Rhythmic movement is common and usually harmless. When it comes with a night full of wakings, the wakings are the part Actually Sleeping fixes.
Is it harmful
The AASM says typical cases in infants and toddlers pose little risk of serious injury, although strong movements can make loud noises against the bed or wall. Many children appear to use the rhythm to settle, much as adults might jiggle a foot.
Keeping the crib safe
Don’t add padding. Crib bumpers are banned in the U.S. and the AAP says no bumper pads in the crib. Keep it bare.
Check the crib. Tighten bolts and screws, and move the crib a little away from the wall to cut down the noise and the rattling.
Don’t restrain your child.
When to see a doctor
The AASM says to see a sleep specialist if the movements injure your child or keep them from sleeping well. Talk with your pediatrician too if:
Your child has bruises, cuts or swelling from it.
It happens for long stretches during the day, not just around sleep.
It continues past early childhood or is getting more intense.
You have any concerns about your child’s development, hearing or vision.
The AASM suggests keeping a two-week sleep diary and recording a video of an episode to show the doctor.
When rocking is part of a bigger sleep problem
If your child rocks or bangs for a few minutes and then sleeps, that is often their way of settling. If it happens at every waking, all night, it is usually one sign of broken sleep rather than the cause: a child who wakes between sleep cycles, cannot get back to sleep easily, and rocks or bangs while they try. Parents often respond by rushing in and picking the child up, which can make the waking itself the habit.
The broken nights are the fixable part, and that is what Actually Sleeping does. Dr. Sam writes a plan for your child, whatever their age, that looks at the schedule and how your child falls asleep at bedtime, inside a bare, safe crib. You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Hear from families in our 129 client video reviews. See also frequent night waking.
