# Will starting solids help my baby sleep through the night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/starting-solids-and-baby-sleep/

Will starting solids help my baby sleep through the night?
Probably only a little. In a large UK trial, babies who started solids from about 3 months slept on average about 7 minutes more per night and woke slightly less than babies exclusively breastfed to around 6 months. The AAP advises against cereal in a bottle. When to start solids is a feeding decision for your pediatrician, not a sleep tool.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
What the best study found
The Enquiring About Tolerance (EAT) trial randomized 1,303 exclusively breastfed 3-month-olds in England and Wales. One group started solids from 3 months while continuing to breastfeed. The other followed the standard advice of exclusive breastfeeding to about 6 months. A 2018 analysis in JAMA Pediatrics looked at sleep.
Across the study, babies in the early group slept about 7 minutes more per night on average.
At 6 months, the difference was about 17 minutes per night.
Night wakings were about 9% fewer in the early group.
Parents in the standard group were more likely to call their baby’s sleep a very serious problem.
The authors called the effect small but significant. Only 42% of the early group fully followed the feeding plan, sleep was reported by parents, and the trial was designed to study allergies, not sleep.
What that means for you
A few minutes more sleep and a small drop in night wakings is real, but it is not the jump from waking every two hours to sleeping through. If your baby wakes often, solids are unlikely to be the fix.
If you are hoping solids will end night waking, the research suggests a small effect at best. The waking itself, usually about how your baby falls back asleep, is what Actually Sleeping fixes.
What the AAP says about timing and cereal
The AAP’s parent site recommends breastfeeding as the sole source of nutrition for about 6 months, and suggests waiting until 4 to 6 months, when the time is right, to start solids.
It advises against putting cereal in a bottle unless your pediatrician recommends it. Early cereal from a bottle or spoon can increase the chance of gagging or inhaling the thickened mixture.
When to start, and how, is your pediatrician’s call, especially for babies born early, with reflux, or with allergy risk. Milk feeds stay the main event in the early months of solids unless your pediatrician advises otherwise.
Why babies keep waking after solids start
Most night waking after about 4 to 6 months is not about hunger. Common reasons:
Your baby falls asleep feeding or being rocked, and needs the same help between sleep cycles.
Bedtime or naps are mistimed, so your baby is overtired or under-tired.
A habit feed: a baby used to eating at night will feel hungry at that time.
A baby who is truly hungry at night usually takes a full feed and goes straight back to sleep. A baby who feeds for a few minutes and falls asleep is more often waking for comfort. That distinction, and whether night feeds are still needed, is worth discussing with your pediatrician. See the feed-to-sleep association and why a 6 month old wakes every 2 hours.
The fixable part
Parents often look at solids, or cereal, because their baby is not sleeping and hunger seems like the obvious reason. Most families who come to Actually Sleeping have already tried things on their own. When the waking continues, it is usually because the baby relies on help to fall back asleep, and that is what Actually Sleeping fixes.

The plan never forces dropping night feeds; feeding decisions, including solids, belong to your pediatrician. # Is it normal for my baby to sleep more or be fussy after vaccines?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-after-vaccines/

Is it normal for my baby to sleep more or be fussy after vaccines?
Yes. The CDC lists fussiness and feeling tired among common mild reactions to some infant vaccines, and says mild reactions usually go away within a few days. A study of 2-month-olds found babies slept more in the 24 hours after their shots, especially when vaccinated in the afternoon. Let your baby sleep, offer feeds, and call the doctor if anything worries you.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
A note on scope: this guide is general information about sleep. Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist. Diagnosis and treatment decisions belong to your pediatrician.
What is common
The CDC lists soreness or swelling where the shot was given, fever, fussiness and feeling tired as possible reactions to the DTaP vaccine, which is part of the routine infant series. Rotavirus vaccine can cause irritability or mild, temporary diarrhea or vomiting. The CDC says these reactions are mostly minor and go away within a few days.
Babies often sleep more
A 2011 randomized trial in Pediatrics tracked the sleep of 70 babies, about 2 months old, for 24 hours before and after their first vaccines, using movement monitors on the ankle. Sleep increased in the 24 hours after vaccination, especially in babies vaccinated after 1:30 p.m. Babies whose temperature rose after the shots had larger increases in sleep.
So a sleepier-than-usual day or an early, long night after shots is common. It is not a reason to worry on its own.
A sleepy or fussy day after shots is normal and calls for comfort. If sleep was already hard before the shots, that is the part Actually Sleeping can fix.
Caring for your baby after shots
The CDC and MedlinePlus suggest:
Comfort. Hold and cuddle your baby. A soothing voice helps.
A cool, damp cloth on the injection site to ease redness, soreness or swelling.
Feeds and fluids more often. The CDC notes it is normal for some children to eat less in the 24 hours after vaccines.
Fever: the CDC suggests a lukewarm sponge bath. If your baby is very young, ask your pediatrician at the visit which temperature should prompt a call.
Pain relievers: ask your child’s doctor whether you can give a non-aspirin pain reliever, and follow the package directions or your provider’s instructions for your baby’s age and weight. Do not give aspirin.
Extra attention. The CDC advises paying extra attention to your child for a few days.
Sleep on the day of shots
Extra naps are fine. If your baby is young and normally fed on a schedule, keep offering feeds; ask your pediatrician if you’re unsure how long to let them go. A day or two of extra holding or feeding after shots is the right response, and it does not undo good sleep habits.
Families in a Actually Sleeping plan pause during a reaction like this and pick up the same plan once the baby is back to normal, with Dr. Sam confirming the restart in the daily 1:1 check-in. If sleep was already broken before the shots, or extra night feeds and holding linger long after your baby is well, that pattern is what Actually Sleeping fixes, with a plan written for your baby and bootcamp-style coaching before the first night. Night feeds stay in the plan until your pediatrician says otherwise. See also getting back on track after illness, and hear from families in our client video reviews.
When to call the doctor
MedlinePlus says to contact your child’s provider right away if your child:
Develops a high fever
Cannot be calmed
Becomes much less active than normal
The CDC notes rare, more serious reactions to DTaP, such as seizures, nonstop crying for 3 hours or more, or a fever over 105°F. After rotavirus vaccine, the CDC describes a small risk of a type of bowel blockage called intussusception, usually within a week of a dose; ask your pediatrician what signs to watch for. The CDC notes a very remote chance of a severe allergic reaction; seek emergency care right away if your baby has trouble breathing or you suspect one.
And the CDC’s simplest advice applies: if you see something that concerns you, call your child’s doctor.

# My toddler is dropping their nap. What is quiet time and how do I set it up?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/quiet-time-when-toddler-drops-nap/

My toddler is dropping their nap. What is quiet time and how do I set it up?
Quiet time is a daily rest period, often 30 to 60 minutes, when your child stays in their room with books or calm toys and may fall asleep. Most children stop napping between ages 3 and 5: a large review found about a third had stopped by 3 and about 80% by 5. How it is set up, and when, depends on your child’s sleep need and bedtime.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
When toddlers stop napping
A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies of napping in children up to 12 years. Its estimates:
AgeChildren who had stopped napping
Before 2 yearsRare, under 2.5%
About 3 yearsAbout 33%
About 4 yearsAbout 57%
About 5 yearsAbout 80%
Over 5 yearsAbout 94%
The ranges between studies were wide, so treat these as a guide, not a deadline. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 11 to 14 hours of sleep per 24 hours at 1 to 2 years and 10 to 13 hours at 3 to 5 years, including naps. A child who drops the nap needs that sleep at night.
Signs the nap is really ending
Your child regularly lies awake for most of nap time and is still in a good mood by evening.
On nap days, bedtime takes a long time or gets pushed much later.
This has gone on for a few weeks, not a few days.
Before age 3, nap refusal is often a phase: a new skill, a cold, a move, or a schedule that has drifted. Because stopping napping before 2 is rare, a 2-year-old who skips naps for a week usually still needs one. See a 2 year old’s sleep schedule.
The move from nap to quiet time is a common point for toddler sleep to unravel. Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on and plans this transition for your child.
What quiet time is
Quiet time replaces the nap with a predictable rest period at the same time of day. Your child stays in their room or a calm spot, with low-key activities. If they fall asleep, that’s fine. If they don’t, they have still rested, and you have had a break. Screens are not rest, and they make the transition back harder.
Because your child will be awake and alone in the room, it has to be safe: childproof the room, anchor furniture to the wall, and use a gate at the door if your child is young.
Why the transition so often goes wrong
The nap is dropped too early. A toddler on a nap strike is treated as finished, and evenings fall apart.
Bedtime does not move. A child who has lost an hour or two of daytime sleep is put down at the old bedtime, overtired.
Late naps creep in. A 4 p.m. doze in the car pushes bedtime late.
Quiet time becomes a battle. Without a clear, consistent limit, it turns into an hour of coming out.
Getting it right depends on your child’s age, actual sleep need, nap history and how bedtime is going. Generic advice cannot see any of that.

You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins while the new day settles. Naps are coached until they are solid. # How do I protect my toddler’s sleep when a new baby arrives?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-sleep-new-baby-sibling/

How do I protect my toddler’s sleep when a new baby arrives?
If you can, make big sleep changes, such as moving to a bed, well before the baby arrives; otherwise wait until the baby is settled at home, as the AAP advises. Expect some regression, and keep the newborn in their own sleep space. If your toddler’s sleep does not settle, Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn on, so both children can be covered.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Timing big changes
The AAP’s advice on preparing your family for a new baby is to finish toilet training or switching from a crib to a bed before the baby arrives if you can. If that isn’t possible, put it off until after the baby is settled at home.
The same logic applies to moving rooms or dropping a nap. Your toddler should not lose their crib and gain a sibling in the same week. If you need the crib for the baby, a second crib or a bassinet avoids rushing your toddler into a bed. A newborn can sleep in a bassinet in your room for the first months.
Expect some regression
The AAP says to expect your child to regress a little, such as toilet accidents or wanting a bottle again. It advises against telling them to act their age. Instead, give them the attention they need and praise grown-up behavior. The AAP also suggests setting aside special time for your child, such as reading, playing or talking together, or a one-on-one outing.
Sleep can follow the same pattern: more night waking, a harder bedtime, or wanting you to stay. That is a normal response to a big change.
A new baby is a big change, and some disruption is normal. When your toddler’s sleep does not recover, Actually Sleeping can fix it, alongside the newborn’s foundations.
Why it often does not settle on its own
The problem is rarely the regression itself. It is what exhausted parents do to get through it: lying down with the toddler until they fall asleep, bringing them into the big bed, letting bedtime slide while the newborn feeds. Each choice makes sense at the time. A few weeks later, the toddler has new sleep habits, the newborn is waking at night, and two children are taking turns keeping everyone up.
Bedtime also gets harder to run. A newborn often needs feeding right at the toddler’s bedtime, one parent is short of sleep, and the routine changes from night to night depending on who is free.
How Actually Sleeping helps a growing family

You get bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. Hear from families in our 129 client video reviews.
Safe sleep with a toddler and a newborn
The newborn sleeps in their own crib, bassinet or play yard. The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign lists a sibling sharing a baby’s sleep surface as a high-risk situation.
Keep toys out of the baby’s sleep space. Toddlers love to “share” blankets and stuffed animals. Explain that the baby’s bed stays empty, and check it before each sleep.
No bed sharing with the newborn, even when a toddler is in the bed too. The AAP does not support bed sharing under any circumstances.
When the toddler and baby will share a room
The AAP recommends your baby sleep in your room for at least the first 6 months. After that, siblings can share. See a baby and toddler sharing a room.

# Can my baby and toddler share a room, and how do I make it work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-and-toddler-sharing-a-room/

Can my baby and toddler share a room, and how do I make it work?
Yes. Most families wait until after the first 6 months, the minimum the AAP recommends for a baby sleeping in the parents’ room. The baby needs their own crib with only a fitted sheet, and siblings should never share a bed with a baby. Room sharing usually works once neither child depends on a parent to fall back asleep at night.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Safety first
Separate sleep spaces. The NIH Safe to Sleep campaign lists a sibling sharing a baby’s sleep surface as a high-risk situation. Each child has their own bed.
A bare crib. The CPSC’s advice is “Bare is Best”: nothing but a fitted sheet in a crib, bassinet or play yard. For the first year, keep blankets, pillows and stuffed toys out.
Toddler-proof the crib. Toddlers like to share. Teach that the baby’s bed stays empty, and check it before every sleep.
Toddler-proof the room. Small toys, coins and batteries go somewhere your crawling baby can’t reach. Anchor furniture to the wall.
Cords. Keep monitor and lamp cords well away from both beds. The CPSC warns never to place corded cameras within three feet of a crib.
White noise at a low volume, if you use it, with the machine across the room. A 2014 study found some infant sleep machines were loud enough at maximum volume to raise concern about hearing.
Two children in one room is workable. When they keep waking each other, the waking is the fixable part, and Actually Sleeping fixes it with both children in mind.
When to move the baby in
The AAP recommends your baby sleep in your room for at least the first 6 months. After that, the timing is up to you. Many families find it easier once the baby has fewer night feeds, because night feeds in a shared room wake the toddler. Night feeds are your pediatrician’s call, not something to cut to make a room share work.
Why siblings keep each other up
Most children learn to sleep through ordinary noises from a sibling. What wakes a roommate is usually a pattern: a baby who cries at every sleep cycle because they need help to fall back asleep, a parent who comes in and talks or feeds, lights going on, a toddler who climbs out to see what is happening. When one child wakes often, the room share takes the blame. In most families the room is not the problem; the night waking is.
Different bedtimes and nap times add to it. Babies usually need to go to bed earlier than toddlers, and naps rarely line up, so the room is often in use by one child while the other needs it.
Why this needs a plan
Fixing sleep for two children in one room is a logistics problem as much as a sleep one: whose bedtime goes first, where naps happen, what happens when one child is learning to fall asleep alone and the other is trying to sleep. The answers depend on both children’s ages, schedules and habits, and on your home.

# How do I keep my baby or toddler sleeping well when we move house?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/moving-house-and-toddler-sleep/

How do I keep my baby or toddler sleeping well when we move house?
Make the new home safe for sleep first: set up the crib, or a play yard with only its fitted sheet, never an adult bed or sofa, and anchor dressers and TVs to the wall. Keeping the same crib, sleep sack, routine and bedtime makes the new room feel familiar. Some unsettled nights are common; habits that start during the move are what tend to last.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
Make the new room safe
A new home has new hazards, and moving week is when furniture is most likely to be left unsecured. The CPSC reports that from 2000 to 2021, 482 children were killed in tip-over incidents, and 88% of them were under 5. It also estimates an average of 19,400 emergency department visits a year for tip-over injuries.
The CPSC advises:
Anchor TVs and furniture, such as bookcases and dressers, securely to the wall.
Store heavier items on lower shelves or in lower drawers.
Don’t put toys or remotes where children might climb to reach them.
Keep TV and cable cords out of reach.
The AAP adds: use a safety gate at the top of the stairs, and consider one at the bedroom door, so a toddler who gets out of bed can’t wander. Check where the crib sits too: away from windows, blind cords, curtains, lamps and anything your child could pull in. Corded cameras should be at least three feet from the crib, per the CPSC.
Safety comes first in a new home. If sleep does not settle after the move, the habits that started during it are the part Actually Sleeping fixes.
Safe sleep on moving night
If the crib isn’t assembled yet, use a play yard that meets federal requirements, with only its fitted sheet. The CPSC lists cribs, bassinets, play yards and bedside sleepers as products safe for sleep. Not an air mattress, an adult bed, or a sofa, even for one night.
Why a move unsettles sleep
A new room means new sounds, new light, new shadows and new smells. Many toddlers are also unsettled by the packing and the change in routine before the move. More waking, earlier waking or a harder bedtime are common in the first week. The AAP’s advice for a new baby, to make big changes well before or wait until things are settled, makes sense for a move too: switching to a bed, dropping a nap or toilet training in the same month adds to the disruption.
Why it sometimes does not settle
Most of what lasts after a move is not the move. It is what happened to get through it: lying down with your toddler until they fall asleep, bringing them into your bed in the new house, a later bedtime while boxes were unpacked. Each makes sense in a stressful week. A month later, the move is over and the habits are not.
That is the fixable part, and it is what Actually Sleeping does. For babies and toddlers alike, Dr. Sam writes a plan for your child in the new home, with bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins. If you are moving soon, the plan can be timed around the move. Hear from families in our 129 client video reviews.
Moving across time zones or into a shared room
If the move also changes the clock, see sleep and time zones. If siblings will share a room in the new house, see a baby and toddler sharing a room.

# How do I prepare my baby’s sleep for when I go back to work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-when-parent-returns-to-work/

How do I prepare my baby’s sleep for when I go back to work?
Plan around the fixed points of your new day: when you leave, the daycare or caregiver schedule, and when you get home. Your baby will need to fall asleep for more than one person and in a crib, not only on you or while feeding. Night feeds stay your pediatrician’s call. Starting a sleep plan a few weeks before your return gives it time to settle.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
The new day starts from fixed points
Fixed pointWhat it decides
When you leaveWake-up time, allowing for a feed, getting dressed and the trip
Daycare or caregiver scheduleNap times on workdays
When you get homeHow much evening time there is before bedtime
Total sleep needHow late bedtime can be
For sleep need, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours for babies 4 to 12 months and 11 to 14 hours for children 1 to 2 years, including naps. Where your baby sits in that range decides how much room the evening has.
If your baby only falls asleep on you, going back to work is a good reason to fix that now. Actually Sleeping writes a plan around your return date.
Why going back to work is hard on sleep
Someone else puts your baby down. A baby who only falls asleep on you, or while feeding, has nobody to do that at daycare. Naps there get short, and evenings get hard.
Evenings get later. Many parents want to keep their baby up to get more time together. A little later is fine. Much later usually means an overtired baby who falls asleep less easily and wakes earlier.
Mornings get earlier. The wake-up time is set by your commute, not your baby’s body clock.
Feeding changes. Pumping, bottles with a caregiver, or more feeds in the evening and at night.
New germs. The first months of daycare often bring a run of colds, each one unsettling sleep.
A study of more than 10,000 young children found that the more nights a week a bedtime routine happened, the better children slept. Doing the routine yourself is a reliable way to reconnect after work.
Feeding
Changes in feeding are decisions to make with your pediatrician or a lactation consultant. Don’t drop night feeds to fit work unless your pediatrician agrees your baby no longer needs them.
Why timing matters
Starting a plan two to three weeks before your return gives you time to see progress without the pressure of early mornings. Starting in the middle of the first week back is usually harder.

The plan teaches your baby to fall asleep in a crib, for more than one person, and naps are coached until they are solid. Night feeds stay in the plan until your pediatrician says otherwise. # How fast does sleep training work? What 129 families reported
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-fast-does-sleep-training-work-129-family-reviews/

How fast does sleep training work? What 129 families reported
In 129 client video reviews of Actually Sleeping, 115 parents said how many nights it took to see the change they describe. 45 of those 115 (39%) named the first night, 76 (66%) said within three nights, and 102 (89%) within a week. The median was 2 nights.
Reading this at 3 a.m.? Tomorrow night can be different. Actually Sleeping builds a plan for your baby, coaches you hard before night one so you go in confident, and checks in 1:1 every day until they are sleeping through, with a full-refund guarantee. Book a free consultation →
These are our families’ results. Every number below is counted from the 129 public client video reviews of Actually Sleeping, in the parents’ own words. Each family had a sleep plan written for their baby by Dr. Sam, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins until it was working.
The numbers

14 of the 129 reviews did not state a number of nights and are left out of the percentages. A few families described a longer stretch, up to 45 nights; they are included.
By the child’s age at the start
AgeFamilies with a numberMedian nightsWithin 3 nightsWithin 7 nightsUnder 4 months15211 (73%)12 (80%)4–6 months24218 (75%)22 (92%)7–9 months262.517 (65%)24 (92%)10–12 months263.513 (50%)22 (85%)Over 12 months24117 (71%)22 (92%)
89% of the families who gave a number saw the change within the first week, and the median was 2 nights. That is what a plan built for one baby, with someone checking in every day, is designed to produce.
What these numbers are, and what they are not
It is not a study. These are families who hired one coaching service and then chose to record a video review. Families with slower or mixed results are less likely to record one, so the real spread is wider than this table.
Results are self-reported. “Night 1” means the parent said they saw the change on the first night. Parents described different changes: falling asleep without help, fewer wakings, or a full night.
There is no comparison group. The numbers say nothing about how these babies would have slept without coaching, or with a different approach.
Every family had 1:1 support. A custom plan, bootcamp-style coaching before the first night and daily check-ins. Timelines for families working alone may differ.
What published research says
An American Academy of Sleep Medicine task force reviewed 52 treatment studies of behavioral approaches to bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. 94% of the studies reported that the approaches worked, and more than 80% of treated children showed clinically significant improvement that was maintained for three to six months. That review is about behavioral approaches in general, not about any one company.
Why the results come quickly
Most families who come to us have already tried things on their own. What changes is not effort. It is a plan written for their baby’s age, feeds, temperament and current way of falling asleep, and support while they carry it out: bootcamp-style coaching before the first night, a coach reading the sleep log every morning, and naps coached until solid. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. We back it in writing: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If not, you get a full refund.
Where the data comes from
Each number is counted from the public video reviews at actuallysleeping.com/reviews, summarized on our reviews page. No names or identifying details are used here. Counted on November 9, 2026.
